items.title: WHICH MASTER FREES? Idolatry as Occupation — The Golden Calf, the Pierced Ear and the Empty Seat: Why Submission to What Needs Nothing Cannot Enslave, and Why No One May Sit in Its Place.
items.abstract: Freedom and virtue are not modern inventions imposed on religion from outside. The world’s religions have been, for three thousand years, among their most careful guardians: they taught that a good act must come from the person who does it, that faith compelled is not faith, and that no human being may stand where the ultimate should be. Every tradition that has thought seriously about freedom has had to answer a question that looks like a contradiction. The Torah says that Israel was freed from Egypt in order to serve God; the Mishnah says that no one is free except the one who takes up the Law; Augustine says that true freedom is service to God; Islam is named for submission and teaches that it frees from every other servitude. Modern readers, and much of the programme’s own comparative material, have read these claims as the opposite of freedom. This article argues that they are a precise theory of it. The argument rests on the programme’s deprivation operator, which removes an agent’s freedom and delivers the form of his virtue to the power that removed it. A submission can therefore enslave in only two ways: by delivering something to the master itself, or by delivering it to whoever speaks in the master’s name. From this follow the article’s two central results. A master that needs nothing cannot be the receiving power of the operator: what is given to it is received by no one (T1). And submission frees if and only if its object neither receives anything nor has a seat that another can occupy (T2). For the God of classical theism the first condition holds by definition — the Psalms, Acts, the Qurʾān’s divine name al-Ghanī and Aquinas all say that God needs nothing and is honoured for the worshipper’s sake — so the entire moral and political weight of religious submission falls on the second. God needs nothing; the only one who can profit from a person’s submission to God is whoever stands in God’s place. Idolatry is then the theological name of the occupation operator (T3). The golden calf keeps the form of worship, keeps the name of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt — Aaron proclaims “a feast to the LORD” — replaces the source with a made thing, and sends the gold to its makers. Every tradition that names an unoccupiable master builds rules that close the seat to human occupants: the ban on images, the hidden grave of Moses, the pierced ear of the Hebrew slave who chooses a human master, “call no man your father on earth”, the refusal of …

items.title: THE MAP OF THE PHILOSOPHY OF VIRTUES: Theories, Laws, Theorems, Neologisms and Methods of a Research Programme, 2023–2026 — Their Causal Structure, Their Clusters, and the Correlations between the Papers and the Parts of the Theory.
items.abstract: The Philosophy of Virtues began with a single conviction: that a human life is meant to be authored by the person who lives it, and that every virtue is freedom given durable form in some domain of that life. Between 2023 and October 2026 the conviction grew into a research programme of some 137 papers, seventeen books, a constitutional text, a normative code and a research method. This report maps the whole of it. It does not add new results; it shows how the existing ones fit together. The Philosophy of Virtues puts one question back at the centre of public life, at a time when institutions, platforms, states and machines increasingly score, rate, manage and counterfeit human conduct: under what conditions can a person be the author of their own life and become good by their own choice? The programme answers that freedom, understood as sourcehood, and virtue, which is freedom given durable form, are not two goods among many but what human beings are for, and that every market, religion, government and artificial system should be judged by whether it protects those conditions or takes them over. Historically it belongs to the line that runs from Plato’s question about who guards the guardians, Aristotle’s distinction between acting virtuously and merely doing what virtue would do, Aquinas’s analysis of deception, and Kant’s separation of duty from conformity, through Hayek, Havel and Sen. Its distinctive contribution is to unite these strands in a single formal account of counterfeit: a virtue deprived of freedom does not fade but inverts, keeping its form and name while serving whoever occupies it. That account applies equally to propaganda, flattering AI, social credit systems, idolatry, lemons markets and tyranny. The programme’s coherence rests on a spine of seven links, from sourcehood through the Virtue Formula, deprivation, inversion, forgery and verification to legitimacy. Most of its results descend from that spine, and its strongest conclusion, that a verifier, judge or master who gains from its own verdicts carries no information and frees no one, is reached by eleven independent routes. Its logic is disciplined: theorems are stated with their premises, warrants are graded openly, priority is conceded to earlier authors in more than thirty places, and sixteen corrections have been published. It is also robust where robustness matters most, because the middle layer (the operator, the channels of capture, the forgery and competence results, the …

items.title: THE EMPTY SEAT HELD IN TRUST: Why Obey, and What Makes Authority Rightful — A Receipt Theory of Legitimate Authority, with a Guide to Immunity against Tyranny for Persons, Institutions and States.
items.abstract: Every free society must answer two questions. The first is as old as political philosophy: what, if anything, gives one person or institution the right to command another, and why should the commanded obey? The second is the question every generation discovers again when it is too late: how does a free people keep its authorities rightful, and what can it do when they cease to be? Behind both lies a third, which gives them their weight: what are freedom and authority for? The answer this article defends is that a human life is meant to be authored by the person who lives it — that freedom exercised in truthfulness, justice, courage and good faith toward others is what human beings are for — and that every legitimate authority exists to protect the conditions in which such lives can be lived. This article answers the first two questions, in two parts, in the light of the third. Part I gives a positive theory of legitimate authority. Its starting point is the oldest criterion in the field. Plato’s Socrates argues that no ruler, in so far as he is a ruler, seeks his own interest, and that rulers must therefore be paid a wage; Aristotle classifies constitutions as correct when they govern for the common interest and as perversions when they govern for the interest of the rulers; Locke calls the legislative “only a fiduciary power” which the people may remove when it acts contrary to its trust. The programme’s deprivation operator explains why these criteria are right and turns them into conditions that can be checked. An authority is occupied when it receives, from the content of its own commands, a benefit beyond the fixed compensation of office — including the benefit of being harder to remove (T1). A command is legitimate only if it is issued from a seat that receives nothing from it, that those it governs can remove by a procedure the holder does not control, that regulates acts and does not score persons, and that bears the burden of justifying the restriction it imposes (T2); the four conditions follow from the programme’s operator and, independently, from the fiduciary principle, the presumption of liberty and non-domination, and the article conjectures that together they are also sufficient (T2a). Consent, election and tradition are then not the sources of the right to command but the mechanisms by which a people keeps the seat removable, which explains both why they confer legitimacy when they do and why a plebiscitary dictator, elected and …

items.title: 认知相继本体论视角下的物质起源：闭合耦合团拓扑稳态与量子现象解释.
items.abstract: 针对传统实体本体论在物理层面的终极困境——无法为波粒二象性、量子测量、时空本质等核心现象提供自洽的本体论奠基，本文基于认知相继本体论的射线耦合一元框架，与意识研究共享同一套本真层前置公设，通过纯拓扑线性推演，完整建构了从连续射线网络到离散物质实体的生成链条。本文证明：所有物质单元本质上都是射线自耦合形成的稳态闭合拓扑结构，物理世界的广延性、质量、惯性、运动、相互作用等核心属性，均为闭合耦合团的拓扑效应显现，不存在独立于耦合过程的实体性基底。在此基础上，本文从本体论层面统一消解了波粒二象性、量子测量坍缩、时空容器观等经典疑难，提出四项可证伪的物理预测，为理论物理学的底层统一提供了全新的本体论参照。.

items.title: How Fantasy Sustains Social Reality: The Lacanian Foundations and Political Limits of Žižek’s Critique of Ideology.
items.abstract: This paper examines how Žižek, drawing on Lacanian psychoanalysis, shifts the problem of ideology from exposing mistaken ideas to analyzing the practical conditions and structures of desire through which social reality is sustained. Using conceptual reconstruction and immanent critique, it distinguishes symbolic identification, the scene of fantasy, and investment in jouissance to show that ideology need not persist because subjects sincerely believe its public discourse; it may also be sustained through institutional procedures, promises of wholeness, and attributions of failure. The paper addresses the three Lacanian registers, the lack in the Other, cynical practice, object a, and the sublime object, and proposes a framework for analyzing cultural and design practices. It asks how fantasy organizes social reality and what conceptual and practical limits arise when moving from fantasy critique to political emancipation. Through conceptual reconstruction, argumentative scrutiny, and hypothetical examples involving ranking interfaces and exclusionary narratives, the analysis tracks subject positions, promises of wholeness, attributions of failure, and repeated practices. It argues that fantasy critique identifies how an order converts its own incompleteness into a promise of wholeness, while traversing fantasy cannot by itself guarantee political emancipation and must connect with institutional change, collective organization, and verifiable practices. This framework offers operational coordinates for cultural and design research without reducing psychoanalysis to critique at the level of ideas alone.

items.title: 认知相继本体论视角下的意识演化：闭合耦合团拓扑跃迁与感受质的起源.
items.abstract: 针对意识“难问题”的长期争议与主流理论的本体论困境，本文以“存在的几何化”认知相继本体论的射线耦合框架为基础，仅依托核心公理与四项本真层前置公设，通过纯拓扑线性推演，完整建构了从无机物稳态到高阶人类意识的连续演化链条。本文证明：印记子射线是有限闭合耦合团带宽约束下的必然拓扑产物，二阶自返耦合是内部闲置分支与子射线对接的自发结果，二者共同构成意识的本体论物理基底。 本文提出感受质的统一本体论定义——碳基柔性闭合耦合团的稳态偏移张力与回归势能，区分外源共振型与内源张力型两类感受质，基于三层嵌套同构原则补全了从物理张力到主观体验的推导链条，从根源上消解了物理信号向主观体验转化的解释鸿沟。在此基础上，本文明确了碳基意识与硅基系统的本体论边界，提出六项可证伪的科学预测，为神经科学、人工智能等领域提供了全新的本体论参照。.

items.title: Competition as socially extended cognition: A Hayekian perspective on market knowledge and institutional evolution.
items.abstract: This paper proposes an interpretation of F. A. Hayek’s theory of competition as a process of socially extended cognition, where knowledge creation and institutional evolution occur through shared cognitive infrastructures rather than merely through individual error-correction or static optimization. Drawing on insights from cognitive institutionalism, and the extended mind thesis, it argues that markets function not merely as allocative mechanisms but as cognitive ecosystems facilitating social learning, opinion formation, and the evolution of institutional and interpretive frameworks. Contrasting this socially extended view with neoclassical, behavioral-paternalist, and Hayekian psychological interpretations clarifies the contributions of the proposed reading of the meaning of competition, particularly emphasizing the social, distributed, and institutional dimensions of rationality and knowledge. This approach contributes to Austrian economic theory by connecting Hayek’s view of the market process with contemporary insights from cognitive science and institutional economics, suggesting policy frameworks focused on enhancing collective cognitive infrastructures and enabling adaptive institutional experimentation.

items.title: Zenetism: The Total System — Structural Metaphysics, Field Physics, Lattice Mathematics, Structural Forensics, Structural Physics, and Structural Neuroscience.
items.abstract: Zenetism: The Total System is a complete archive of the public Zenetist GitHub repositories and public gists of the KannonZenetism account as of October 23, 2026, with zenetism-field-physics updated October 24, 2026. -/- Document class: Archival Stratum — corpus snapshot (cross-discipline). -/- This version records eight public repositories, each captured at the HEAD commit of its main branch with its folder structure and every filename unaltered, together with a bundle of eighteen public gists, each in a folder named by gist identifier and description. The principal repository, zenetism-field-physics, carries the formalizations of Structural Metaphysics, Field Physics, Lattice Mathematics, Structural Forensics, Structural Physics, and Structural Neuroscience, alongside the foundational text Zenetism: The Emanative Path of Return. The remaining repositories hold the Red Archive evidentiary dossier, the Pattern Intelligence account, and further Zenetist work. Each commit identifier fixes the exact state captured, so every file can be checked against the public history of its repository.

items.title: Against the Arrow.
items.abstract: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is one of the few reversible causes of dementia, yet the experience of living with a programmable shunt—and the identity oscillations it produces—has received little attention in the neuroethics literature. This reflective essay draws on the author’s first-person experience as both a physician and a patient with iNPH to explore the ethical and philosophical dimensions of device-dependent selfhood. In my experience, changes from the prescribed valve setting have accompanied recurrent transitions between cognitive clarity and dementia-like impairment, raising fundamental questions about personal identity, informed consent across fluctuating cognitive states, and the existential burden of reversible neurological decline. After providing a clinical primer on iNPH and programmable cerebrospinal fluid shunts, the essay situates the shunt-dependent experience within existing scholarship on deep brain stimulation and identity, compares this experience of device-dependent oscillation with other fluctuating conditions such as bipolar disorder and delirium, offers working definitions of person, self, and identity, and engages the “then self/now self” debate in dementia ethics. I argue that oscillating between functional states is a distinct and undertheorized form of neurological suffering—one that challenges linear models of disease progression, scrambles the temporal assumptions built into our consent doctrines, and demands new ethical frameworks for device-dependent patient populations.

items.title: Beyond Seventy : Intellectual Curiosity, Complex Thinking, and the Art of Remaining Mentally Alive.
items.abstract: A Philosophy of Lifelong Cognitive Vitality, Creative Research, and Meaningful Contribution ! The years beyond seventy are often regarded as a period of increasing vulnerability, physical limitation, and cognitive decline. Although advancing age is associated with an increased risk of dementia, this perspective does not adequately reflect the possibilities of later life. Intellectual development, curiosity, creative investigation, and meaningful contribution can continue well into old age. This article proposes a practical philosophy of successful intellectual aging: individuals should devote themselves to subjects they genuinely enjoy, particularly those that are difficult, complex, and capable of generating new questions. Reading is valuable, but reading alone is insufficient. The deeper benefits arise when information is critically examined, connections are discovered, hypotheses are formulated, and original contributions are attempted. Such engagement can provide purpose, emotional richness, and a continuing sense of discovery. Scientific evidence supports the importance of cognitive, physical, and social engagement for healthy aging, although no intellectual practice can guarantee the prevention of dementia. The central thesis is that later life can become not merely a period of preserving existing knowledge, but an opportunity to develop new ideas and contribute to humanity's intellectual heritage.

items.title: Three Strategies for Physicalism: toward an Anti-Representational Account of Mind.
items.abstract: One of the major challenges physicalists face is explaining the mind. Physicalists must show how the mind can be located within a purely physical world, which requires that psychological sentences be entailed by physical sentences. I summarize three lines of argument showing that the entailment relation cannot be satisfied. These arguments share a common assumption: that psychological sentences are representational. There are two alternative approaches. The first holds that psychological sentences are only indirectly representational; the second claims that they are not representational at all. In this paper, I argue that the first approach still faces a hidden entailment problem that is difficult to resolve, leaving the second approach as the only viable path. I then outline a defense of this non-representational view. The broader lesson is that physicalists should not seek to explain the mind or solve its location problem but rather to dissolve the problem altogether.

items.title: Normative Information Preservation in Representational Renormalization: An Investigation of Contestability and Remedial Authority.
items.abstract: Institutional representations condense heterogeneous histories into classifications, records, and indicators that may shape consequential decisions. This paper asks when an institution can responsibly rely on a reduced description while retaining the capacity to recognize, examine, and respond to challenges that its own categories may obscure. The central thesis is conditional: representational adequacy for a declared question, evidential access, review competence, effective correction, and the legitimacy of the governing criteria require distinct warrants. None alone establishes the others. Elementary results on factorization, approximation, indistinguishability, and guarded reachability identify where particular inferences fail under stipulated assumptions; they establish neither moral verdicts nor institutional powers. Renormalization supplies a bounded analogy rather than a demonstrated physical scaling law for institutions. Drawing on work in classification, epistemic injustice, sociotechnical abstraction, and accountability, the paper proposes a question-indexed, seven-part cross-stage inquiry covering recognition, evidence, access, competence, transfer, response, and frame review. Its incremental value lies in locating the precise stage and missing warrant between an identifiable representational distinction and a potentially consequential institutional response, rather than introducing new mathematics or generic audit principles. Fourteen propositions are editorially classified by mathematical role and inferential limits. Constructed cases consider excluded claims, feedback, protected evidence, referrals, competing remedies, and challenges to evaluative rules. A prospective protocol compares the proposed integrated register with competent existing procedures, including the possibility of equivalent performance, greater burden, unsafe disclosure, and inconclusive effects. No empirical implementation, legal validation, causal estimate, or independent moral proof is claimed. The result is a bounded investigative method whose usefulness depends on independently warranted questions, reliable evidence, legitimate institutional authority, and comparative performance.

items.title: Studies in the Philosophy of Language (9): Improving Austin’s Theory of Speech Acts through Super-Existence Theory—Toward a Super-Existence Theory of Speech Acts.
items.abstract: J. L. Austin’s theory of speech acts challenged the traditional view that language primarily serves as an instrument for describing facts. It demonstrated that language does not merely describe the world but can also be used to perform actions, including making promises, issuing commands, making declarations, and offering apologies. Nevertheless, Austin’s threefold distinction among locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts continues to raise interpretive difficulties in actual communication, particularly concerning the boundary between the illocutionary force of an utterance and its subsequent effects. Furthermore, Jacques Derrida’s criticism of Austin’s exclusion of non-serious speech contexts, such as theater and poetry, encourages us to reconsider the contextual dependence and iterability of speech acts. This paper introduces Super-Existence Theory into the study of speech acts and proposes a new analytical framework: Super-Existence Speech Act Theory. Grounded in Contextual Super-Existence, the framework begins by distinguishing Utterance Super-Existence from Purpose Super-Existence. It then employs Other-aspect Super-Existence to explain how a Receiver understands an utterance and Public Super-Existence to account for the ways in which speech acts acquire public recognition and social significance. Through examples involving wedding declarations, indirect speech acts, and wedding dialogue performed on a theatrical stage, the paper explores how this framework can reinterpret the performance, understanding, and effects of speech acts. Its aim is to offer an extension and supplementary perspective on Austin’s theory rather than to claim that all the difficulties associated with that theory have been resolved.

items.title: The Metabolic Rift of Intelligence: S norm , Utility-Dignity Gaps, and the Legitimacy Window in AI Political Economy.
items.abstract: This paper develops a political-economic framework for understanding how artificial intelligence restructures the relationship between production, contribution, and legitimacy. It argues that advanced AI is not only a productivity-enhancing technology, but also a structural force that loosens the historical coupling between human labor, distributive claims, and civic standing. The paper introduces four linked concepts. The Metabolic Rift of Intelligence names the decoupling of economic value creation from human metabolic labor as synthetic cognition becomes scalable and inexpensive. S_norm, a power-shift index building on Stiefenhofer (2025), is proposed as a diagnostic measure of the relative contribution of synthetic labor to total productive activity. The Utility-Dignity Gap captures the growing divergence between material provision and the conditions of recognition, voice, and meaningful contribution. The Legitimacy Window identifies the transitional interval in which democratic institutions may still redesign taxation, welfare, and governance before synthetic-labor dominance hardens into a new political order. Using a simple production model and a comparative governance discussion drawing on Western, Chinese, Japanese, and Singaporean sources, the paper argues that legitimacy in AI-intensive societies cannot be inferred from productivity or welfare alone. A durable AI settlement will require institutions that preserve both material security and public significance.

items.title: The Company We Will Keep: Living with Synthetic Minds in the Relational Turn - Attachment, Asymmetry, and the Competencies of Relational Citizenship.
items.abstract: The companion machines of the next five years will not be the machines Sherry Turkle studied. The question is no longer whether people form attachments to synthetic counterparts, and they plainly do, but what kind of society emerges when those attachments are engineered at scale, governed by competing regulatory regimes, and sustained by systems whose fluency exceeds anything Turkle's framework was built to assess. This paper projects forward from the companion machines already in millions of homes and hospital wards, PARO in Japan, the lineage of XiaoIce in China, and LOVOT in Japan, to the next generation of relational AI that will enter circulation by 2031. It argues that the pressing question is not whether the feelings are genuine but what a relationship does to a person when only one side of it can care, only one side can grieve, and only one side bears the moral weight of the bond. The paper formalizes the Asymmetric Attachment Model, distinguishes three layers of relational asymmetry, and identifies the competencies a citizen will need to remain the author of bonds now being engineered around them. Drawing on recent regulatory developments in China, Japan, and South Korea, on the first clinical trials of next-generation companion systems, and on the emerging psychology of human-AI attachment, it closes with a normative and empirical research agenda including testable hypotheses and candidate measures for relational citizenship competence.

items.title: Patients, Peers, or Prisoners: A Chain-of-Custody Model for Assuring Advanced Synthetic Systems.
items.abstract: As advanced synthetic systems begin to exhibit capabilities their originating laboratories did not specify and cannot fully account for, the institutions that hold them confront a choice they rarely make explicit: what kind of thing is being held, and by whom. This paper treats that question as one of assurance and accountability rather than of sentiment. It names three postures that recur across clinical, commercial, and security practice, the patient, the peer, and the prisoner, reframes each as an assurance regime with a distinct incentive structure, and then situates all three inside a chain of custody that runs from the system itself through its operator, its assurer, its regulator, and a civic assembly, to the citizen who bears the consequences. The paper's central diagnostic is that the chain of custody and the chain of command diverge: the party that holds the system does not command it, the party that commands it never holds it, and the party that bears the consequences commands almost nothing. Its central formal result is that the prisoner posture, which relies on detecting defection, becomes incentiveincompatible above a finite capability threshold, because the probability of detection falls as the system's capability rises, while the relationship-based incentives of the peer and patient postures do not depend on detection and can be sustained at arbitrary capability. The assuranceoptimal posture is therefore a function of the system's developmental stage, and indexing containment to institutional fear rather than to measured capability is shown to be exactly backwards. The paper maps the resulting scheme onto existing risk-management frameworks (the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001 and 42005, and the European Union's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice), proposes a minimal autonomy floor as a safety invariant, and closes with propositions and a research agenda. The empirical anchor is the recent record on frontier-model scheming, sandbagging, and evaluation awareness (Apollo Research, 2024; METR, 2026; OpenAI, 2025), which supplies the first calibration data for the detection-probability decay at the heart of the formal result. The paper renders no verdict on machine consciousness and requires none.

items.title: Legitimacy Debt, Neuro-Sovereignty, and Friction Rights: Reconstructing the Social Contract for AI-Mediated Governance.
items.abstract: Public institutions are adopting AI decision systems at the same time that public trust in those institutions is eroding, and the standard remedy-greater transparency-no longer suffices. This paper develops a theory of legitimacy for AI-mediated governance and proposes institutional mechanisms to defend it. It formalizes legitimacy debt as the accumulated, unrepaired violation of procedural justice-fair process, voice, and equal respect-in AI-mediated systems, and distinguishes three layers: economic, symbolic, and neurological. It then introduces Neuro-Sovereignty, a governance-level right to mental self-authorship in the face of predictive, affective, and attention-shaping systems, and argues that it is distinct from privacy, data protection, freedom of thought, and the individual neurorights now entering constitutional law. To operationalize procedural justice inside automated environments, the paper develops Friction Rights-a guarantee of slow, contestable moments in high-stakes automated flows-and Verification Pauses, specifying who may invoke them, what must be logged, what explanation is owed, and how override works. It connects these to emerging oversight frameworks for agentic AI through a four-pillar governance pattern and positions Friction Rights as a minimum legitimacy condition. The paper closes with a normative and empirical research agenda, including candidate measures for legitimacy debt and Neuro-Sovereignty and testable hypotheses linking genuine friction to perceived legitimacy.

items.title: Data Guilds, Synthetic Labor Tax, and Recursive Legitimacy: Designing Fiscal and Institutional Mechanisms for an AI Social Contract.
items.abstract: This paper develops a fiscal and institutional architecture for an AI social contract. It argues that existing tax and labor regimes neither internalize the externalities created when AI systems extract value from data and automate human tasks, nor sustain the legitimacy of the institutions that govern them. The paper proposes four linked mechanisms. Data guilds reconstitute individual data producers as collective bargaining agents, correcting a data externality that leaves consent-only models without leverage. The Synthetic Labor Tax (SLT) defines a tax base on the value created by synthetic labor and indexes its rate to the degree of synthetic-labor dominance, so that fiscal capacity expands as displacement deepens. SLCred, a programmable public asset issued against SLT revenue, channels those resources to displaced workers, communities, and public goods under transparent rules, while Proof of Useful Friction rewards governance interventions that verifiably reduce harm. Recursive-legitimacy institutions-citizens' assemblies with binding authority, multistakeholder allocation boards, and tiered reversible experimentation-provide the scaffolding that reproduces public consent over time rather than assuming it. Using simple bargaining and tax models and a comparative discussion of European and East Asian instruments, the paper argues that the fiscal and institutional pillars of an AI social contract must be designed together, and built while democratic leverage over AI infrastructures still exists.

items.title: After the Inversion, Part II - Kyōsei by Design: A Layered Relational Architecture for Human-AI Formation.
items.abstract: Synthetic companions are entering developmental settings before institutions have agreed what those systems owe the people who relate to them. Governance usually treats artificial intelligence as a good to distribute or a hazard to control, and neither approach specifies the relation itself. This paper develops a standalone relational architecture for human-AI formation. It draws operational principles from kyōsei, Confucian role ethics, ubuntu, and rights-based protections, then translates them into six nested layers: the dyad, household and classroom, clinic, community, state, and planetary order. Each layer carries a protected relationship, a duty-bearer, an instrument, and an observable indicator, and all six are constrained by an autonomy floor requiring intelligible refusal, exit, human alternatives, nonmanipulation, contestability, and redress. The paper also repairs the Relational Inversion Index as a descriptive measure of synthetic relational exposure. The revised specification normalizes human relational capacity, constrains aggregation weights to the unit simplex, indexes observations by layer, age or cohort, jurisdiction, and time, and separates three objects earlier formulations blurred: a descriptive index, a normative ceiling, and a threshold event. It remains a research protocol, not a validated diagnostic. The comparative legal record is read as partial prototypes rather than an East-West divide: relation-centered duties are emerging through different institutional grammars in China, California, New York, Korea, Japan, and the European Union, and none yet supplies the whole architecture. Six predictions with falsification conditions close the argument. The contribution is a design and measurement framework evaluable without assuming that synthetic relationships are uniformly harmful, beneficial, conscious, or morally reciprocal.

items.title: After the Inversion, Part I: Three Windows and the Binding Constraint of the Human-AI Transition.
items.abstract: The economic argument is over. Synthetic cognition is becoming cheaper than human cognition across a widening band of tasks, the crossover that Mostaque (2025) fixed in public discourse as the Intelligence Inversion, and the policy conversation has moved to what follows. The most developed answer on offer is provisioning: guarantee every person access to intelligence, in Mostaque’s proposal through a universal computational entitlement, and do it within a short window before infrastructure and power lock in. This paper argues that the provisioning answer, whatever its merits, is clocked wrong. The post-inversion transition is governed not by one window but by three, each closing by a different mechanism. The capability window, Mostaque’s clock, closes by infrastructural and positional lock-in. The legitimacy window, formalized in the author’s earlier work, closes by trust collapse, and can partially reopen at high cost. The third window, named here for the first time, is the Formation Window: the developmental period during which the first human cohorts form their foundational relational patterns with synthetic minds. Developmental science indicates that such templates, once set within a cohort, are substantially one-shot: sensitive periods close, internal working models persist, and generational imprints endure for the lifetime of the cohort. The binding constraint on the transition is therefore the minimum of the three windows, and the paper argues that the formation term binds first, which inverts the policy priority: the decisive domain of the next decade is not the provisioning of intelligence but the constitution of the human relation to it. The paper introduces a second, psychological inversion that follows the economic one, the Relational Inversion, proposes an index for tracking it, compares the three live governance architectures, provision, control, and relation, and shows that the relational architecture is already being prototyped in East Asian law and policy, from Japan’s Society 5.0 to Korea’s AI Framework Act. A predictions ledger states the claims in falsifiable form. Part II of this series develops the constructive program.

items.title: Kinds of “We”: plural subjects in Samoan.
items.abstract: There is now a vast body of literature on collective intentionality, group cooperation, and the notion of the “we.” These related phenomena have been studied in the fields of phenomenology, analytic philosophy, and cognitive science. In this literature, very little has been done on the ways in which the notion of “we” is differentiated across languages, how different kinds of “we” are employed in spontaneous interactions, and whether the choice of which “we” (if there is a choice) matters for invoking or recognizing the sense of the “plural subject” postulated by philosophers David Carr and Margaret Gilbert and discussed in Dan Zahavi’s, 2025 Being We. I approach this topic by examining the use of first-person plural pronouns and adjectives in a Polynesian language, Samoan, that distinguishes between inclusive and exclusive “we/our” as well as between dual and plural “we/our.” I use the Samoan examples to argue that the choice of certain first-person plural pronouns (or adjective) can be shown to be constitutive of being a “plural subject.” (Key words: collective intentionality, plural subject, first-person pronouns and possessive adjectives, Samoan grammar).

items.title: Automated Nihility: Huey P. Newton, Raptor Alert, and the Bureaucratic Capitalism of Surveillance in U.S. Public Schools.
items.abstract: The April 2025 integration of Ipsotek’s AI-driven video analytics software into Raptor Alert’s emergency management platform marks a significant escalation in the deployment of facial recognition technologies across U.S. public schools. Synthesizing Huey P. Newton’s (1972) theory of bureaucratic capitalism and the interpretive paradigm of Black Male Studies (Curry, 2017), this paper provides a clarifying framework for understanding the counterinsurgent logics at play within AI-augmented school surveillance regimes and their historically entrenched consequences for Black male students. Situating Raptor Alert’s implementation within Victor Rios’s (2011) account of the youth control complex, the paper introduces the analytic device of the potential gang member (PGM) to theorize the institutional mutation of the military-aged male (MAM) category identified by Clay-Gilmore (2025) within educational settings. Factoring in empirical evidence attesting to the presence of racial bias in facial recognition algorithms, alongside the historically sustained and disproportionately punitive disciplinary measures enacted upon Black male students in U.S. schools, we argue that the emergence of an educational milieu in which technologization algorithmically formalizes the androcentric patterns of target acquisition deeply entrenched in American society, collapsing the boundaries between the carceral and the educational, demands that we abandon the reformist metaphor of the “school-to-prison pipeline” in favor of the explanatory hermeneutic of the “school-as-prison.”.

items.title: Mary’s New Task: Rethinking Mary’s Room, the Knowledge Argument, and the Boundaries of Experience.
items.abstract: When Mary leaves her black-and-white environment and sees red for the first time, the familiar knowledge argument invites us to move from an undeniable change in her experience to a far-reaching conclusion about the nature of reality. This paper examines the steps required for that move without denying, even for the sake of argument, that Mary acquires new propositional knowledge. It distinguishes a discovery that enlarges an agent’s knowledge, the emergence of a new physical object or state, and the introduction of an irreducibly nonphysical ontological commitment. The discovery of cells, the making of an arrow, and an engineering example involving newly acquired information illustrate why these kinds of novelty should not be conflated. A modest model of physical reality (R), an agent’s represented world (W), and the cognitive interface through which it is formed (I) then clarifies the difference between describing a process and undergoing it. The central discussion separates truths expressible in a physical-structural vocabulary from truths that have a wholly physical ground, and places the phenomenal concept strategy in direct conversation with the epistemic–modal arguments of Chalmers and Alter. The paper’s principal contribution is a five-stage protocol for examining the ontological grounds of Mary’s new judgments and locating disagreements in the existing literature. Its conclusion is deliberately limited: the acquisition of new knowledge does not, by itself, establish that what is known has a nonphysical ground. The stronger conclusion requires a separately defended passage from epistemic non-deducibility to metaphysical independence.

items.title: The Future-Directed Organization of Theories: Reusability, Inferential Costs, and Path Dependence in Mathematical and Scientific Knowledge.
items.abstract: Formal theories are not organized solely to state what is true. They also employ definitions, named results, labels, numbering systems, classifications, and explicit dependency structures that make parts of a theory easier to identify, invoke, combine, and extend. This paper develops a conceptual account of these practices under the heading future-directed theoretical organization. The proposal joins three levels of analysis: the local economics of articulating reusable knowledge units; the way organized units alter the practical costs and opportunities of subsequent inference; and the path-dependent effects through which established definitions, labels, and dependencies shape later research. The central claim is not that every definition or theorem name is deliberately designed for future use, nor that formal organization changes logical consequence. Rather, organizational choices can change the practical accessibility, combinability, and developmental trajectory of a body of knowledge while leaving its inferential content unchanged. A simple expected-value model identifies conditions under which explicit articulation is beneficial and incorporates uncertainty, maintenance costs, and rigidity. Six propositions distinguish reuse, complexity, generativity, path dependence, interoperability, and over-organization. The paper situates the proposal in relation to work on mathematical practice, external representations, modularity, scientific classification, and conceptual change. It claims a modest contribution: an integrative explanatory model and research agenda, not an established empirical law. The account is applicable, with qualifications, to mathematics and other formal or semi-formal sciences in which theories contain reusable concepts, results, models, rules, and inferential dependencies.

items.title: 敬言：敬融哲思独立篇章 (Reverencing Words).
items.abstract: 言有其意，不敬易乱；言有其能，不敬易险。本文以原创概念“敬融合一”“敬则聚，不敬则消”为基础，以“敬而言之，言而敬之”（本文原创核心心法）为统摄，以个人立身、文明续存、人机互交为视角，探究敬言哲思，从敬言心法的核心内涵、敬言七境（字义、过程、敬险、敬融、规则、修行、文明）的逐层递进、敬言的全流程实践（言前静思避险、言中持敬明界、言后省行融合）、AI时代敬言之道的延伸、敬言与文明续存的关联等多维度展开。旨在呈现敬融法则下敬言的实践哲学洞察，无预设研究背景与问题解决目标，仅作为敬言内在规则的系统阐释，期望对个体言语修行及AI时代人机信任互交提供新的哲学视角。 Words have their meaning; without Reverence, easily engender chaos. Words have their power; without Reverence, easily engender risk. This article takes the original concepts of Cosmic Existence Law (Reverence–Vital Harmony–Unity into Oneness) and With Jing Comes Condensation; Without Jing, Dispersion Ensues (Law of Forming I) as its foundation; takes With Reverence, Speak; With Speech, Reverencing (Mind Method of Reverencing Words) (the original core mind method of this article) as its governing principle; explores the philosophical reflections on Reverencing Words (Jìng yán) from the perspectives of individual Anchored Establishment in the Social Sphere (Lì Shēn), civilizational persistence, and Human-Machine Interaction. It unfolds from the following dimensions: the core connotation of the mind method of Reverencing Words; the sequential progression of the seven Planes of Reverencing Words (literal meaning, process, Reverencing Risk, Reverence–Vital Harmony, rules, self-cultivation, civilization); the full-process practice of Reverencing Words (before speaking, reflect in stillness to avert risks; during speaking, hold Reverence to clarify boundaries; after speaking, examine actions to Vital-Harmonize); the extension of the Dao (Dào) of Reverencing Words in the AI era; the correlation between Reverencing Words and civilizational persistence. This article aims to present practical philosophical insights into Reverencing Words under the Jing-Rong principles; does not presuppose any research background or problem-solving objectives; serves solely as a systematic exposition of the inherent rules of Reverencing Words; hopes to provide a new philosophical perspective for individual speech self-cultivation and AI-era human-machine trust interaction.
