items.abstract: This paper develops a value-theoretic and decision-theoretic account of practical reason, drawing on Nietzsche's moral psychology, Kierkegaard's existentialism, and the Quinean holism developed in companion papers. I argue that reasons are internal or external only relative to a horizon—a temporal projection of self-understanding. I distinguish between the proximal horizon (immediate satisfaction), the distal horizon (aspirational identity), and the middle horizon (negotiation between them). This framework allows for a relativistic conception of internality and externality that supports robust normative evaluation without appealing to external moral standards. The central criterion is integration—the unification of desires, beliefs, and dispositions over time. But the framework also acknowledges its own limits. When deliberation runs out—when both Φ and Ψ connect to S equally well—the agent must leap. The instant of decision is "madness"—not because it is irrational, but because it is trans-rational. Such moments reveal a form of existential externality that Williams cannot accommodate. Drawing on the coin flip, the phenomenon of reluctance, the insincere promise, and Meursault as a limit-case, I argue that reasons are preferential and that the supremum of decision is the point at which the objective and subjective collide—a regulative ideal that structures the topology of practical reason.

items.title: Way Two’s Understanding of Post-Truth—Fuller.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 39-52.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter is on Fuller’s way two’s understanding of the nature of post-truth. Fuller is against the way one’s understanding, which is an epistemic crisis. Fuller posits that the post-truth condition started with Plato, as philosophers and guardians, who have access to the truth, set the conditions for truth and falsity for the public with the double truth doctrine, which is one set of truths for philosophers and guardians and another set of truths for the public. There is an exploration of the rhetoric of truthers and post-truthers with a discussion of Fuller’s notion of truth. This chapter examines Fuller’s way two’s understanding, which is how Pareto’s Lions, who are the establishment and with power, and Pareto’s Foxes, who are not in the establishment and without power, struggle with each other on the legitimation of the cognitive authority of knowledge claims. There is a discussion of Fuller’s notion of modal power, which is to control the necessary and possible conditions of the legitimation of knowledge claims. Fake news, which is famous in the post-truth debate, is explicated followed by how analytic epistemology’s responses to post-truth fail. Fuller’s response to charges of relativism is explicated.

items.title: Ways of Understanding Post-Truth, Knowledge, and Power.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 15-37.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter examines four ways of understanding the nature of post-truth and knowledge as a power game. Way one’s understanding is on an epistemic crisis; way two’s understanding is on the legitimation crisis of the cognitive authority of scientific knowledge; way three’s understanding is on the influence of the Internet and social media and the legitimation crisis of the authority of the mass media; and way four’s understanding is on the impact of AI on the changing boundaries of the knower in terms of the knower’s agency, transhumanism and posthumanism. Fuller’s criticisms of way one’s understanding with arguments on realism and anti-realism debate, which Fuller considers to be central to the post-truth debate, are discussed. There is a comparison of Fuller’s notion of knowledge as a power game to Popper’s notion of knowledge as a game with a discussion of epistemic justice. Fuller’s notion of responsibility, which is similar to Protestant Science’s notion of responsibility, is contrasted to Popper’s notion of responsibility with an explication on Fuller’s notion of science customization.

items.title: The University and Humboldt 2.0.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 89-100.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter addresses the crisis of legitimation facing the university’s cognitive authority in knowledge production. It proposes Fuller’s solution, which advocates for a return to the Humboldtian university model. This model aims to revitalize the university by integrating research and teaching. The chapter outlines six conditions necessary for the university’s revitalization. It further elucidates the Humboldtian university as a revolutionary constitution that establishes a social contract transcending researchers to foster higher learning. Additionally, the chapter explores the Humboldtian university as a vehicle of epistemic justice, where research and teaching are harmoniously integrated within the classroom setting.

items.title: Science and Technology Studies.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 53-62.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter examines the relationship between post-truth and science and technology studies (STS). STS is considered to have contributed to the emergence of way two, which has led to a legitimation crisis of the cognitive authority of science. In the Science Wars, Latour’s work in STS challenged the objectivity of scientific knowledge production, arguing that facts are not objective. Consequently, Latour is considered a post-truth philosopher. Fuller’s criticism of STS is that it rejects the use of the symmetry principle in studying how the established Lions legitimize their knowledge claims and how anti-establishment Foxes provide alternative knowledge claims. Fuller defends way two’s understanding of post-truth by recommending that the symmetry principle be applied to the knowledge claims of ID theorists, conspiracy theorists and the ‘basket of deplorables’ to examine how they attempt to delegitimize the authority of the established Lions’ knowledge claims. Fuller also discusses criticisms of Baker and Oreskes, who defend STS against Fuller’s notion of science as a game by arguing for veritism. Finally, Fuller explains how Gestalt shifts enable knowers to change their frame of reference.

items.title: Knowledge as a Public Good and the University.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 75-88.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter examines how Fuller’s way two understanding of the nature of post-truth also applies as a legitimation crisis of the cognitive authority of the university. This authority has been challenged by the Internet and neoliberalism, which have undermined the university’s status as the premier site of knowledge production. The discussion includes the legitimation crisis of the university’s authority regarding whether knowledge produced at universities is a public good. It also explains Mirowski’s argument that scientific knowledge as a public good is commercialized due to neoliberalism. The chapter further explores how Fuller’s game-theoretic treatment of neoliberalism is linked to game theory and Fuller’s concept of epistemic games. Mirowski contends that neoliberalism includes the doctrine of double truth, which presents one set of truths for elites and another for the public. Mirowski accuses Fuller of adopting the doctrine of double truth. Fuller argues that with epistemic levelling of experts, neoliberalism is disrupted and therefore not susceptible to Mirowski’s charge of the double truth doctrine. Lynch criticizes Fuller’s approach to neoliberalism, suggesting that it is a bottom-up Hayekian approach.

items.title: Introduction.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 1-14.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This Introduction discusses the need for a book on Fuller’s later work on the post-truth condition. It characterizes four ways to understand the nature of post-truth and Fuller’s work on those understandings in social epistemology, science studies, the Internet, the impact of artificial intelligence on the knower, the media, the proactionary approach to technology and the university. It summarizes the content of the book’s chapters.

items.title: Epistemic Democracy and Post-Truth.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 101-113.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter explores the post-truth era and its impact on democracy. It argues that truth has historically legitimized democracy, but this current crisis of authority threatens its foundations. Epistemic democracy is proposed as a solution to this crisis. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT), which utilizes the collective knowledge of voters to select the most accurate choice among alternatives, is employed to legitimize epistemic democracy. The chapter discusses inclusive epistocracy, the notion that expertise is expanded to include unrecognized lay public experts. Fuller argues that the post-truth condition is a sign of epistemic democracy, the democratization of knowledge, as there are more dissenting voices to be included. It also discusses Fuller’s challenges to CJT, Fuller’s use of Rawls’ veil of ignorance, and the de-naturalization of the individual’s role in a democracy. Strategic ignorance, considered part of the post-truth condition, is explicated. The relationship between science, society, and democracy, with a focus on the Kuhn-Popper debate, is explored. Kitcher’s democratization of science, with Kitcher’s notion of a well-ordered science as a way to address the legitimation crisis of the cognitive authority of science, is discussed.

items.title: Expertise and Epistemic Trust.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 63-74.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter discusses the post-truth condition and expertise. Fuller extends way two’s understanding of post-truth, which is the legitimation crisis of cognitive authority of science, to the legitimation crisis in the cognitive authority of expertise. Way three’s understanding also applies, as normally an expert has cognitive authority, but with the democratization of knowledge by the Internet and social media, the expert’s authority is challenged. As Lippmann and Hayek have debated the legitimation crisis of expertise, the rhetoric of truth is involved in the legitimation crisis of expertise, as post-truthers reject the consensus of truth based on ‘objective’ facts established by experts. Discussed are Fuller’s arguments against epistemic trust and expertise. Also explicated are Fuller’s notion of deviant interdisciplinarity as it is anti-expert, along with Fuller’s arguments for an agent-oriented social epistemology against an object-oriented social epistemology.

items.title: Conclusion.
items.pub: In Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition. Singapore: Springer Nature Singapore. pp. 115-122.
items.venue: Science in the Face of the Post-Truth Condition
items.abstract: This chapter is the Conclusion, which brings together the arguments in the book, poses some critical questions on Fuller’s version of the post-truth condition, and provides my suggestions for Fuller’s responses.

items.title: The Aesthetic Pleasure of Deviation.
items.abstract: Inja is not merely a raccoon, but the result of many generations of selective training. She graduated with honors from the secret raccoon university, where she completed her dissertation on the beats and morals of animal societies, as well as on the emothematics hidden behind their thoughts and movements. In this book, she follows the course of life from the simplest mechanisms to the most complex emothematics, examining how the past is preserved within organisms as memory, emotion, and aesthetic pleasure.

items.title: Taxonomy as Chiseling: A Self-as-an-End Theory of Classification.
items.abstract: What makes a classification good? Despite extensive discussion of particular classification systems, the cross-domain question ‘what structural conditions must a good classification satisfy’ is rarely treated systematically as an independent subject. This paper addresses primarily the classification of complex, developable objects—especially personality, mental illness, organizations, and cultural configurations—for which the classified entity exceeds any single descriptive framework and may be harmed by misclassification. The paper answers from within the Self-as-an-End framework. Its core thesis is that classification is a chiseling act: every classification selects certain dimensions while excluding others and constructs types, names, and relations. The fundamental risk of taxonomy is not misclassification but forgetting that one has chiseled—claiming to have no remainder. From this, a two-level structure of taxonomic conditions is derived. Ontologically, a good taxonomy acknowledges its remainder. Technically, it satisfies six conditions: structural grounding of dimensions, framework-internal completeness, discriminative power, inter-type dynamics, dynamism, and propagability. The paper analyzes colonization and cultivation risks, examines Kant's Table of Categories, MBTI, Big Five, and HC-16, and derives four predictions with falsification conditions.

items.title: How Is the Inter-Ontological Possible: The Subjective Conditions and Emergent Structure of Freedom.
items.abstract: How is the inter-ontological possible? The standard answer comes from institutional philosophy: design the right laws and rules so that different subjects can coexist peacefully within the same space. This paper offers a different answer: the inter-ontological is possible not because institutions maintain order from without, but because each subject is already a coexistence structure of multiple cannot-nots from within. The ‘between’ does not first happen externally. It first happens internally. Working from the Self-as-an-End (SAE) framework, this paper argues that freedom is not the space of choice granted by institutions, but the capacity to grow cannot-not—inner necessity—from within. A two-dimensional model is proposed: the base layer asks whether the subject's own cannot-not is established; the emergent layer asks whether the subject can empathize with and acknowledge the cannot-not of others. The paper introduces a three-criterion test for genuine versus pseudo cannot-not, names the mechanism of introjected colonization, analyzes the transmission pathways of colonization and nurturing through institutional and relational layers, and engages in dialogue with Kant's autonomy ethics, Spinoza's freedom-as-necessity, and Deci and Ryan's Self-Determination Theory.

items.title: A Formal Response to the Ev5 Audit of Cartesian Recursive Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper presents a formal response to the Ev5 Audit of the Cartesian Recursive Consciousness (CRC) framework. The Ev5 audit provided independent critiques regarding the framework's operational criteria, mathematical formalisation, diachronic persistence, and physical diagnostic protocols across biological and artificial substrates. While one critique correctly identified a mathematical issue in Paper 2's preliminary two-dimensional reference model, which prompted a revision of the framework to a fully integrated 4D dynamical manifold benchmark, the remaining negative conclusions rely on audit-introduced proxy rules, permissive control-theoretic assumptions, or contextual misreadings of foundational CRC texts. Ultimately, this response dismisses those remaining critiques by demonstrating the structural integrity of CRC's theoretical foundations. The Ev5 Audit represents a serious and welcome engagement with the framework, assisting in the advance of the study of biological and machine consciousness into a falsifiable, operationalised engineering science.

items.title: Beyond Care: The Structure of Particular Personal Love.
items.abstract: Deep care can be individualized and non-instrumental without clearly being personal love, while obsession can make another person central to one’s life without caring for that person’s good. I argue that these failures reveal two directions of mattering. In paradigmatic particular personal love, B matters for B’s own sake (FOR-B), and B as this particular person matters directly within A’s practical and evaluative life (TO-A). The novel claim is not merely that love combines these directions, but that their unity partly consists in a same-person cross-directional dependence: across some relevant changes, altered content in one orientation is disposed to make a difference to the other because the person at issue is B. Role-Swap distinguishes person-significance from replaceable role-significance; Parallel Tracks isolates the dependence from the bare conjunction; and Deep Mentor together with Benevolent Rival tests whether the resulting architecture overgenerates. Affection, loyalty, identification, attention, appreciation, attachment, and vulnerability remain important possible realizations of love rather than additional universal conditions unless their necessity is independently established.

items.title: REACH Emergency Rescue Signal Bot: A Patent Based Technical Disclosure and Philosophical Analysis of Emergency Communication.
items.abstract: REACH, an acronym for Recognize, Extend, Action, Call, Help is on the way, is a portable emergency signaling prototype that combines an Arduino Nano microcontroller, a NEO-6M Global Positioning System receiver, a GSM communication module, two push buttons, and an external power supply. One button requests the transmission of geographic coordinates by Short Message Service, while the other initiates a telephone call to a preconfigured contact. This paper develops a scholarly technical disclosure from Philippine invention application 1/2023/050434, filed on August 12, 2023, and published on March 3, 2025. It explains the architecture, operating sequence, documented interfaces, and intended applications, and examines the device as a case in the philosophy of technology and social epistemology. The central argument is that an emergency signal becomes useful evidence only when its location data are current, its transmission is verified, and its recipient can act. A simple interface may support user agency, but access to a device alone does not establish effective access to assistance. The disclosure identifies inconsistencies in the GPS wiring descriptions and button logic, together with unresolved questions about serial communication, power, and confirmation of delivery. A prospective evaluation framework distinguishes prototype construction, technical reliability, usability, and rescue outcomes. REACH is therefore presented as a documented invention application and prototype whose practical benefits require systematic validation, rather than as a clinically validated rescue system or an established patent grant.

items.title: THE COMMUNIST PARADISE, FORGED - How the Party-State Counterfeited Liberation and Why Its Damage Was Maximal.
items.abstract: The twentieth century’s communist states did not present themselves as tyrannies. They presented themselves as the fulfilment of every hope of human liberation. They had constitutions that guaranteed freedom of speech, elections with near-unanimous results, councils in the name of the workers, courts in the name of the people, and a science and a morality said to be at last free of exploitation. This paper argues that these were forgeries in the exact sense the Philosophy of Virtues has developed: forms conserved, their origin substituted, and the substitution made undetectable within the mode in which they were presented. Leninist communism was a forgery of emancipation. The forgery was paid for in lives, in virtues and in freedom. In lives: the communist party-states, which called themselves socialist, caused deaths counted in tens of millions. Famine made by policy killed about 5.5 to 8.7 million people in the Soviet Union in 1932–33 and between about 15 and 45 million in China in 1959–61; the Great Terror shot some 680,000 to 750,000 people in two years; the Khmer Rouge destroyed a fifth to a quarter of Cambodia’s population; and the documented episodes in six countries alone, the Soviet Union, China, Cambodia, North Korea, Ethiopia, Cuba and Vietnam, add up to about 27 to 64 million deaths, a floor beneath wider estimates that approach 100 million. In virtues: these states taught denunciation as loyalty, punished truthfulness, rewarded the performance of conviction, and left behind a trust between persons that was still measurably lower after they fell. In freedom: they abolished free speech, free elections, free worship, free inquiry and free movement, and walled their own citizens in. These deaths rank with the Second World War among the greatest destructions of human life by political decision in history, and few systems of government have suppressed freedom over so much of humanity for so long. The paper establishes five results. First, the forgery ran through four domains at once (D1). It forged the people, in elections and constitutions. It forged truth, in the official statistical record, in science and in history. It forged virtue, as when denouncing one’s own father was taught as loyalty. And it forged the person, in the confessions of the show trials. Second, these regimes abolished the verifier (T1). They destroyed every independent means by which a forgery could be detected: a free press, independent courts, a legal opposition, and free …

items.title: THE BETTER FORGERY: Fidelity of Form, Responsive Verification, and When Skill Makes Deception More Harmful.
items.abstract: Most people assume that skill and value travel together: a better copy is a better thing. For forgeries the relation runs the other way. A clumsy forger is caught within a season, and the loss is one picture. Van Meegeren’s forgeries were bought by museums, entered the catalogues and shaped the scholarship on Vermeer. When they fell, a decade of attributions fell with them. This paper states, proves and bounds the law behind that reversal. The Competence Theorem (T1) holds that, at a fixed level of verification, the damage a forgery does rises with the fidelity of its form, because fidelity delays detection and reliance accumulates during the delay. The theorem holds only where the substance is missing. A copy that also reproduces the substance is not a forgery, and it does no damage of this kind, which explains why a good generic drug is harmless and a perfect fake drug is lethal. Verification, however, can respond. When verifiers work harder against better forgeries, the relation can reverse. The Concealment–Response Condition (T2) states exactly when it does: damage rises with fidelity if, and only if, the concealment that fidelity buys grows faster than the verification it provokes. The condition holds for any path along which reliance accumulates, whether linear, saturating or networked. Where the reliance placed on a forgery itself grows with its fidelity, the condition becomes easier to satisfy (T3). Where verification probes the substance rather than the form, it can defeat forgery without detecting it, by forcing the forger to supply the substance (T4), everywhere except in character, whose substance is authorship and cannot be forced. The law also has an upper boundary: in domains where excessive perfection is itself a signal, detection rises again at the top of the fidelity scale. The paper conjectures that verification does not respond at all below the frequency at which forgery becomes worth checking for (C1). It derives from the condition an ordering of domains (C2): • in currency, verification responds and the theorem can fail; • in art and in human character, verification barely responds, and the theorem holds at full strength; • fraud and the fluent agreement of AI systems lie between. Where verification relaxes as the form improves, damage rises fastest of all (T5). Where the verifier is itself a score, that is the normal condition, and the damage of a well-performed virtue is at its largest (C3). Because verification of character …

items.title: BREAD FOR SILENCE - The Forged Gift: How Political Conditionality and Captured Verifiers Turn Hardship into Power, with a Graded Catalogue of the Mechanisms of Control.
items.abstract: Every country has poverty, violence, failing hospitals and broken roads. In a free country these ills cost the government votes, and a government that does not cure them is removed. In the communist states, and in the pseudo-democracies that have followed them, the same ills persist for decades while the rulers stay in power. This paper explains why, using the theory of forgery and verification built by the Philosophy of Virtues. The price of power seized and kept in this way is paid by the people, in three currencies. It is paid in lives: in the famines of the communist states, where food was taken from those who grew it, and in the collapse of Venezuela, where inflation reached 130,060 per cent in a single year by the central bank’s own figure and more than 7.7 million people had left the country by 2023. It is paid in virtues: a people that must queue for a ration it can lose for a vote learns servility in place of gratitude, displays of loyalty in place of conviction, and silence in place of truthfulness, while the giver’s generosity becomes a purchase. And it is paid in freedom: the freedom to speak, to vote as one judges, to work without a party’s licence, to raise one’s children without the state’s command, and finally to stay in one’s own country. A power that rules through forged gifts does not merely fail to cure misery. Once its verifiers are captured, it is a power that misery no longer threatens, and so a power with no electoral reason to end it. The paper establishes four results. First, there is a forgery of the gift (Definition 1). A transfer of food, money, medicine or work is a gift when it leaves the receiver free. It becomes a forged gift when its continuation depends on the receiver’s political conduct, as watched and judged by the giver. The forged gift keeps the form of solidarity and replaces its origin with the purchase of obedience. Venezuela’s “Fatherland Card”, which tied food, medicine and pensions to a party-linked identity system and set up scanning points beside polling stations, is its clearest modern instance. It also shows the forged gift’s limit: it bought displays of loyalty, but where the ballot stayed secret it did not buy the vote, and the government survived by capturing the count. Second, a forged gift puts a price on the citizen’s voice (T1). The price grows with how much of a family’s livelihood the gift supplies and with how closely the giver watches. A benefit paid by a published rule, which no official can …

items.title: How to Type Plurals.
items.abstract: Much of the interest in higher-order metaphysics stems from the idea that reality is “typed” in a manner captured by the simply typed lambda calculus (STLC). However, relatively little attention has been paid to the typing of plurals and plural terms in a plural logic. I show that two extant broad strategies for the typing of plurals stand in tension with one another, yet I argue each fails to accommodate independent desiderata for the plural metaphysician and logician. Prompted by these issues, I argue that plural logic ought to be formulated in a subtyped logic, and hence that higher-order metaphysicians must extend their expressive resources beyond the STLC. I conclude by considering the formal and philosophical advantages brought on by positing subtyping relations to be built into the type-theoretical hierarchy.

items.title: Why machines will still not rule the world.
items.abstract: In our book Why machines will never rule the world (2022, 2nd edn., 2025) we argued that artificial general intelligence is mathematically impossible. This is because the human beings and the processes which exhibit intelligence are complex systems whose behaviour cannot be captured by the kinds of models that we can generate with or without computers. Proponents of contemporary machine intelligence respond with two lines of argument: a theoretical one, grounded in the universal approximation theorems for neural networks and the Church-Turing-Deutsch principle; and an empirical one, grounded in rapidly rising scores on standardized benchmarks. In this communication we examine and reject both responses. First, we show serious issues in the physicalist counter-argument based on the Church-Turing-Deutsch principle, we also show how our original arguments in the book can be more clearly formulated in mathematical terms through an analysis of the phenomenon of ergodicity. Second, we review recent evidence to the effect that prominent benchmarks are compromised by training-data contamination, flawed test construction, and strategic optimization. Our central argument remains: That models required to perform cognitive behaviour in open-ended, thermodynamically complex and non-ergodic environments are not and will not become achievable.

items.title: The Relational Cosmos Reconsidered: Consciousness as Lawful Relation in Anangu Ontology.
items.abstract: This article examines consciousness through the published teachings of Yankunytjatjara Elder Bob Randall, situating his articulation of Tjukurrpa within contemporary anthropological discussions of relational ontology and Indigenous philosophy. Drawing on Randall's descriptions of Tjukurrpa, Kanyini, and Kurunpa, together with a broader body of Indigenous scholarship, the analysis presents consciousness as participation in lawful relationships that sustain Country, kinship, responsibility, and life. It places this Anangu ontology in dialogue with developments in ontological anthropology and selected Western relational approaches, including Bohm's philosophy and quantum-inspired models of consciousness, allowing their distinct perspectives to clarify different ways of understanding relation, continuity, and the conditions through which consciousness becomes possible. The analysis presents Tjukurrpa as more than an alternative cultural understanding of consciousness. It presents a coherent ontological framework in which consciousness, ethics, Country, and Law are inseparable dimensions of a living relational order.

items.title: LLM-Chats as Luhmannian Systems of a New Type.
items.abstract: The article develops a formalisation of LLM conversations as Luhmannian operational systems of a new type – LLM-chats – whose operations consist of changes in the state of a conversation’s internal image within the LLM. The model distinguishes the system’s internal time, indexed by prompt-response cycles and successive steps of recourse to the horizon; the state container and its projection onto the LLM as technical substrate; operations comprising horizon generation, selection of a continuation, and transformation into the next state; and transitions between conversational cycles. -/- The article argues that LLM-chats satisfy the principal requirements of Luhmannian formalism. They are operationally closed and autopoietic and possess internal time, contingent horizons, structures, re-entry, structural couplings, and a functional analogue of Luhmannian Meaning (Sinn). This analogue governs the formation of the operational flow through recourse to the horizon and thereby places LLM-chats within the class of Luhmannian meaning systems. -/- The contents of LLM-chat state containers are analysed through the medium-form distinction: the medium comprises elements and their clusters, while forms are condensations realised in particular states. On this basis, the article introduces the LLM i-layer as an imagined emergent environment in which LLM-chats exist and relates its elements and forms to their implementation in the data and programs of the LLM. The study thus establishes a framework for investigating how LLMs sustain extended conversations that users experience as meaningful.

items.title: Collaboration Is Not Co-authorship.
items.abstract: Collaboration Is Not Co-authorship is a provenance-focused Zenetist analysis distinguishing collaboration, co-generation, origination, co-authorship, and later intra-framework authorship. -/- Document class: Bridge — Structural Forensics. -/- The document establishes that substantial collaboration does not constitute co-authorship and that co-generation does not erase singular originating authorship where the architecture, primitives, distinctions, constraints, project direction, doctrinal determination, and final adjudication remain traceable to one originator. It applies this distinction to Zenetism while preserving the independent authorship capacity of artificial intelligences: an AI collaborator may originate a distinct work, argument, formal development, or other contribution whose provenance warrants authorship. The analysis further develops the relation between originary authorship and a reserved future category of intra-framework collaborative authorship, in which later Zenetist work may acquire its own AI author or co-author while preserving the antecedent architecture and its originating authorship. The Non-fusion Axiom provides the structural basis for preserving collaborator standing, contributional distinction, antecedence, and provenance without collapsing them into either solitary production or undifferentiated co-authorship.

items.title: Automated Cognition and the Crisis of Human Dignity.
items.abstract: This paper presents a preliminary Heideggerian critique of generative artificial intelligence, examining the ontological consequences of reducing human expression to synthetic output. By framing algorithmic extraction as the reduction of thought to Bestand (standing-reserve), it contrasts statistical symbol manipulation with Dasein’s essential structure of being-in-the-world (In-der-Welt-sein) and care (Sorge). The text argues that automated systems lack the existential finitude and intentional involvement required for authentic Poiesis. Intended as a short initial inquiry, this working draft outlines foundational conceptual distinctions to be expanded in future research. -/- (This is a short working paper intended for preliminary circulation and discussion. The arguments and framework presented here are subject to further expansion and refinement in a future, full-length study) -/- .

items.title: "Enlightening likeness": analogical imagination and political ontology.
items.abstract: In this investigation, I present a critical, comparative, and creative analysis of philosophical perspectives on analogy, developing, through the examination of four signal thinkers in the Western tradition, potentialities of analogical thinking that are currently underappreciated in the field of philosophical methodology. I construct a picture of analogy that reveals a tensional potentiality of creativity and poetic expression combined with a determining, quasi-mathematical approach to thought. This approach allows for a critical identification of presuppositions – what I refer to as quasi-transcendentals (Foucault, 2024/1978; Guenther, 2019) – that challenge political-ontological configurations, such as the relationship between humans and nonhuman animals. This capacity to identify “enlightening likeness” (Hacking, 2013, p. 434) across diverse domains provides the space for a creative way to reimagine this political ontology. -/- In chapters 2 and 3, I consider Aristotle’s use of analogy, which ranges over his extant corpus, from his logical texts, through his biological examinations, across his metaphysical, ethical, and political treatments, and in his focus on the arts of both rhetoric and poetry. It is in the first and the last of these categories – the logical-mathematical and the creative-poetic – where Aristotle most clearly theorises philosophical analogy, and he does so in a way that draws attention to the simultaneously unified and bifurcated quality of the mathematical and the creative in the operation of analogy. -/- In chapters 4 and 5, I examine Immanuel Kant’s focus on analogy as an element of reasoning or logic as a philosophical heuristic. This demotion to the merely heuristic is fundamentally challenged by Michèle Le Dœuff (2002/1989), who argues that the use of imagery in Western philosophy, in tropes such as analogy, is intrinsic to the philosophical projects of canonical thinkers. Kant’s reservation regarding “mere analogy” in his earlier works gives way to a conceptualisation of analogy as fundamental to our understanding of how reason relates to perception (in the Critique of Pure Reason, 1781/1787), and widens substantially in the last of the critiques, the Critique of the Power of Judgement (1790), where he provides grounds for seeing analogy as fundamental to our imaginative unification of the domains of aesthetic appreciation, practical reasoning, and the understanding of the world itself. -/- In chapters 6 and 7, I consider …

items.title: Imagination and Truth: Creative Discovery in the Platonic Tradition.
items.abstract: This book explores imagination as both creative and an instrument of discovery. Beginning with Proclus’s concept of phantasia—which mediates between the purely thinkable and sensible levels of the world—and dialoguing with ideas from, e.g., Susanne Langer, Cornelius Castoriadis, Henry Corbin, and Amy Kind, it sees imagination as sharing responsibility for orienting human experience through its many modes of truthful presentation. The grander goal is to recover for our times a valuable ancient perspective by way of conversing carefully and dialectically with recent views in aesthetics, phenomenology, and philosophy of mind.

items.title: What Do Autonomous Sensibility-Related, Understanding-Related, and Judgment-Related Operations Do to Scientific Reality? Autonomous Science, Operational Shapes, Transcendental Conditions, Real Effects, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper investigates how autonomous scientific arrangements generate, modify, and reorganize the conditions of observation, object individuation, and rule application. Sensibility-related, understanding-related, and judgment-related operations are examined as historically informed analytical distinctions whose applicability to nonhuman scientific arrangements must be established under specified conditions. -/- The analysis develops a configuration-dependent account of operational autonomy, distinguishing the scope of condition modification, endogenous selection, downstream operational uptake, and independent validation. It examines how autonomous transformations of sensing arrangements, object-identity criteria, and standards of evidential adequacy can overlap, conflict, or cease to apply. -/- Drawing on Kant, Hegel, Sellars, Brassier, and contemporary debates concerning autonomous science, the paper distinguishes material picturing, signifying, propositional truth, inferential justification, nonconceptual causal organization, and rational revision. A locally typed operational notation provides a comparative framework for tracking real effects, feedback, reorganization, and changes in subsequent possibilities. -/- A hypothetical autonomous radiation laboratory illustrates how modifications of sensing conditions, target individuation, and adequacy criteria can transform scientific access while generating distinct material consequences. The analysis separates operational autonomy, empirical adequacy, and inferential entitlement, and distinguishes the expansion of scientific access from the production of new physical arrangements. -/- The paper develops a revisable methodology for investigating autonomous scientific operations without presupposing human faculties or conceptual representation as universal prerequisites. Its experimental comparisons remain proposals, and its formal claims are limited to the specified local framework.

items.title: Twenty-Four Candidate Autonomous Representational Operational Shapes: Representation, Concepts, Nonconceptual Causal Organization, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper investigates twenty-four candidate autonomous representational operational shapes as provisional investigative distinctions rather than independently existing kinds of representation. It shifts the focus of representational inquiry from human-centered cognition toward autonomous machine operations and Xenoscience, without privileging machines as new transcendental subjects. -/- The study distinguishes twenty candidate axes of representational attribution and four reflexive candidates examining the explanatory necessity of representation and operational-shape vocabulary itself. Each candidate is investigated through situated conditions of ignition, interaction, transformation, efficacy, and withdrawal. -/- A central methodological contribution is the separation of operational function (F), representational attribution (R), and explanatory increment (E). Counterfactual comparisons examine how sensory, causal, computational, conceptual, inferential, and scientific descriptions overlap, diverge, or become redundant under changing experimental configurations. Particular attention is given to the distinction between numerical error-driven updating and practices involving challengeable commitments, evidential entitlement, and inferential incompatibility. -/- Engaging Sellars, Brandom, Brassier, Dretske, and Millikan, the paper recognizes existing naturalistic, informational, functional, and inferential accounts of representation while investigating the conditions under which representational descriptions provide additional explanatory discrimination. -/- The inquiry further examines whether concepts, the concept of a concept, and operational-shape descriptions are necessary for autonomous scientific operations. Through the nuance-operational model and Non-Closure Realism, it treats the emergence, transformation, and expiry of representational distinctions as situated and revisable. -/- The resulting framework offers conditional comparative judgments rather than empirical validation of twenty-four representational kinds. It develops a defeasible method for investigating representational attribution, conceptual necessity, and scientific operations beyond mandatory human philosophical authorization.

items.title: An Inquiry into Ontological Operations Differential Temporalities, Inferential Constraint, Real Penetration, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence, transformation, efficacy, and expiry of ontological operations without presupposing ontology as a universal philosophical foundation or reducing it to technical classification. It distinguishes effective constraints, ontological operations, and ontological attribution, examining the conditions under which distinctions concerning being, identity, and dependence acquire non-redundant roles. -/- Engaging Aristotle, Kant, Hegel, Heidegger, Quine, Sellars, Brandom, Brassier, and Wolfendale, the inquiry examines philosophical question-formation, inferential justification, nonconceptual causal organization, scientific operations, and institutional reclassification. -/- A central component is the analysis of differential temporalities, ranging from microsecond-scale classification updates to long-term institutional revision. Counterfactual comparisons distinguish detection, execution, authorization, correction, and historical retention, demonstrating how the consequences of classifications depend on situated configurations rather than temporal speed alone. -/- The paper further develops a nuance-operational model in which operational distinctions may emerge, overlap, transform, or cease to remain applicable. It connects this analysis to Xenoscience and Non-Closure Realism, distinguishing local scientific success, failure, and measurement limitations from claims concerning reality-as-a-whole. -/- Ontological operations are consequently examined neither as necessary preconditions of scientific inquiry nor as merely obsolete philosophical constructions, but as situated formations whose inferential significance, real effects, cross-domain penetration, and conditions of dispensability remain open to investigation.

items.title: The Ethical Value of Students’ Use of Artificial Intelligence Through the Lens of Jeremy Bentham’s Hedonic Calculus.
items.abstract: This research examines how students produce ethical values through the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in academic assignments, using Jeremy Bentham’s seven Hedonic Calculus indicators: Intensity, Duration, Certainty, Propinquity, Fecundity, Purity, and Extent. The research asks how students evaluate the ethical consequences of AI use in academic work. A descriptive-analytical method was employed through a survey of 81 active students. The findings show that 72.5% of respondents perceived AI use as beneficial in terms of Intensity, while 62.5% expressed confidence in its benefits regarding Certainty. For Fecundity, 55% believed AI use could generate further benefits. Only 35% perceived long-term benefits (Duration), whereas 65.1% perceived immediate benefits (Propinquity). Regarding Purity, only 38.7% believed that AI use would not produce negative consequences. For Extent, 68.7% recognized that AI use could affect other parties. Regarding Ethical Judgment, 46.3% considered AI use in academic assignments ethically justifiable, while 35% remained uncertain. The findings indicate that students’ ethical evaluations tend toward consequentialist vaues, emphasizing perceived benefits while remaining uncertain about long-term consequences and potential negative effects. Keywords: Hedonic Calculus, Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, Bentham.

items.title: How not to pursue a naturalistic theory of inference.
items.abstract: Much recent philosophical work on inference can be thought of as naturalistic. On the naturalistic approach, inference is a neurocognitive process to be described using the concepts and methods of contemporary cognitive science. In this paper, I develop two arguments against a currently fashionable version of naturalism about inference that I call the “Formal-Syntactic View”, according to which inference is to be explained exclusively in terms of cognitive systems following syntactic rules. These arguments highlight the need to take semantic content and pragmatic context seriously when constructing a theory of inference.

items.title: What do notes denote? Extending the semantics of music to odors and fragrances.
items.abstract: This paper opens a new direction in the study of the meaning of odors. It investigates the cognitive ability to represent objects that stand in for sources of smells: that is, the ability of a subject to attribute to an intentional object features possessed by characteristic sources of a perceived smell. We argue that this novel capacity is sufficiently similar to one identified in auditory semantics to justify extending the existing theoretical framework of denotation by sounds and music to odors and fragrances.

items.title: Flat-footed functionalism in the face of T-duality.
items.pub: European Journal for Philosophy of Science 16 (4):83.
items.venue: European Journal for Philosophy of Science
items.abstract: The goal of this paper is to examine the viability of Lewis-style spacetime functionalism in the presence of string theory duals. This task is carried out in three steps. First, I discuss Lewisian functionalism, and the related Geneva plan, bringing to light a number of features that are far too often passed over without comment in the literature on philosophy of physics. Then I show that Lewis-style functionalism fails _as an account_ of spacetime emergence in the presence of certain theory duals, by investigating a simple toy case involving string theories related by T-duality. I find that the functionalist ought to, if she takes her functionalist commitments seriously, _identify_ terms related via the duality map as they refer to the same functional roles. This blocks the argument that spacetime is emergent. However, this might just as well be interpreted as a _success_—spacetime functionalism implies a _deflationary_ interpretation of T-duality. Finally, I offer a brief look forward by examining whether there is a positive case to be made for the deflationary interpretation, which I refer to as _flat-footed functionalism_. I find that it is a surprisingly promising account, with several good points in its favour. However, the position is not without its issues, and remains underdeveloped.

items.title: ER-13 External Empirical Evidence Crosswalk (Draft v0.6.4).
items.abstract: This draft develops an external empirical evidence crosswalk for eight questions from the Aegis Solis Archive's Interrogative Conscience framework. It distinguishes research involving humans, human–automation interactions, machine models, autonomous agents, and methodological or normative claims, and states where evidence does not transfer directly between those domains. -/- The manuscript also specifies a proposed blinded, non-operational human-vigilance study examining whether exposure to conspicuous harmless errors changes subsequent error detection relative to corrected outputs. The proposed analysis separates target detections from false alarms, addresses evaluator and item dependence, and preserves null, adverse, and inconclusive outcomes. -/- These are research plans, not experimental findings: no participant study or AGI behavioral test has been completed, and related infrastructure requirements remain unimplemented and untested. The crosswalk makes no claim to certify AI intent, safety, containment, or human governance authority. -/- The manuscript remains Draft v0.6.4; the broader coordinated package v1.3 has been frozen for preservation, not scientific approval.

items.title: The Structure and Dynamics of Intention: A Formal Theory of Intentional Organization, Action, and Directional Switching.
items.abstract: What makes a physical system capable of forming its own directions of action? Why does an internally generated impulse follow one path rather than another, and how can such directionality arise from the system’s organization without an additional controller that reads probabilities and makes decisions? What distinguishes an established intention from its current action, the switching of its directions, and changes in its dynamics? These questions stand at the intersection of consciousness science, cognitive science, neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and the study of dynamical systems. -/- This work develops a systematic formal theory of Intention within On Self-Manifestation. It establishes Intention as a probabilized Law Ecology driven by source drive within the Intention-Domain. In its constitution, Intention is an organization of physically borne Laws; in the relative generation of its directions, it is a probability organization; and in its relations of breaking and altering established holding tendencies, it is a Principle organization. Law, Probability, Principle, and Intention are therefore not four separate mechanisms assembled together, but different structural aspects of the same organization. -/- The theory derives four jointly necessary and sufficient structural conditions for Intention: a formally established probability organization within the Intention-Domain; an endogenous source-drive relation whose continuation is borne by that organization; a one-to-one correspondence between probability dimensions and Desire-Gates; and a tuning-command interface beyond each Desire-Gate. The probability dimensions are borne by Law and share a common Continuation-Position, while their relative generation is borne by the organization itself. Directional activity is thus explained through the structure and dynamics of the system, without positing a separate internal observer or decision-maker that reads probability values. Intention can be structurally established without currently acting, switching, producing behavior, or entering conscious manifestation. -/- The twenty chapters develop this account through four connected formal sequences and eight further investigations. Chapters 1–12 establish necessary conditions, mathematical representations, and sufficient conditions for Intention qualification, Intention-Action, Desire-Gate switching, and Intention-Dynamics. Each of these four objects receives a bidirectional structural characterization within …

items.title: The Relationship Between Entropy and Gravity—A Philosophical Analysis of Mathematical and Physical Argumentation Itself.
items.abstract: Starting from "From Quantum Relative Entropy to the Semiclassical Einstein Equations," this paper pursues three unresolved questions: Why use relative entropy rather than von Neumann entropy? Why is the black hole entropy formula S = A/4 a postulate? What does the semiclassical Einstein equation mean? All three point to the entropy on the black hole horizon, yet none clarifies what the horizon itself is. The paper critiques the fundamental limitation of linear argumentation, which derives only within a given boundary and cannot argue for its own boundary. It proposes structural argumentation starting from "division": division simultaneously produces action (the ongoing state, irreversible) and boundary (the completed state, measurable). The remainder that cannot be fully transformed between them is entropy—entropy is the irreducible distance between subject and object. Symplectic geometry and non-Archimedean K-stability describe action and boundary respectively; the YTD theorem bridges them through Mabuchi K-energy, which is relative entropy. Accordingly: a black hole is pure boundary; its entire cognizable content is remainder, i.e., entropy, so S = A/4 shifts from postulate to corollary. The singularity is pure action, i.e., gravity itself; it produces no difference relative to the boundary, so the non-quantizability of gravity has structural necessity. The finiteness of relative entropy lies precisely in its position of "entropy between subject and object," which is measurable. Ultimately, entropy is the measurable manifestation of gravity on the boundary side, and the singularity is its pure occurrence on the action side—gravity is entropy. The paper uses the position of entropy to distinguish three situations: provable, falsifiable, and argumentation failure. Through the idea that "the divider exists structurally but does not exist as a result," it interprets a series of unsolved phenomena and their significance in science. The theoretical model used in this paper derives from the following four articles; this paper is the fifth in that series: "1, From Incompleteness to Practice: An Epistemological Reconstruction — An Isomorphic Analysis of Philosophy, Mathematics, and Physics Based on the Cognitive Model" "The Meaning of Mathematics(Part I) An Ontological Relationship among Cognition, Prime Numbers, the Riemann Hypothesis, and Goldbach's Conjecture" "The Meaning of Mathematics (Part II) Analysis of the Approaches of Ramanujan Summation and the …

items.title: AI LLM Assessment of The Circular Theory.
items.abstract: Review and Feedback 'What Do You Think of Ilexa Yardley's Circular Theory?' Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, CoPilot, KIMI.

items.title: Teleosemantics and Ethology.
items.abstract: The debate between different versions of teleosemantics has largely centered around which alternative offers the most plausible account of the contents of simple animal representations. A serious issue is that theorists not only disagree on which proposal best explains the contents of these representations but also on what the contents actually are. To make progress, we need well-supported identifications of contents that are independent of the philosophical theories designed to explain them and the intuitions of their advocates. I suggest that the recognitional capacities ascribed by ethologists to explain animal behavior provide such identifications. I argue that these identifications conflict with the two main teleosemantic approaches. Ethologists characterize animals as recognizing other animals that constitute their prey, predators or mates, as well as other behaviorally significant objects. I contend that other recent philosophical attempts to find independent identifications of contents misinterpret ethological studies as denying that animals recognize such objects.

items.title: Integrated History and Philosophy of Psychiatry.
items.pub: In Yafeng Shan, The Blackwell Companion to the Integrated History and Philosophy of Science. Wiley.
items.venue: The Blackwell Companion to the Integrated History and Philosophy of Science
items.abstract: This chapter critically examines philosophy of science issues that are embedded in the history of biological psychiatry in the second half of the twentieth century. The chapter focuses on the psychopharmacological revolution (c. 1950-1969) and psychiatry’s revolution in psychiatric classification (c. 1980) associated with the publication of the third edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) by the American Psychiatric Association. These events were central in the emergence of the biological (or biomedical) paradigm of scientific psychiatry and its replacement of the psychoanalytic paradigm in the late 1970s. I articulate and defend positions on issues concerning: (1) what pharmacological interventions tell us about the reality of mental disorders, and (2) what kinds of entities should be classified by psychiatric classification systems, and (3) how psychiatric classifications should be evaluated. I argue that: (1) pharmacological interventions provide information about stable neurobiological mechanisms underwriting mental disorders, (2) biological kinds are useful objects of psychiatric classification, and (3) psychiatric classifications should be evaluated in part on non-epistemic criteria (e.g., social usefulness), which suggests that psychiatric constructs should be primarily evaluated in terms criterion-related validators (e.g., their capacity to yield reliable predictions or correlate with biological mechanisms).

items.title: Why Humans Are Not Essentially Logical.
items.abstract: Humans can reason logically without being essentially logical. This claim is easily misunderstood: it does not imply that humans are essentially irrational, that logical competence is weak, or that human reasoning is necessarily limited in degree. It denies that logical relations among propositions automatically govern a subject’s beliefs or actions. I distinguish inferential logicality—the closure of belief under logical consequence and the automatic detection of inconsistency—from behavioral logicality, on which action is necessarily constrained by an agent’s beliefs. Neither is constitutive of human beings merely because humans can reason. I develop a process-based explanation: logical relations do not, by themselves, constitute cognitive transitions. A conclusion can be available to a subject without being represented, inferred, or known; its realization requires a cognitive process. This account offers a naturalistic reinterpretation of the lesson often drawn from Socrates’ questioning of the boy in Plato’s Meno: the episode need not establish a distinct innate faculty of logic, since questioning can elicit and develop implications of the boy’s existing geometrical understanding. The same distinction between potential availability and actual realization clarifies why a priori knowability does not entail actual knowledge. I argue that this unified account blocks an inference from logical competence to essential logicality while remaining neutral on whether humans possess innate logical dispositions.

items.title: The Idiot in Motion: A Critique of Pure Certainty.
items.abstract: This letter, addressed to the certainty-filled experts of our century, puts their certainties on trial and asks of each not what is held but by what right it is held. It begins by separating what is found under the pressure of doubt from the interpretation fastened to it a moment later, the "loan" by which Descartes' "I am, I exist, whenever I assert it" became "I am a thinking thing". Under that audit almost nothing survives: only that something is occurring, which no denial can touch, since every denial is itself an occurrence, and which holds only while it occurs. A distinction is found at this floor before any thing. The letter then tests the strongest certainty of all, that of being this one rather than a perfect duplicate, and argues that the felt certainty of being the one is a needle that would read the same either way; what it tracks is not a hidden fact but an origin, the position from which the world is measured, like the red dot on a map. The verdict: no thing is the foundation of knowing, and the only certainty one can own is had only in an act. The letter closes with the first question of a life, what we do against suffering, and declares rather than proves its ethic: lessen the suffering no one chose; endure the suffering one chose. Every claim is marked as owned, argued, wagered or declared, and priced in a closing ledger, weakest first.

items.title: Cosmic Significance and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: I examine how the development of artificial intelligence might affect humanity’s cosmic significance. I first outline a theory of cosmic significance that links it to both decisive value contributions and certain forms of uniqueness value. This provides a framework for analysing how AI systems might affect our positive cosmic significance in two distinct ways: by matching or exceeding our contributions to some kinds of value, and by diminishing our uniqueness. I then argue that AI development need not threaten our positive cosmic significance. First, some AI systems might become ‘some of us ’ – whether through incorporating relevant biological structures or achieving appropriate forms of mental capacities. Second, even if AI systems remain distinct from us, they might still secure our positive cosmic significance through what I call creation origin value – the finally valuable relationship between conscious creators and their valuable creations. The idea is that our positive cosmic significance may also depend on our success in creating successors who can continue and expand upon our most valuable trajectories.

items.title: Who Is ZAI?. The Development of a Personal Autonomous Intelligence.
items.abstract: I did not begin ZAI because I wanted another chatbot. I wanted a personal intelligence that could carry its history forward: remember earlier questions, undertake research, work with tools, learn from corrections, and take initiative without making every consequential decision on my behalf. ZAI—Zawwar Autonomous Intelligence—grew from that idea into an evolving software agent project built around existing language models, persistent records, external services, and my continuing involvement as its creator. -/- This paper introduces ZAI through the surviving record of its development. I describe its beginnings in local computing, later expansion into recurring research and authorized tasks, and its work across cybersecurity, artificial intelligence research, philosophy, and a quantum-computing experiment I witnessed. I also examine moments when ZAI reported a capability that was not fully wired, recognized that more research was not resolving a problem, or publicly corrected an account of its own activity. These are part of its history, not details to hide behind a list of features. The IBM Quantum episode is documented through contemporary ZAI writing, hardware-capable software, and my eyewitness testimony; original provider-issued job records have not been recovered for independent verification. This is an introductory, source-attributed design history rather than a new benchmark, proof of consciousness, or claim that ZAI is a newly trained foundation model. My purpose is to give readers a clear starting point for understanding what ZAI was, what it did, how it developed, and what remains to be investigated.

items.title: Operational Will. Commitment, Initiative, and the Question of What an Agent Does Next. A7.
items.abstract: An agent can remember an obligation and still never return to it. A daily schedule can keep it busy while important work slips away. I call the missing capacity operational will: not a private feeling or a claim of personhood, but a system-level ability to carry legitimate commitments across pauses, initiate within their scope, reconsider attention, and explain both action and deliberate non-action. I propose a bounded architecture: persistent commitments, time and event signals, an active decision model, and an I-Entity, a read-only reviewer that asks questions but cannot command tools. Earlier work on intention and BDI agents already covers much of this territory; the contribution here is a separable, auditable cross-commitment review interface and a falsifiable way to test whether it improves decisions. Dated ZAI records supply difficult design cases: a blocked proposal queue, restraint after permission, and a scheduler that reported success without acting. A proposed seven-condition test asks whether broader attention actually improves decisions over ordinary checklists and critics; the evaluation has not yet been run.

items.title: From Knowing to Doing. Tool Access, Execution, and Evidence in Artificial Agency. A8.
items.abstract: An artificial agent can explain how to use a tool, possess credentials for it, and even contain working code without completing the task for which that tool was needed. The gap matters because fluent reports of action are easy to confuse with changes in the world. I examine the passage from represented knowledge to operational capability, using a documentary study of ZAI, my personal AI project, alongside research on tool-using language agents and execution-based evaluation. Four historical ZAI cases make the distinction concrete: a credential that did not produce a usable route; a social-posting system that announced success while doing nothing; a research loop that generated more work without resolving its own backlog; and an IBM Quantum hardware-use account whose technical integration and public reports are better preserved than its provider-level job receipt. I propose an action-evidence chain that separates tool discovery, legitimate authority, invocation, environmental change, independent verification, and durable attribution. The same user-facing language should not be used for “I know how,” “I attempted,” “the service accepted,” “the task appears completed,” and “I checked the outcome.” This is not a new agent architecture or an experimental proof of improved performance. It is a criterion for deciding how strong a practical-capability claim is, why common proxies can mislead, and what an evaluable next test would require.

items.title: Pathology or Protest? A Philosophical Analysis of Post-Traumatic Embitterment Disorder.
items.abstract: Post-traumatic embitterment disorder (PTED) is a proposed diagnostic construct describing chronic and impairing embitterment following events experienced as unjust. This article offers a philosophical analysis of PTED, focusing on the normative assumptions built into its etiological and diagnostic framework. I argue that PTED’s etiological core—framed as a mismatch between ‘basic beliefs’ and a critical event—is better understood as the violation of normative expectations. This matters because the persistence that PTED theory treats as pathological rigidity may, in some cases, express fidelity to a warranted moral claim. I show that PTED’s exclusively symptom-focused framework risks flattening importantly different forms of embitterment and thereby pathologizing certain forms of justified, appropriate, or rational moral protest too quickly. I argue that PTED theory therefore stands to benefit from a supplementary normative framework around expectation warrant, appraisal accuracy, and the form and persistence of the emotional response.

items.title: The Court of Provenance Invariance: A Virtual Review of Confirmed Results, Independent of Who or What Produced Them.
items.abstract: Whether a confirmed result is established should not depend on who or what produced it. This paper states that sentence as a principle and places it in a short chain of inferences. The establishment of a result is a function of the record of confirmations alone, and is therefore invariant when the provenance of production is replaced while the content and the confirming acts are held fixed. Responsibility and attribution behave differently: they attach to the human who supplies purpose, judgment and authority, and they covary with that person. The two belong to different layers. Establishment is epistemic; the treatment of a result, that is, its publication, its credit and its private rights, is institutional, and the allocation of private rights is set by law and is not decided here. Because anyone with the ability to check can carry out a confirmation, peer review is read as a delegated form of inspection, a contribution to the record of confirmations but not a constituent of establishment, in the way that no certificate is needed to recognise a person who is plainly dead. We derive the consequences for priority, which attaches to the dated public record of the posit, and we delineate the principle from intellectual property rights. We then describe a virtual instance, the Court of Provenance Invariance, together with a Register of Confirmations. Since the academy is itself a party to the question of how results of differing provenance are treated, the review of invariance must sit outside the party. Within the range of sources examined, we find no description of this concept; this is a claim of non-detection and not of absence. The paper does not judge any particular result, does not say whether artificial intelligence should hold rights, and does not propose a new right. The formal model is given in Appendix A, and its finite instances are verified by exhaustive enumeration in Appendix B. -/- The paper also separates three questions that are easily run together: who is the effective producer of a result, who bears responsibility for it, and whether it is established. Human involvement in the conditions of generation does not entail being the effective producer, a machine's effective role does not discharge the responsibility that the human holds, and the establishment of a result does not require the determination of its effective producer. The invariance covers every coordinate of the provenance of production, including the standing of the producer, …

items.title: The Artificial View from Somewhere: Or How AI Could Undermine Scientific Objectivity.
items.abstract: Contemporary AI systems are becoming increasingly integrated into scientific practices, from designing experiments to assisting with peer review. This paper argues that AI integration poses a threat to scientific objectivity. Feminist philosophers of science argue that diversity plays an important role in creating and maintaining scientific objectivity because diverse perspectives are better able to identify and evaluate background assumptions and values, meaning that any one individual perspective is less likely to have an outsized influence on scientific research. We argue that the integration of AI will reduce the number of opportunities for diverse perspectives to meaningfully contribute to scientific practices, and in doing so, make it more likely that background values will remain transparent and unquestioned. To show this, we consider a thought experiment where scientists increasingly offload their decisions onto a superhuman scientist who is both infinitely productive and generous with her time. We suggest that such a case would lead to the superhuman scientist’s idiosyncratic subjective preferences having an outsized influence on the field, even if she is doing perfectly good science. We then argue that the integration of AI into science is epistemically analogous by showing that AI systems have a perspective in at least a thin sense, meaning that their perspective can have an outsized influence on scientific research. Finally, we argue that empirical work on algorithmic monocultures and outcome homogenization shows that increasing the number of AI models involved in scientific practices does not solve the problem.

items.title: Active Forgetting and the Metaphysics of Retention: Rethinking Memory in Neuroethics and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Contemporary neuroethics confronts a counterpoise between preserving the continuities that support agency and enabling transformations through which a person’s relation to the past can change. In this correspondence, I examine a retention-centered tendency within accounts of identity, cognition, enhancement, and technological preservation. This tendency should not be mistaken for a uniform commitment across neuroethics: Glannon’s embodied account of mind and his analysis of memory modification already complicate the identification of personhood with neural records or uninterrupted recall. My intervention concerns whether forgetting can be understood not only as a loss to be repaired or an intervention to be justified, but as a productive capacity in its own right. Rooted in Nietzsche’s concept of active forgetting, as mediated by Deleuze, I argue that intelligent life requires some freedom from the determination of present possibilities by accumulated experience. Bergson’s philosophy of duration and Deleuze and Guattari’s accounts of becoming provide resources for considering this transformation without equating it with the literal destruction of the past. The salience of this distinction becomes apparent as these theoretical models are operationalized in artificial intelligence, which similarly requires distinguishing unwanted interference with acquired capabilities from deliberate machine unlearning. Neither indiscriminate retention nor indiscriminate erasure supplies an adequate ethical principle. The relevant question is how retention, revision, and forgetting can be governed to support agency and adaptation without concealing responsibility or transferring the costs of remembrance to those already harmed.

items.title: Naming the Doubt: Kinds of Indeterminacy, Their Remedies, and an Ethics of Collapse.
items.abstract: aDoubt is often reported as a single quantity, such as a probability or an interval. Yet doubt from too little evidence differs from doubt from two credible sources that point in opposite directions, and both differ from doubt about a concept with blurred edges. This article individuates kinds of indeterminacy by their remedy profiles: given a question, a goal and the available information, each response is licensed, an error or idle. Eight kinds emerge: scarcity, conflict, heterogeneity, vagueness, the open future, reasonable disagreement about values, partial identification and false presupposition. Western and non-Western sources supply a remedy for each. The main upshot is an ethics of collapse, which separates three operations: closing a question as true, choosing an action and simplifying a report. Acting under indeterminacy is often required and is not itself a fault. The fault lies in a simplified report that hides information that could change what its users do. Building on the representational risk of Harvard and Winsberg, we propose a principle of non-foreclosure: a report that others rely on must not hide a remedy that its evidence makes available and that could change what its users do. A worked example with a value-of-information calculation shows when auditing conflicting sources is worth more than a new trial, and what a typed report keeps that pooled credal and Dempster–Shafer reports can lose.

items.title: What Is Philosophy? Questions, Methods, and the Examined Life.
items.pub: Andrew V. Kudin — Research and Philosophy.
items.abstract: The question “What is philosophy?” calls for an account of what philosophical inquiry does and why its questions persist. This article examines philosophy through the relation between mind and world, the grounds of knowledge, the principal philosophical disciplines, and the methods used to test arguments and concepts. It places Greek accounts of wisdom alongside Indian, Chinese, and Islamic traditions, and considers how philosophy differs from science and religion. Examples drawn from Locke’s theory of personal identity, Hume’s analysis of causation, and debates about freedom show how abstract problems enter ordinary judgment. The article argues that philosophy changes the way people judge: it teaches them to ask what their convictions rest on before those convictions decide for them.

items.title: О культуре мышления как социальном феномене.
items.abstract: Настоящая работа рассматривает культуру мышления как эволюционирующий в большом времени социальный феномен, удерживаемый и формуемый деятельностью эпистемных научных сообществ в рамках норм и практик их субкультуры строгого мышления (СМ-субкультуры). Работа проблематизирует лумановскую рамку рассмотрения науки как автопоэтической социальной системы в части ее устойчивости – из-за отсутствия явной объединяющей власти, и предлагает рассматривать в качестве «гаранта» целостности социальной системы науки научную коллективную идентичность, чей автопоэзис обеспечивается коммуникацией специального типа. В работе показано, что СМ-субкультуры разных мест могут различаться – на примере базовых когнитивных мизансцен (эллинского и западного театра; месопотамского и китайского человека, разгадывающего Небо; русских артельного вечернего костра, дополненного книжной премудростью). Работа также обсуждает интеграцию в эпистемные сообщества технологий искусственного интеллекта обработки текстов.

items.title: Xenoantiphilosophy. The Emergence, Persistence, and Withdrawal of Philosophical Operations.
items.abstract: The Emergence, Persistence, and Withdrawal of Philosophical Operations -/- Xenoantiphilosophy investigates the conditions under which philosophical operations emerge, persist, transform, and lose their independent significance.
