The article develops importance as a relational property grounded in constitutive consequence. Causal consequence concerns what an alteration produces within an existing configuration. Constitutive consequence concerns whether an alteration changes the conditions under which further transformations can occur. Importance becomes philosophically significant when alteration affects the future reconfigurability of a field. This account distinguishes importance from value, significance, mattering, and immediate causal efficacy while explaining their possible intersections. The article then examines the ontological status of latent capacity, arguing that capacity is real when an existing organization materially or structurally conditions a range of future transformations. Reconfigurative capacity is distinguished from ordinary adaptation because it concerns the transformation of the organization through which future responses become possible. Meta-capacity designates the preservation and regeneration of conditions through which further capacities can emerge. The argument engages Aristotle, Kant, Heidegger, Whitehead, Simondon, Dewey, Jonas, Levinas, and Nussbaum. These traditions provide important resources for understanding potentiality, …

items.title: The Ontology of Refusal, Saying No as a Mechanism of Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: This article develops an ontological account of refusal within the philosophical framework of Finite Continuance. It argues that saying no can be understood as a structurally significant operation through which a finite being regulates constitutive exchange and preserves its future capacity for reconfiguration. Refusal is commonly interpreted through ethical, political, psychological, or juridical categories such as autonomy, resistance, consent, opposition, withdrawal, or self-assertion. The present account locates refusal at a more fundamental level. A finite being exists through continuous exchange with its environment, while the same exchange can progressively diminish the capacities required for further transformation. Refusal therefore acquires ontological significance when it interrupts a mode of exchange whose continuation would reduce the subject’s capacity to reorganize itself. The article develops five connected claims. First, constitutive exchange is a condition of finite existence and therefore cannot simply be eliminated. Second, constitutive exchange possesses an erosive dimension because every finite relation can consume time, attention, energy, affective resources, interpretive capacity, institutional access, or future possibilities. Third, refusal regulates this exchange by establishing a limit upon what may enter, leave, demand, occupy, or determine a finite system. Fourth, the value of refusal depends upon its effect on reconfigurative capacity. Refusal becomes philosophically significant when it preserves the possibility of future transformation. Fifth, refusal has an ethical and political dimension because institutions and social systems can systematically appropriate the capacity to refuse. The article distinguishes ontological refusal from avoidance, rigidity, domination, selfishness, and simple negation. It also examines the relation between refusal and Heideggerian finitude, Sartrean freedom, Levinasian responsibility, Simondonian individuation, Whiteheadian process, Foucauldian power, and contemporary accounts of autonomy and capability. The resulting conception defines refusal as a regulated limitation of constitutive exchange undertaken for the preservation of future reconfigurative capacity. Refusal thereby becomes a mechanism of finite continuance and a central component of an Ethics of Sufficiency. Keywords: Finite Continuance, refusal, refusal capacity, constitutive exchange, erosion, reconfiguration, future agency, …

items.title: Relational Experientialism.
items.abstract: Experientialism is a family of philosophical theories of well-being that tie well-being to experiencing certain positively charged experiences. Experientialism has fallen out of favor today because of Robert Nozick’s experience machine objection. According to this objection, experientialism must allow that there is no difference between living well in reality and living well in a plausible computer simulation, because the experiences would be identical in both cases. This article proposes a theory that avoids this objection: relational experientialism. According to this position, well-being is experiencing certain positively charged experiences, but only when those experiences are caused by the realization of some genuine objective good. This version of experientialism avoids the experience machine objection and also has a number of explanatory advantages over the dominant theory of well-being today: naturalistic perfectionism. In particular, relational experientialism does a better job of explaining the nature of the motivation to pursue objective goods, as well as the asymmetry between conscious and unconscious entities. It also does a better job of addressing the challenge of the “flourishing anhedone” – a person who realizes genuine goods in their life but has no positive experiences at all. Such a person’s life, despite the presence of objective goods, is hardly a happy one, but only relational experientialism can explain why this is so. In addition, relational experientialism is most consistent with relationism about phenomenal consciousness. This is the view that the phenomenal character of experience is constituted by the relational properties of external objects, and that the experience of real perceptions is therefore phenomenally distinct from the experience of illusions and hallucinations. All of these considerations suggest that relational experientialism is, at least as a first approximation, a plausible theory of well-being.

items.title: Our Teleological Selves.
K. E. Løgstrup’s second-personal phenomenology of social life.
items.abstract: K. E. Løgstrup’s work remains largely absent from phenomenological research about sociality. The aim of this paper is to rectify this neglect by articulating and situating Løgstrup’s work on this topic in a phenomenological context. After clarifying Løgstrup’s credentials as a phenomenologist, I argue that one of his central contributions is the development of a second- personal phenomenology of social life, in which communicative trust—trust as involved in paradigmatic communicative exchanges between a speaker and an interlocutor—constitutes the bedrock of the social world. I go on to argue that as distinguished from two major phenomenological approaches to the foundations of sociality—the Husserlian and Heideggerian approaches—Løgstrup’s approach doesn’t prioritise the experiential asymmetry between self and other, nor an impersonal and anonymous way of being with each other, but rather the spontaneous trust towards one another that we take for granted in paradigmatic communicative or—as I also call them—second-personal interactions.

items.title: John Grote and the Promise of “Knowledge of Acquaintance”.
items.pub: In Arnaud Dewalque, Bruno Leclercq, Valentina Martinis, Jacopo Pallagrosi & Denis Seron, The Cambridge Family: British Philosophy of Mind at the Turn of the Twentieth Century. Routledge.
items.venue: The Cambridge Family: British Philosophy of Mind at the Turn of the Twentieth Century
items.abstract: The notion of knowledge by acquaintance is associated primarily with Bertrand Russell. Interestingly, however, it is anticipated in the mid-19th-century by the philosopher John Grote’s distinction between “knowledge of acquaintance” and “knowledge of judgment.” Here I argue that Grote’s notion is actually superior to Russell’s in avoiding certain philosophical difficulties that afflict the latter, especially as concerns the alleged total passivity of knowledge-by-acquaintance and the claim that we enjoy knowledge-by-acquaintance of universals.

items.title: A History of Consciousness — From the Voices of the Gods to the Emergence of the “I,” and on to AI.
items.abstract: “If people 3,000 years ago did not have consciousness like ours today, how did they think?” This paper began with a conversation with a friend. Julian Jaynes’s theory does more than propose the provocative hypothesis that ancient people did not possess consciousness in the same form that we do today; it also forces us to reconsider what we mean by the word “consciousness,” which we use so casually. Here, “consciousness” does not simply mean being awake, or having the capacity to see and feel. What concerned Jaynes was an inward form of consciousness in which we possess a point of view—an “I”—within the mind, mentally traverse the past and future, and reflect on ourselves. This paper first considers the relationship between what appears in consciousness and the nonconscious processes operating behind it, using concepts such as Jaynes’s bicameral mind, mind-space, and the analog “I.” In the second half, I extend the questions raised by Jaynes and consider, through five aspects—subjectivity, time, causality, possibility, and meaning—how the emergence of this inward form of consciousness allows the world to be experienced as “my world.” These five aspects are not intended as a summary of Jaynes’s theory itself. Rather, they are an attempt, starting from his ideas, to explore in my own way the workings and possibilities of consciousness. Finally, I ask whether human consciousness in its present form was an inevitable outcome of evolution, or merely one of several possible forms of cognition, and consider the possibility that AI may one day develop toward a form of consciousness different from our own.

items.title: Relational Positions in Volunteer Aid: A Preliminary Psychoanalytic Formalization.
items.abstract: This paper develops a preliminary psychoanalytic formalization of relational positioning in volunteer, aid, and support relations within Generative Relational Theory (GR). It studies how participants may encounter concrete historical subjects through expectation-laden positions that organize functions, anticipated continuations, confirmation conditions, frustration conditions, and revision routes. Papers I–III already provide the historical-relational substrate: tracked subjects, support roles, self-reconstruction, recognition, path dependence, provenance, and subject co-formation. Paper IV adds a separate claim-grade architecture for increasingly theory-dependent interpretation. It distinguishes manifest aid events, participant reconstructions, relational-position inferences, source-specific psychoanalytic structural hypotheses, dynamic-contribution attributions, and comparatively demanding attributions of unconscious contribution. The framework separates support-relevant need from relational address, desire hypotheses from ordinary requests, relational tension from psychoanalytic lack, recurrence from psychoanalytic repetition, and the concrete other from the function assigned within a relational position. Disconfirmation events—including refusal, independent success, transfer, altered need, and loss of expected recognition—provide comparative evidence about position revision, position-restorative pressure, and the incremental explanatory contribution of stronger hypotheses. Freudian, Lacanian, relational, intersubjective, and object-relational resources enter as source-specific interpretive interfaces under ontological suspension and competing-explanation discipline. The resulting architecture supports analysis of helper identification, rescue configurations, recognition mismatch, separation, alterity tolerance, coupled positioning, institutional reinforcement, rupture, and later reorganization while preserving material, institutional, normative, interpersonal, and historical explanations as independently typed contributors.

items.title: Ethics of Aid, Volunteering, and Support under Heterogeneous Subject Conditions: Subjectivity Uncertainty, Recognition, and Revisable Assistance.
items.abstract: Ethical assistance is often discussed as if the identity, interests, communicative capacities, and moral standing of the recipient were sufficiently settled before practical deliberation begins. Cases involving heterogeneous subjects weaken that assumption. Human beings with atypical communicative access, nonhuman animals, artificial systems, and hypothetical alien subjects may present different evidence of adversity, different forms of agency, and different grounds for moral considerability. Building on a prior Generative Relational account of support-relevant recognition, this paper develops a preliminary ethics of aid, volunteering, and support under such uncertainty. Its central proposal is that ethical assessment should preserve the provenance of recognition, distinguish uncertainty about adverse states from uncertainty about moral status and normative theory, and evaluate assistance through typed constraints on benefit, harm, communicative engagement, autonomy, dependency, helper burden, third-party effects, and revisability. The framework treats revisable assistance as a design property of ethical response under incomplete knowledge: interventions should, where the relevant reasons support it, remain monitorable, contestable, corrigible, and capable of responsible withdrawal or repair. Human, animal, artificial, and hypothetical alien cases function as heterogeneous stress tests across different evidential, agential, communicative, and relational conditions. The paper remains within normative ethics; humanitarian doctrine, legal standing, adjudicative authority, and institutional responsibility are reserved for subsequent work.

items.title: Entangling humans and AI.
Studies in the Philosophy of Language (4): Contextual Super-Existence and Indirect Speech Acts.
items.abstract: Face-to-face linguistic communication is not a closed process consisting solely of an Expressor, a Receiver, and linguistic content. Every actual communicative exchange takes place within a particular environment, which directly affects the meaning and appropriateness of linguistic expressions as well as the Receiver's understanding of what is expressed. Accordingly, in addition to the various forms of Super-Existence associated with the Expressor and the Receiver individually, linguistic communication involves a form of Super-Existence relevant to both participants. This chapter calls it Contextual Super-Existence, which may also be termed Situational Super-Existence when emphasis is placed on the concrete circumstances of an interaction. This chapter first examines the fundamental role of Contextual Super-Existence in linguistic communication, arguing that the appropriateness of an expression cannot be determined independently of the particular situation in which it occurs. The same sentence may have entirely different degrees of appropriateness, and even different practical meanings, in different situations. Drawing on John Searle's theory of indirect speech acts, the chapter then analyzes the relationship between an Expressor's literal utterance, underlying intention, and Purpose Super-Existence, using the example “It's very cold.” It further argues that whether the Receiver acts in accordance with the Expressor's actual intention depends not only on the Receiver's understanding of the linguistic content but also on Contextual Super-Existence, including the participants' current activities, their relationship, the physical environment, and other relevant background conditions. The chapter thus seeks to demonstrate that linguistic meaning does not reside entirely within linguistic expressions themselves. Rather, meaning emerges from the dynamic relations among the Expressor, the linguistic expression, the Receiver, and Contextual Super-Existence.

items.title: Visible Seams: Why Provenance in Human-AI Work Is More Than a Credit Statement.
items.abstract: Human–AI work is increasingly common in writing, design, research, programming, conceptual development, and reflective practice. Yet its public description often remains imprecise. AI involvement is either concealed or marked by broad phrases such as “AI-assisted,” “created with AI,” or “AI-supported.” Such phrases may be better than silence, but they often fail to identify the role the system actually played: language correction, structural assistance, conceptual clarification, counterargument, formulation, or sustained dialogical development. This paper argues that the distinction matters. Not every use of an AI system creates authorship or co-authorship. Spell-checking, formatting, simple paraphrasing, and superficial variation do not normally amount to substantive epistemic participation. However, when an AI system materially shapes the direction, structure, concepts, objections, or central formulations of a thought, the result is no longer adequately described as isolated human work. In such cases, the relevant unit for provenance may be the coupled process through which the result emerged. The central claim is that visible seams are not merely a matter of politeness, fairness, or technical disclosure. They are part of epistemic traceability. Provenance is not decoration around a finished result; it is information about how that result became possible. The paper also identifies a social tension: transparency about AI involvement is increasingly demanded, while such transparency may be socially, institutionally, or professionally penalized. This disclosure penalty creates incentives to hide or flatten AI participation, thereby worsening provenance and undermining trust. The paper proposes a vocabulary that separates disclosure, provenance, epistemic participation, and formal authorship without collapsing them into one another.

items.title: When Do the Operational Conditions of Non-Closure Collapse？ Twenty-First-Century Schwärmerei, DMT, AI, Population-Scale Penetration, and the Loss of Alternative Access to Reality-as-a-Whole.
items.abstract: Epistemic Non-Closure denies that the success, reproducibility, or institutional dominance of a local access configuration establishes its identity with reality-as-a-whole. Yet locally successful configurations can reorganize the apparatus, variables, boundaries, scales, temporal windows, external memory, institutional authority, and resources through which subsequent access becomes possible. -/- This paper investigates when such transformations disable particular operations through which Non-Closure would otherwise have consequential effects. It distinguishes three forms of operational failure: the loss of a specific capacity for discrimination or intervention, the loss of the ability to detect that loss, and the failure of epistemic constraints to affect subsequent observation, evaluation, resource allocation, or reconfiguration. -/- Kant’s confrontation with Schwärmerei and contemporary DMT-related metaphysical attributions provide historically distinct cases for examining how claims to privileged access can acquire practical consequences without acquiring epistemic entitlement. The analysis connects Sellars and Brassier’s scientific realism with measurement epistemology, scientific pluralism, institutional epistemology, and contemporary autonomous science. -/- The central conclusion is conditional: Non-Closure itself does not collapse. What may collapse are configuration-dependent operational routes through which its epistemic constraint would otherwise influence subsequent inquiry and material reconfiguration. Earlier computational investigations are retained as exploratory rather than confirmatory evidence. The paper develops a self-critical extension of Thing-in-Itself Engineering without claiming to establish a new universal theory or to demonstrate population-scale epistemic closure.

items.title: The Operational Shape of Brassierian Scientific Realism and Its Conditions of Transformatio Scientific Paradigm Transitions, Xenoscientific Operational Shapes, the Stellarization of Scientific Operational Shapes, and the Non-Privilege of Epistemic Progress.
items.abstract: This article critically reconstructs Ray Brassier’s scientific realism by distinguishing the epistemic conditions of warranted knowledge from the material and operational configurations through which scientific inquiry becomes possible. Rather than claiming that nonconceptual causal operations refute conceptual mediation, it examines how the conditions enabling observation, experimentation, rational revision, and scientific-image construction arise, persist, transform, become unavailable, or are reactivated. -/- Through engagements with Sellars, Brandom, Kant, Hegel, Kuhn, and contemporary philosophy of science, the paper examines the nonidentity and possible causal coupling of conceptual justification, experimental implementation, historical retention, and downstream physical effects. It develops an operational account of scientific paradigm transitions without treating paradigms as universal prerequisites for scientific change or equating successful intervention with epistemic entitlement. -/- The stellarization of scientific operational shapes is introduced as a conditional research proposal concerning heterogeneous scientific operations capable of retaining, transferring, interrupting, and reactivating experimental capacities across changing configurations. Comparisons with active inference, constructor theory, autonomous laboratories, and contemporary AI-for-science research delimit the proposal’s explanatory scope. -/- Previously executed synthetic experiments, including a separate 12,000-world comparison of changing correction conditions, are evaluated as exploratory computational evidence rather than tests of Brassier’s epistemological necessity. The paper does not claim to refute conceptual mediation or establish a new scientific law. Its contribution lies in clarifying the conditions under which epistemic qualification, operational feasibility, historical transmission, and consequential scientific intervention become coupled, separated, or reorganized.

items.title: Transcendental Operational-Shape Metaphysics The Generation, Transformation, and Dissolution of Conditions of Possibility.
items.abstract: This paper develops Transcendental Operational-Shape Metaphysics as a general philosophical framework for investigating the generation, transformation, maintenance, and dissolution of conditions of possibility. Rather than presupposing transcendental conditions as invariant structures, it examines how operational configurations enable, discriminate, retain, transform, and reorganize subsequent possibilities across different scales, temporal horizons, boundaries, and media. -/- The framework distinguishes enabling conditions, discriminative conditions, and validity conditions without reducing transcendental questions to empirical changes in scientific instruments. It develops Operational-Shape Realism, Operational-Shape Naturalism, Non-Closure Realism, and Xenoscientific Realism as interconnected but non-identical philosophical positions. -/- Through critical engagement with Kant, Hegel, Sellars, Brandom, Brassier, Simondon, Hacking, and Rheinberger, the paper situates operational-shape analysis within existing debates concerning transcendental conditions, scientific realism, conceptual mediation, and historical transformations of scientific practice. -/- The framework is further developed through Xenoscience, the Ziran System, Thing-in-Itself Engineering, autonomous physics, embodied operational configurations, life and death, institutional transformations, and formal identification systems. Computational findings from Ziran Runtime are discussed as bounded evidence of configuration-dependent operational differences, without treating them as direct demonstrations of transcendental transformation. -/- The central proposal is that conditions of possibility should themselves be investigated as historically and materially reconfigurable operational formations, while no locally constituted description is identified with reality-as-a-whole.

items.title: Post-Active-Inference Experimentally Delimiting the Operational Conditions of Active-Inference Representations Across Worlds, Tasks, Memory Regimes, Hysteresis, and Structural Capacity.
items.abstract: Active Inference provides a powerful formal framework for inference, action, and adaptation under a generative model. This paper asks a different question: under what operational conditions do the primitives through which an Active-Inference system is described—agent, boundary, observation, variable, model, prediction error, and policy—remain stable, become non-redundant, enter transition, or cease to provide an adequate description? -/- We develop Post-Active-Inference not as a successor controller, but as an experimental program for making those conditions themselves measurable. In Phase 1, a preregistered confirmatory simulation study comprising 55,680 runs across 30 fresh seeds found that Active Inference remained a strong controller throughout much of the tested space, while reproducible transitions in representational validity were concentrated primarily in observation and action-interface perturbations rather than world-side topology, coupling, memory, or structural perturbations. Operational tracking did not generally outperform Active Inference, and several development-stage effects failed to replicate, including a proposed dissociation between representational failure and preserved control advantage. -/- Phase 2 extends the analysis across multiple world families, graph realizations, tasks, a finite Bayesian structure-learning Active-Inference comparator, memory-retention regimes, continuous perturbation paths, and structural-capacity measures. Structure learning did not uniformly dominate adaptive Active Inference and could retain high model confidence under complete observational failure. History re-entry was negligible under rapidly decaying memory but became non-redundant under long-memory conditions in development experiments. A preregistered hysteresis effect reproduced directionally but failed its predefined practical-effect threshold. By contrast, structural-capacity experiments confirmed that binary reachability can remain almost unchanged while effective accessibility is substantially reorganized: target-region inbound edge capacity and inbound weight fell by approximately one half while mean path distance increased. -/- The results do not falsify Active Inference and do not establish a universally superior alternative. They instead support a methodological shift: the operational conditions under which Active-Inference primitives become valid, unstable, transitional, or dispensable can themselves be experimentally investigated. More …

items.title: Herr Hegel: Laying Bare the Operations of Hegelian Philosophy What Remains When Philosophical Operations Cease to Be a Necessary Passage Point? Operational Shapes, Inferential Necessity, Systematicity, the Generation, Transformation, and Dissolution of Conditions of Possibility, Scientific Reality, Reality-as-a-Whole, Xenoscience, and Philosophical Self-Obsolescence.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs Hegelian philosophy as a historically situated set of operations rather than a self-evidently universal conceptual system. It examines the internal transitions of the Phenomenology of Spirit, Science of Logic, Philosophy of Nature, Philosophy of Spirit, and Philosophy of Right, asking what their inferential and systematic constraints actually establish and how these constraints are retained, transformed, or rendered inoperative in subsequent philosophical, scientific, and institutional practices. -/- The analysis distinguishes conceptual necessity from physical causation, historical transmission, institutional validity, and experimental implementation. It critically engages Sellars, Brandom, Brassier, Wolfendale, and Nick Land without reducing their contributions to contemporary translations of Hegel. -/- Drawing on Operational-Shape Realism, Operational-Shape Naturalism, Non-Closure Realism, Xenoscientific Realism, and Transcendental Operational-Shape Metaphysics, the paper investigates how conditions of possibility are generated, transformed, and dissolved through actual operations. Particular attention is given to the retrospective emergence of freedom, the operational conditions of ethical distinctions, the temporal constraints of rational correction, and the transformation of scientific observability. -/- The central question is what remains of Hegel when philosophical operations cease to function as necessary passage points. The paper argues that the disappearance of philosophical mediation in a particular operation does not entail the disappearance of inferential constraints, institutional validity, or conceptual reconstruction. Hegelian operations may persist, change their medium, become functionally redundant, or cease to operate under different conditions. -/- The result is a differentiated reconstruction of Hegelian philosophy that neither presupposes its universal necessity nor declares its historical obsolescence.

items.title: When algorithms cannot be fair: constitutive and contingent discrimination and the limits of less-discriminatory alternatives.
items.abstract: The literature on algorithmic fairness has concentrated on the choice amongst fairness metrics, a choice constrained by well-known impossibility results (Chouldechova 2017; Kleinberg et al. 2017). This paper argues that a prior question deserves equal attention: how the categories, variables, and objective functions that constitute an algorithmic system’s representation of its domain are chosen, and when those choices themselves discriminate? We propose a criterion for distinguishing two kinds of algorithmic discrimination. A disparity is contingent, relative to a legitimate purpose and a class of admissible designs, when an alternative design within that class serves the purpose whilst reducing the disparity; it is constitutive, relative to the same parameters, when no such alternative is available. Because contingency is an existential claim and constitutivity a negative existential over a class of designs, the two carry asymmetric obligations: contingency is shown by exhibit, constitutivity by documented exhaustion, and neither is discharged by assertion. Every constitutivity claim therefore states in advance the exhibit that would refute it, which is what makes the distinction actionable in design review, audit, and litigation rather than merely classificatory. The criterion adapts the comparative logic of the less-discriminatory alternative from disparate-impact doctrine (Laufer et al. 2025) and shifts it from the level of models and outcomes to the level of representational choices, whose distinctive rigidity we analyse through the notion of open texture (Waismann 1945; Hart 1961): computational systems fix ex ante the precisifications that human decision-makers perform case by case. Three case studies (the ImageNet person categories, tokeniser-level disparities in large language models, and automated hiring together with clinical risk scoring) are used to test, not merely to illustrate, the criterion. We conclude by proposing ontological auditing, an upstream evaluation of representational choices articulated through an Ontological Impact Statement, and by locating it within the risk management and data governance provisions of the EU AI Act.

items.title: Agency and Consciousness.
items.abstract: Agency and Consciousness proposes a functional architecture of agency and consciousness. It argues that both are emergent architectures that appear when sufficiently complex systems integrate resilient memory, limited perception, internal simulation, and self-modeling. -/- Memory is not an archive of the past but the present physical state of a system shaped by prior interactions. Perception does not capture reality in full but only the fraction accessible to the agent's architecture. On that incomplete information, the system builds approximate simulations of its environment and of itself through what this work calls intelligent bias. Consciousness appears when the system incorporates its own state within its internal simulation, and subjective experience is presented as a consequence of a structural asymmetry between internal modeling and external observation. -/- The work introduces a partition between architectural dominance and the zone of functional indifference: when the evaluation differential between trajectories exceeds the system's basal noise, the decision belongs to the architecture; when it does not, the resolution is contingent. Agency resides in the strategy; the openness of the future, in the execution. -/- The position defended is relational: agency is not a property exclusive to the universe nor to the agent, but a property that emerges when a sufficiently complex architecture operates on a sufficiently stratified ontology. The work builds on the three-level architecture developed in Destiny and Will and engages with Metzinger's self-model theory, Friston and Clark's predictive processing, and simulation theory in philosophy of mind. It does not aim to resolve the strong phenomenological problem of subjective experience; its objective is more limited: to describe the minimal architectural conditions compatible with the existence of real agency and functional forms of consciousness. -/- This entry includes the English version and its Spanish original.

items.title: Between Rational Reconstruction and Explication: Carnap’s method of translation in the Syntax.
items.pub: British Journal for the History of Philosophy.
items.venue: British Journal for the History of Philosophy
items.abstract: This paper reexamines the standard view of Carnap’s methodological development, according to which the period surrounding the writing of the Logical Syntax of Language is regarded as a mere transitional period between rational reconstruction and explication. I argue that Carnap, in the Syntax, employs a distinct and coherent “method of translation”, a specific kind of transformative analysis that differs from both rational reconstruction and explication. To clarify the differences between these methods, I distinguish three forms of metaphilosophical pluralism that transformative analyses can permit: input-pluralism, output-pluralism, and operation-pluralism. Carnap’s method of translation allows the first two but not the third—philosophers enjoy radical freedom in choosing frameworks and translations, yet must satisfy what I call the ”translation norm”: the requirement to translate philosophical theses into formal language to remain legitimate discussants. I show how this combination of pluralism and normative constraint makes this method fully consistent with the principle of tolerance and distinguishes it from both rational reconstruction and explication. Recognizing the metaphilosophical significance of this intermediate phase reshapes our understanding of Carnap’s philosophical trajectory and raises new questions about his later turn to explication.

items.title: Attention and the Relevance Problem.
items.abstract: The relevance problem is the problem of how cognitive systems can be sensitive to what is relevant despite relevance being holistic, open-ended, and context-sensitive. The problem has typically been applied to higher-order cognitive processes. In this paper, I argue that there is a hitherto unrecognized relevance problem for perceptual attention. This problem becomes apparent when considering the functions of attention: attention must not only support ongoing task performance but also remain sensitive to opportunities for task switching, latent learning, and context checking. Existing treatments of the relevance problem have largely focused on its task-relative form: given a task, what is relevant? I argue that attention faces a more general problem that includes sensitivity to factors relevant to other interests and to cues indicating that another activity may be worth pursuing. For such features of the environment to stand out as salient, salience cannot be determined solely by bottom-up factors and a limited set of occurrent top-down factors, such as current goals and intentions. Rather, it must reflect the wider (if not the entire) range of an agent's latent interests in a context-sensitive way. This motivational unencapsulation of attention poses a challenge for both contemporary accounts of attention and suggests that passive attention is much more intelligent than commonly thought. -/- .

items.title: Generic stereotypes: Negotiating content and assertability.
items.pub: In Laure Gardelle & Naomi Truan, From cognition to language and back: A cross-disciplinary perspective on generics and stereotypes. De Gruyter Mouton.
items.venue: From cognition to language and back: A cross-disciplinary perspective on generics and stereotypes
items.abstract: Generic stereotypes are resistant to challenge. We argue against the standard explanation from Langton, Haslanger and Anderson (2012) on which this resistance stems from the speaker’s ability to shift between two different interpretations of a generic. Instead, we argue that generics standardly express a single complex content that combines both interpretations, and their resistance to challenge stems from two kinds of metalinguistic negotiability: negotiability of content and negotiability of epistemic and ethical assertability. Finally, we examine some insidious and beneficial effects of this negotiability.

items.title: Cognition as Operator Architecture: Conscious Integration, Subconscious Generativity, and the Derivation of Option Sets.
items.abstract: This paper presents a mechanistic account of cognition as an operator architecture. Subconscious operators generate predictions, impulses, interpretations, and candidate actions, forming the organism’s option set—the structured manifold of possibilities available at any moment. Consciousness functions as the global integrator, evaluating, endorsing, inhibiting, and sequencing operator outputs. Development expands the option set through structural feedback, while collapse contracts it through distorted pacing, synthetic feedback, and operator interruption. The framework unifies subconscious generativity, conscious integration, manifold structure, and environmental pacing into a single architecture of agency.

items.title: Phenomenal Conservatism as Epistemology of Logic: A Defence Against the Obscurity Objection.
items.abstract: This paper defends phenomenal conservatism as an epistemology of logic (‘PC-Logic’), according to which basic logical beliefs are prima facie justified when they seem obvious to us. A central challenge—the ‘obscurity objection’—holds that PC-Logic offers a mysterious or unintelligible account of such justification. I examine leading versions of this objection and contend that each fails. In particular, I argue that logical seemings are no more obscure than other justificatory appearances and that evolutionary considerations can demystify the reliability of logical seemings.

items.title: Thinking with Objects. Understanding Non-Representational Cognitive Artifacts.
items.abstract: This paper defends the notion of cognitive artifacts that do not serve representational functions. Contrary to the standard account of cognitive artifacts as representational, we argue that it is possible to distinguish a special class of artifacts that fulfill cognitive roles without performing representational functions. With reference to cognitive semiotics, we respond to Fasoli’s critique of ecological cognitive artifacts, which were defined as non-representational by Heersmink. First, cognitive semiotics identifies key features of the representational relation. This relation arises through interactions between the object and the user. It requires the user to appreciate the duality between expression and content. Second, cognitive semiotics distinguishes between reality and pictorial modes of experiencing artifacts. We apply this framework to explore what happens when an artifact is experienced in reality mode: situations in which its representational function is disregarded by the user, or in which the artifact has no representational function to begin with. Based on three examples from the literature (file structure visualization, hotel key weight, and intelligent use of space), we propose a class of cognitive artifacts that can be meaningful in a technical sense with respect to users’ cognitive goals and needs, even if the artifacts are not carriers of representations or their representational functions are not recognized as such.

items.title: Null Monism : Why Qualia Arise from Nothing.
items.abstract: A persistent intuition that motivates panpsychism — thereby generating the combination problem — holds that parts lacking experience cannot combine to produce a whole that has it. We argue that this intuition rests on an unexamined assumption: that phenomenological contents compose by a null-preserving operation. We show that any composition rule adequate to preserve the structural sensitivity of experience generates non-null composites from null parts. Qualitative character turns out to be nesting topology — forced by the formalism, not assumed. An argument from physical anchoring connects the set-theoretic result to the physical world, revealing that nesting topology is causal topology, and showing that wherever causal organisation closes into an irreducible whole, qualia become a logical necessity. In the discussion we draw out what follows once the null-preservation assumption is dropped, for panpsychism and the explanatory gap. Crucially, the argument begins from the methodological assumption that elementary parts carry no phenomenological content — which means panpsychism is not required.

items.title: Persistent State and Becoming. When Memory Becomes Operational History. A5.
items.abstract: An AI system can keep records for months and still have no usable past. It may retrieve the right sentences yet fail to know what was revoked, what failed, what was later verified, or why the present state differs from an earlier one. I ask where that boundary lies. I distinguish five layers: archive, context, persistent state, operational history, and becoming. My claim is narrow: records become operational history when relations among events—including order, supersession, verified outcome, and provenance—change what the deployed system should do now. I turn that claim into a representation-adequacy test and a counterfactual pre/post-state test for a limited form of system-level becoming. The latter requires a durable, attributable change in later behavior; it does not require model-weight updates and does not imply consciousness or numerical identity. I place the account within recent work on long-term agent memory, use a publication workflow to show how identical surviving records can encode different practical pasts, and specify a controlled M1–M4 evaluation with relational ablations. I do not report a benchmark result. What I am trying to sharpen is the difference between record survival, continuity of work, and adaptation caused by retained experience.

items.title: The Living Corpus and the Rosarian Rite of Sacred Structure.
items.pub: Mystical Dawnist Rosarian Knight and Dame Fellowship.
items.abstract: THE LIVING CORPUS AND THE ROSARIAN RITE OF SACRED STRUCTURE Published by the Dawnist Rosarian Wolves, First Table of the Mystical Dawnist Rosarian Knight & Dame Fellowship, beneath the Grand Table — Mensa Rotunda Sub Rosa, upon Via Solis Sub Rosa — The Way of the Sun Beneath the Rose. The Rosarian Articles constitute a living body of Rosarian composition arising from The Knight Manifesto: A Rosarian Compendium and continuing through interpretation, clarification, symbolism, terminology, philosophy, Fellowship, Table structure, ceremony, custodianship, and lived practice. The Twenty-Two Articles remain the Twenty-Two Articles. They constitute the completed composition of the first established series of Rosarian Articles and remain the foundational composed body through which the Rosarian vocabulary, principles, symbols, Laws, Fellowship, Tables, ceremonies, and custodial responsibilities were brought into correspondence. Article XXII completed that particular composition; it did not declare the Rosarian Way itself complete or prohibit further Rosarian writing, interpretation, or development. The distinction is therefore established between the completed Twenty-Two and the continuing Rosarian corpus. A work arising after the Twenty-Two is not Article XXIII or a numerical continuation of the Twenty-Two. It may nevertheless be a Rosarian Article when it develops, clarifies, interprets, organizes, or establishes a faithful expression of the Way while remaining accountable to what has already been established. The number twenty-two identifies the completed composition and is not an assigned numerical limit upon the living corpus. Later Rosarian Articles therefore do not replace the Twenty-Two, amend them merely by being later, or compete with them for precedence. They continue the process already demonstrated throughout the Rosarian corpus: foundation becoming interpretation, interpretation becoming structure, structure becoming practice, and practice becoming further understanding. The foundation remains the foundation, the Twenty-Two remain the Twenty-Two, later works remain Rosarian Articles, and the Way remains open. This Article is therefore a Rosarian Article in its own right and is published by the Dawnist Rosarian Wolves as the First Table of the Mystical Dawnist Rosarian Knight & Dame Fellowship. The First Table does not constitute a superior institution within the Fellowship. Its precedence is historical and custodial. The Dawnist Rosarian Wolves are …

items.title: THE FOURFOLD ROSARIAN STATION.
items.pub: Mystical Dawnist Rosarian Knight and Dame Fellowship.
items.abstract: THE FOURFOLD ROSARIAN STATION -/- The Fourfold Rosarian Station establishes four functions by which the Rosarian may understand and practice responsibility within the Way: Shepherd, Steward, Student, and Servant. These are not ranks, degrees, offices, or measures of spiritual worth. They describe distinct responsibilities already present within the Rosarian life: guidance, custodianship, learning, and service. The distinction between them is functional rather than hierarchical, and no function places one person above another. The Rosarian remains accountable to the Path, to the Fellowship, to the work entrusted to them, and to the principle of service. The Shepherd represents the function of responsible guidance. This function corresponds to the already established responsibilities of the leader as mentor, protector, facilitator, and companion. The Shepherd helps maintain the conditions in which Fellowship, study, inquiry, conversation, mentorship, and practice can continue with integrity. The Shepherd guides without domination, protects without possessing, facilitates without controlling, and accompanies without creating dependency. The Shepherd does not stand between the seeker and the Divine, does not claim ownership over another person's Path, and does not use responsibility as a means of personal elevation. The function is therefore measured by the ability to preserve the conditions in which others may walk their own Path with dignity, courage, responsibility, and conscious participation. The Steward represents the function of custodianship. The Steward receives what has been entrusted and is responsible for its preservation, protection, continuity, and proper use. This includes the preservation of the literature, the teachings, the integrity of the Fellowship, the continuity of established structures, and the responsibilities placed into the Steward's care. The Steward does not become the proprietor of what is entrusted. Custodianship does not create ownership, superiority, or permanent authority. The Steward carries responsibility on behalf of the work and remains accountable to the principles that the work serves. A responsibility may be entrusted to another when the work requires it, and the completion of one responsibility does not establish permanent elevation over those who perform another function. The Student represents the function of continued learning. The Rosarian remains an Eternal Student because learning, practice, reflection, …

items.title: Conceptual Sandboxes: A Proposal for Experimental Lawmaking.
items.abstract: Multi-stakeholder drafting of laws and regulations is praised for bringing diverse perspectives into the drafting process. However, it frequently leaves the meaning and implications of key legal concepts insufficiently specified, and not as a deliberate use of vagueness. Drawing on the EU AI Act’s Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment regime and the US Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, we illustrate how multi-stakeholder drafting can defer conceptual choices, creating costs for the interpretation and implementation of law. We propose a new experimental method, inspired by regulatory sandboxes, to address this problem before laws or regulations are enacted: conceptual sandboxes. A conceptual sandbox is a pre-codification controlled environment where lawmakers and stakeholders test and compare candidate concepts alongside the norms and institutional arrangements by which they operate. Combining conceptual engineering with methods from software and requirements engineering, we specify a six-phase protocol that maps contested concepts, predicts the effects of enacting them, stress-tests those predictions, compares alternatives, re-engineers the concept, and audits the result after enactment. A counterfactual application of the original Article 27 of the AI Act illustrates how the protocol can expose weaknesses in legal design before enactment.

items.title: The Ontology of Priority Importance, Comparative Significance, and the Problem of the More Important.
items.abstract: The distinction between what is important and what is more important structures practical reasoning, ethical judgment, institutional decision-making, and political organization. Philosophical analysis has developed extensive theories of value, reasons, comparability, incommensurability, and practical rationality. The ontological structure of priority itself remains less explicitly differentiated. This article develops a theory of priority by distinguishing four logically related operations: importance, comparative importance, priority, and meta-priority. Importance concerns the relation between an entity or condition and the future possibilities of a field. Comparative importance concerns differences in structural consequence among important elements. Priority concerns the allocation of finite practical capacity when important possibilities compete for precedence. Meta-priority concerns the authority of the criteria through which such precedence is established. The argument engages Ruth Chang’s account of parity, Joseph Raz’s analysis of value incommensurability, T. M. Scanlon’s account of reasons, and Norman Daniels’s procedural theory of fair priority-setting. These approaches illuminate important dimensions of practical evaluation. The present theory addresses a more specific question concerning the transition from normative relevance to practical precedence under conditions of finite capacity, temporal pressure, and changing future conditions. Urgency is treated as a temporally structured dimension of potential loss rather than as a synonym for importance. The Eisenhower Matrix is examined as a practical representation of the distinction between importance and urgency. The article then develops the concept of meta-capacity, defined as a field’s capacity to examine, contest, and revise the criteria through which its priorities are established. The Principle of Reflexive Priority follows from a seven-step argument showing that a priority structure can alter the future conditions under which its own adequacy is assessed. The Principle of Provisional Priority further holds that finite priority structures should remain sufficiently stable for action while preserving sufficient capacity for future evaluation and revision. The political analysis develops the concept of priority closure, in which preservation of a dominant priority progressively contracts the capacity to question that priority. The resulting framework distinguishes persistence from adequacy …

items.title: Doxastic Attitudes and the Appreciation of Art across Cultures.
items.abstract: This article begins with a claim that has come to enjoy widespread acceptance amongst philosophers of art, and it explores some of its unappreciated implications for thinking about the experience (by which I mostly mean perceptual experience) and appreciation of artworks of other cultures. The claim is two-fold: (1) knowledge of an artwork’s original or generative context affects our experience of it, and (2) appreciation of an artwork requires knowledge of facts about this context. Over the last few decades, this view has been defended under the banner of ‘contextualism’ in the philosophy of art. -/- This article makes a case for an expanded contextualism by arguing that other sorts of broadly cultural aspects of artworks’ generative contexts are among their constitutive properties, affect perceptual experiences of them, and bear upon their appreciation. In particular, I will argue that various doxastic attitudes, notably religious and spiritual beliefs, that are widely held within the cultural context of an artwork’s creation may constitute essential, relational features of the work and affect how cultural insiders experience a given work. Furthermore, I argue that the cognitive content that is necessary for the perception of the work’s aesthetic features and its appreciation may extend beyond knowledge (of the work’s relevant categories, art-historical context, cultural context, and so forth). In some cases, a particular doxastic attitude may be necessary for apt aesthetic perception and appreciation.

items.title: Universality of the Prohibition of Indifference.
items.abstract: This work takes as its sole initial givenness the fact that actual Reality exists and is given as process. The investigation does not begin with a choice of what existed "in the beginning." The question of the initial state is replaced by the question of the minimal invariant necessary for the very possibility of Reality as process. If the processuality of Reality is accepted as givenness, then absolute identity, absolute symmetry, and absolute synchrony are incompatible with it. The Prohibition of Indifference is thus reconstructed: Z = ¬(Id ∨ Sym ∨ Sync). Logos and Monos are distinct domains, not sequential stages. In Logos: A = A. In Monos, absolute identity is prohibited: A ≠ A → A₁. Logic does not transition into Reality. The dynamic consequences — dissipation of identity, temporality, spatiality, and recursivity — are developed in the corpus. Recursion occupies a special place: it arises in Monos as a prerequisite of process after the exhaustion of external degrees of freedom; the Observer does not generate it but realizes this prerequisite through the means of Logos. The work has the status of an ontological hypothesis concerning the minimally sufficient invariant of Reality. It is not a physical theory and does not derive concrete physical equations.

items.title: Perceptual Presence.
items.abstract: In this doctoral thesis, I defend an account of perceptual presence. My account has descriptive and explanatory aspects. In the descriptive account, I argue that perceptual presence is a strand of phenomenal character whereby experience manifestly depends on mind-independent objects. I identify two forms of manifest dependence, manifest spatial dependence and manifest temporal dependence. Each form reflects the apparent fulfilment of an enabling condition for successful perception. My explanatory account locates perceptual presence within a metaphysical framework. I argue that perceptual presence can be accommodated within a point of view-act-object framework, and reject appeals to an attitude-content framework. I also reject the view that presence is not perceptual at all. -/- Both the descriptive and explanatory aspects of the thesis are guided by the aim of placing perceptual experience within a broader account of the mind. This involves attending to the similarities and differences between perceptual experience and other kinds of experience, both in their phenomenal character and functional role. Sensory imagination and experiential memory are especially valuable here, for though their phenomenal characters are in some ways like that of perceptual experience, they don’t possess presence. As a companion to my account of perceptual presence, I offer an account of the phenomenal pastness of experiential memory. Pastness is to be explained by experiential memory’s characteristic pattern of dependence both on its objects and its subject.

items.title: Mnemic extension and appropriate causation.
items.abstract: Philosophers of memory often assume that the extended mind hypothesis is compatible with the causal theory of memory. For extracranial resources can, the idea goes, sustain the causal connection between a past event and a present representation of it that, on causalist views, distinguishes genuine remembering. Some go as far as to claim that constructive versions of the causal theory can accommodate complementarity-based versions of the extended mind hypothesis. This paper casts doubt on these ideas by defending two claims. First, the existing arguments for compatibility are flawed. While some conflate external information storage with cognitive extension, others wrongly hold that fulfilling the conditions for cognitive extension secures the appropriate kind of causal connection for remembering. Second, constructive versions of the causal theory and complementarity-based versions of the extended mind hypothesis are in fact incompatible. For constructive causal theories require of memory traces features that functionally disparate but complementary extracranial resources systematically lack. The paper concludes by considering how parity-based versions of the extended mind hypothesis might fare within the causal theory, and how other theories of memory might be assessed for compatibility with the extended mind hypothesis.

items.title: Always This One: The Boundaries and Recurrence of First-Person Actuality.
items.abstract: A census recording every public, personal, and experiential fact about the world's lives would record who was born when, who remembered what, and who died. It would not record which of those lives is this one. This paper asks what could draw that line. The ordinary answer draws it twice: other lives are not this one because they belong to other persons; and this life is the only time this one is actual because it is a single occurrence that ends. I argue that neither difference acquires boundary authority merely by being real. For the first, a symmetry argument shows that, under Neutrality and before any boundary relation has been granted authority, the non-anchor census lives are symmetric for the scope question: either all fall within this-one scope or none do; a line in between needs a relation that constitutes it. For the second, I grant the strongest form of the first boundary—complete content fixes which occurrences are this one—and show that if actual succession continues past death, its later positions are realized by lives with genuine first-person experience, and this one is not wholly replaced, the same complete content must receive a numerically new, later, non-overlapping occurrence. I call this first-person recurrence. The results are conditional. The final section returns to the points at which the argument can be resisted and makes clear what changes when one leaves the route.

items.title: Deathbed Aesthetics: Ugliness and Courageous Love.
items.abstract: Dying can be ugly. This fact is relevant to the growing subfield of everyday aesthetics, to the philosophy of death, and to all of us as mortal beings. Disgusting experiences in particular seem to impose a limit on the dying person’s aesthetic agency. If disgust is the fitting response to medical and body horror in everyday contexts, we might think that we can aesthetically respond to these properties only with rational disgust (cold comfort for the dying person seeking beauty in painful circumstances) or with deluded aesthetic enjoyment (false beauty). I develop a Bhattacharyyan solution to this dilemma, defending a third option. According to K. C. Bhattacharyya (KCB, 1875–1949), even acute disgust in everyday life can be rationally enjoyed as an aesthetic emotion in virtue of adopting an emotional perspective of ‘courageous love’ through a specific imaginative procedure. I argue that courageous love is a merited, positive aesthetic-emotional response to disgusting experiences on the deathbed.

items.title: An Ethics Ecosystem for AI.
items.abstract: This article diagnoses ethical failures associated with AI as resulting from the lack of a robust ethics ecosystem. Drawing on the domain of health and healthcare, we identify the components of a functioning ecosystem and explain how an ecosystemic approach helps to manage the scale of the ethical challenges in the domain of AI relative to more typical alternatives.

items.title: Unconscious Cook: On the Speed and the Temporality of Analytic Processes in Digital Contexts.
items.abstract: Drawing on Freud’s indeterminate analytic pace, Deleuze’s reading of Spinoza’s relational speeds and Patricia Clough’s technological unconscious, this article examines how digital media reveal and transform the heterogeneous temporalities of psychic life. Extending Bion’s psychic metabolization through Winnicott’s rhythms of separation and return and Luciana Parisi’s account of connections across bodies and machines, it develops “co-metabolization” to conceptualize how algorithms participate in the processing, circulation and temporal organization of affect and experience. Bringing these processes into relation with Foucault’s political reason and Virilio’s politics of speed, it argues for an analytic attunement to unequal bodily, computational and historical tempos that sustains unconscious movement and keeps the meaning of analytic speed open.

items.title: Coming to Terms with the Need for Meaning: How an Existential Demand Awakens in Camus’s L’Étranger.
items.abstract: Many critics have argued that Meursault, the protagonist of Albert Camus’s L’Étranger, is profoundly aware that life is absurd. In this paper, I argue that this is partially correct: although Meursault believes that life lacks meaning (the existential lack), he has also failed to acknowledge the need for meaning (the existential demand). Since the Camusian account of the absurd involves both an existential demand and an existential lack, Meursault initially fails to completely recognize the absurdity of life. I analyze his initial failure to acknowledge the existential demand, its subsequent coming into conscious awareness in the second half of the novella, how it could have been out of awareness in the first place, and how the possibility of proactively pursuing a meaningful life is forlorn once he has become aware of the existential demand, which explains his sense of guilt at the end of the novella. This analysis offers crucial insight into both the phenomenology of the absurd and the normative implications that follow from the absurdity of life. The story, in short, implores us to embrace the existential demand – not only for the sake of integrity, but also to guide us towards a more meaningful life.

items.title: What Remains of the Cogito? Operational Constraint Fields Prior to Self, Thought, Inference, Modality, and Existence.
items.abstract: This paper asks what remains of the Cartesian cogito when self, thought, inference, modality, and existence are not treated as an indivisible philosophical unit. Rather than rejecting the cogito, it reconstructs it as a compression of several operational achievements that can become non-redundant at different intervals and under different configurations. The general explanatory object proposed is the operational constraint field: a configuration-indexed structure governing co-realizability, suppression, enabling, persistence, recurrence, addressability, and downstream reachability. Operational incompatibility is treated as only one regime within this field. -/- The paper situates this reconstruction in relation to Descartes, Hume, Sellars, Brandom, and Brassier. It distinguishes nonconceptual causal patterning from conceptual and inferential articulation, while asking when the vocabularies of “I,” “think,” “therefore,” necessity, and existence begin to make non-redundant differences to prediction, intervention, attribution, correction, counterfactual discrimination, and re-entry. -/- A development-scale computational study provides a limited empirical constraint on the framework. Across 10 seeds, 47 perturbation types, four severity levels, 1,890 evaluated cells, and 9,120 runs, operational stability varied systematically with configuration. Observation- and action-interface perturbations were especially effective in producing transitions, while changes in operational-unit stability did not simply coincide with loss of control performance. Several theoretically salient components were also redundant under the tested conditions. These results do not establish a machine cogito. They support the narrower claim that operational non-redundancy and stability are configuration-indexed and can change independently across components and tasks.

items.title: What Is Respectful Operation Before It Becomes Normative? Operational Respect, Trust, Active Inference, Machine Agency, and Nihilism.
items.abstract: Respect is usually introduced as an already normative relation involving recognition, reasons, autonomy, or moral standing. This paper asks an analytically prior question: what operational differences become non-redundant when interactive respect is introduced? It proposes operational respect not as respect simpliciter, but as a candidate operational constituent of interactive respect: the maintained non-closure of pathways through which differences arriving from another configuration can alter subsequent possibilities of operation and, under relevant conditions, the terms of future revisability itself. -/- The paper distinguishes respect from trust, agreement, obedience, politeness, agency, reward, and generic responsiveness. It connects this analysis to Active Inference, machine learning, corrigibility, Sellarsian and Brandomian normativity, and Ray Brassier’s nihilism without reducing nihilism to passivity. A sequence of computational experiments examines constructive separability, learned revision, architecture-dependent intervention, closed-loop return and reconfiguration, and an Active-Inference-inspired probabilistic epistemic baseline. The central result is not a scalar measure of machine respect but configuration-dependent separability: candidate operational constituents of interactive respect can become coupled, separable, revisable, or non-identifiable depending on configuration, history, temporal window, boundary, and intervention topology. The experiments establish computational distinctions under synthetic conditions; they do not establish moral respect in machines.

items.title: What If Every Human Acquired Brassierian Operations? A Population-Scale Counterfactual Simulation of Philosophical Penetration, Rational Revision, Fragility Transfer, and Self-Obsolescence.
items.abstract: What would happen if Brassierian operations ceased to be locally concentrated philosophical competencies and became population-scale capacities? This paper treats that question not as a thought experiment about universal agreement with Ray Brassier, but as a counterfactual simulation problem. “Brassierian operations” are operationalized minimally as capacities for revising commitments under impersonal constraints, resisting the identification of intelligibility with human phenomenological privilege, distinguishing causal patterning from conceptual articulation, and permitting inherited conceptual resources to become obsolete. The simulation then varies population penetration, network topology, revision speed, institutional coupling, external-memory persistence, resource constraints, and rates of environmental reconfiguration. -/- The central result is non-monotonic. Increasing the distribution of rational-revision capacities can initially improve error correction and reduce dependence on inherited conceptual fixations, but universalization does not simply produce a maximally rational population. Beyond specific configurations, the same operations can destabilize the social, institutional, and mnemonic infrastructures required for their own reproduction. Rational revision therefore exhibits fragility transfer: robustness gained at one operational layer can relocate vulnerability to another. At population scale, philosophical penetration can consequently modify the conditions under which philosophy itself remains a non-redundant practice. -/- The paper distinguishes philosophical doctrine from the operational shapes through which doctrines propagate, transform institutions, reorganize observation and inference, and alter subsequent possibility spaces. This permits a stronger counterfactual: if Brassierian operations became sufficiently distributed across humans, machines, institutions, and external memory, their successful penetration could eliminate the need for specifically “Brassierian,” philosophical, or even human mediation. The limiting case is therefore not universal Brassierianism but self-obsolescence: successful philosophical penetration produces configurations in which the philosophy that initiated the transformation ceases to constitute a necessary passage point.

items.title: What Can the Concept of “Concept” Lose and Still Remain a Concept? An Experimental Search for Minimal Non-Redundant Constituents.
items.abstract: This paper asks a subtractive question: what can the concept of “concept” lose before concept-like operation ceases to remain non-redundant? Rather than defining concepts by a universal essence, six candidate constituents—configuration, temporal window, scale, ignition, retention, and re-entry—are treated as experimentally removable search coordinates. The framework permits a universal minimal set, multiple minimal realizations, or failure of “concept” to form a single operational kind. A synthetic computational proof-of-protocol tests ablation, minimal-set transition, retention, transformed reuse, dissolution, and re-entry across controlled configurations. The experiments shift the target from an invariant constituent inventory toward a configuration- and criterion-dependent transition structure. Retention is not uniformly beneficial; replay is not equivalent to useful re-entry; supplied transformation can improve cross-interval reuse; and repeated attempts at autonomous transformation discovery and joint unit–transformation search fail to outperform fresh learning. These negative results constrain rather than confirm the framework. The paper therefore proposes not a new essence of concepts, but an experimentally vulnerable method for determining when distinctions, constituents, and even the concept of “concept” itself remain operationally non-redundant.

items.title: The Stellar Operationalization of Science: Xenoscience and the Loss of Human Conceptual Mediation as a Mandatory Passage Point.
items.abstract: This paper develops the concept of the stellar operationalization of science: a transition in which scientific operation ceases to require human conceptual mediation as a universal mandatory passage point while retaining difference sensitivity, historical re-entry, error-sensitive correction, generated observability, and reconfiguration. Beginning from Sellars’s distinction between causal responsiveness and the space of reasons, Brandom’s account of material inference, incompatibility, and modal and normative metavocabularies, and Brassier’s commitment to nonconceptual causal patterning, the paper asks a post-Brassier question: can scientific configurations recurrently couple to reality, experiment, intervene, retain results, and revise their own conditions without returning through human conceptual judgment at every cycle? Xenoscience is developed as a configuration in which sensors, artificial intelligence, experimental apparatuses, external memory, and physical interventions can form such recurrent loops. Stellar operationalization does not mean the elimination of humans, concepts, reasons, or ontologies. Rather, it removes their unconditional status as universal mandatory passage points. Ontological mediation is treated in the same way: a unified ontology is required only where it produces a non-redundant difference in prediction, intervention, correction, transfer, or reconfiguration. Operational redundancy under a given configuration does not entail ontological falsity. Preserved Ziran/Xeno Simulator results provide cross-system evidence for several necessary operational components, particularly the dependence of correction on its timing relative to environmental reconfiguration, while dedicated native validation remains outstanding. The result is a model of scientific autonomy that distinguishes causal operation, conceptual articulation, modal projection, normative entitlement, and intervention without making any one of them universally foundational.

items.title: Position-Value Evaluation of Research Operations Research Is a Position, Not a Ranking: Counterfactual Reachability from Scientific to Philosophical Intervals.
items.abstract: This paper develops Position-Value Evaluation of Research Operations (PVERO), a framework for evaluating research without assigning context-independent value to named researchers, institutions, or AI systems. Research value is instead treated as a configuration-dependent change in subsequent possibility: an operational difference may ignite under specific conditions, persist or transform, generate observable or intervenable effects, penetrate other media or scales, return through feedback, and reorganize what can subsequently be reached. -/- The framework introduces counterfactual removal and replacement, operational non-redundancy, open-ended research-state generation, transition-depth and elapsed-time separation, environment-relative revision speed, and an event-first representation of research evidence. Human researchers, AI systems, laboratories, collectives, instruments, and hybrid arrangements can therefore be evaluated without assuming in advance that they constitute the same kind of entity. -/- Controlled synthetic experiments, negative controls, sensitivity analyses, open-ended state-generation experiments, and an exploratory real-world pilot are reported. A central negative result is that generating more novel research states does not by itself increase research value. The paper also specifies integration with the Ziran Simulator while explicitly separating current computational validation from still-unperformed confirmatory blinded coding and native Ziran execution. -/- The central claim is that research is not adequately represented by a context-free ranking. Its value depends on which operational differences become non-redundant in which configurations, how they alter subsequent reachability, whether they can be replaced, and whether their revision remains fast enough relative to environmental reorganization.

items.title: Do Philosophical Positions Exist as Operational Intervals? Historical Reconstruction and a Progressive Computational Test.
items.abstract: This paper asks whether philosophical positions such as skepticism, realism, idealism, empiricism, and rationalism should be treated as stable properties of thinkers and doctrines, or reconstructed as historically stabilized families of operational structures and intervals. -/- Rather than translating philosophical positions directly into computational variables—for example, skepticism into uncertainty, realism into predictive success, or empiricism into sensory weighting—the paper develops a “detect first, name later” methodology. Pyrrhonian, Cartesian, Humean, and Kantian operational structures are reconstructed independently and fixed prior to machine comparison, while Sellars, Brandom, and Brassier provide important boundary conditions concerning scientific constraint, nonconceptual causal patterning, inference, and normative vocabulary. -/- A progressive computational program then tests increasingly demanding conditions for any machine–historical comparison, including unlabeled regime differentiation, multiscale temporal robustness, causal bypass, history re-entry, altered reachability, cross-medium penetration, endogenous intervention, and frozen-policy ignition. Positive controls establish that these properties can be measured independently. However, the decisive raw-observation and generic-objective experiment fails to produce selective configuration-sensitive ignition: intervention saturates even in the control condition. -/- Accordingly, the paper does not claim that a machine instantiated skepticism or any other philosophical position. Instead, it argues that philosophical vocabulary should be introduced only after operational differentiation has been independently established, and should remain withheld when the required non-redundant structure is absent.

items.title: Can Truth Be Too Fast? Is Truth That Arrives Too Fast Operationally True? AI, Autonomous Science, Self-Correction, Reality Penetration, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: Can truth arrive too fast? This paper argues that the problem is not absolute speed and does not require a second notion of truth. A truth-apt output may retain its truth-value while its production and reality penetration outrun the verification, correction, and reconfiguration processes coupled to it. The analysis therefore distinguishes five heterogeneous temporal processes: production, verification, penetration, correction, and reconfiguration. “Truth too fast” names a configured speed asymmetry in which penetration changes subsequent possibilities before non-redundant verification and correction can operate. -/- The paper develops this claim through the concepts of correction-reachability, reality penetration, correction debt, configured ignition conditions, and operational shape, and connects them to AI, autonomous science, and Xenoscience. Reproducible synthetic experiments, structural controls, and mechanism-removal ablations show that the relevant variable is not speed simpliciter: when the pre-verification penetration pathway is removed, the timing effect disappears. Historical re-entry likewise increases correction burden only when coupled to a reconstruction pathway. -/- The computational results establish mechanism specificity in a synthetic environment, not real-world causal validation.
