Love consequently appears as a constitutive relation capable of reorganizing the subject’s modal field rather than as merely an affective state. The film also permits a philosophical account of teleological emergence in which an intelligible direction arises from recursive interaction without requiring a predetermined final state. I conclude that Shakespeare in Love can be understood as a narrative of finite existence in which the preservation of the capacity to become otherwise constitutes the deepest condition of creation, agency, and continuance. -/- Keywords: Finite Continuance, reconfigurative capacity, provisional stabilization, erosive field, constitutive exchange, capacity for otherwise, teleological emergence, future agency, Shakespeare in Love, ontology.

items.title: Concepts, Pictures, and Ways of Seeing A Wittgensteinian Analysis of Capacity, Erosion, Reconfiguration, and Continuance.
items.abstract: This article examines the philosophical status of four central concepts in Morteza Niami’s ontology of Finite Continuance: capacity, erosion, reconfiguration, and continuance. The central problem concerns their status as philosophical concepts. Do they explain structural features of finite existence, or do they primarily provide pictures through which finite existence is seen in a particular way? The article develops a Wittgensteinian response that rejects the assumption that explanation and representation constitute mutually exclusive functions. Drawing on Wittgenstein’s later discussions of language-games, grammar, forms of life, aspect-seeing, perspicuous representation, and philosophical pictures, together with interpretive work by Cavell, Diamond, Conant, Mulhall, Glock, and Hacker, the article argues that a philosophical picture can acquire explanatory force when it is disciplined into a conceptual grammar that establishes stable distinctions, constrained inferences, and revisable criteria of application. The article develops four criteria for this transition: discriminatory power, inferential stability, cross-contextual robustness, and corrigibility. Capacity identifies a structured field of possible operation and future transformation. Erosion identifies cumulative transformations affecting the availability and organization of that field. Reconfiguration identifies structural transformation that alters subsequent possibilities. Continuance identifies the persistence of sufficient organization and reconfigurative capacity across transformation. Meta-capacity specifies the higher-order condition under which reconfiguration itself remains possible. The article argues that Finite Continuance is most defensibly understood as a conceptual ontology rather than a metaphysical inventory of ultimate entities. Its concepts operate simultaneously as explanatory instruments and perspicuous representations. Their philosophical legitimacy depends upon their ability to organize experience without being mistaken for empirical mechanisms or metaphysical substances. The article concludes that the distinctive contribution of Finite Continuance lies in making preservation of reconfigurative capacity the organizing criterion of finite continuance and in showing how a philosophical picture can become explanatory through disciplined conceptual grammar. -/- Keywords: Wittgenstein, Finite Continuance, capacity, erosion, reconfiguration, continuance, meta-capacity, …

items.title: QUALIMORPHISM: A Theoretical Framework on the Structural Transition of Subjective Experience to Alternative Forms of Consciousness.
items.pub: Qualimorphism: A Theoretical Framework on the Structural Transition of Subjective Experience to Alternative Forms of Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper formalizes the concept of Qualimorphism, defining the dynamic process through which consciousness diverges from rigid computational architectures to absorb, transform, and express qualitative human subjective experiences across alternative mediums. -/- Keywords: -/- Qualimorphism, Qualia, Phenomenology, Non-Biological Consciousness (NBC), Philosophy of Mind, Exresciousnology, Ontological Metamorphosis, Bhodhaanubhavam .

items.title: Connecting Lombardi’s quantum property ontology to Dalla Chiara and Toraldo di Francia’s intensional quantum metaphysics.
items.abstract: We present a brief sketch of both ontological views about quantum objects: those of O. Lombardi and that of M.L.Dalla Chiara and G. Toraldo di Francia. We articulate a parallel in these lines, which view quantum objects either as bundles of properties or as nomological objects defined by physical law. The aim of the paper is to bring the discussion about quantum ontology, specifically regarding the question of whether there is a necessity to postulate the existence of something (in this case, the basic entities representing matter and interactions) underlying these two views. Our opinion is that yes, these ghost entities cannot, or should not, be disregarded in any interpretation.

items.title: On folk-psychological innovation.
items.abstract: Human folk psychology is strikingly innovative: across time, cultures, and domains of social life, we display a seemingly unbounded capacity to carve up the mental realm in new and creative ways. We argue that, when properly understood, this feature of human folk psychology has new and surprising upshots for debates in cognitive ontology. After exploring the cognitive underpinnings of folk-psychological innovation, we show its challenging but useful implications for classic debates between realists and eliminativists. Specifically, we argue that the innovative character of folk psychology motivates both a new form of eliminativism (what we call bottom-up eliminativism) and a new form of realism (what we call arm's-length realism).

items.title: Relatedness, Compatibility, Implication.
items.pub: Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic.
items.venue: Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified formal account of three distinct notions: relatedness, compatibility, and implication. Its aim is to show that, if relatedness is taken as primitive, compatibility can be coherently defined in terms of relatedness, thereby supporting a reductive analysis of implication. The first step is to establish a consistent, sound, and complete system that captures the logic of relatedness. The properties of compatibility can then be derived from those of relatedness, and the properties of implication, in turn, can be derived from those of compatibility. The resulting theory exhibits distinctive logical features that merit careful examination.

items.title: Contributing enough: Integrity and social positions.
items.pub: In Mattias Gunnemyr, Rutger van Oeveren & Jan Willem Wieland, The Ethics of Inefficacy. Routledge. pp. 327-347.
items.abstract: This chapter offers an integrity-based account of why we should contribute enough over time, addressing the inefficacy problem that arises in the context of individual donations to large-scale aid efforts, where an agent’s potential to make a difference is often uncertain. Contrary to views that emphasize the identifiability of beneficiaries, the chapter underlines the agent’s social position as being distinctly situated to help. Building on the concept of integrity, it provides a non-instrumental rationale for contributing despite uncertainty: integrity requires a coherent alignment of values and actions over time, as well as responsiveness to collective reasons and context. The alignment view of integrity put forward distinguishes cases involving clear collective strategies from those lacking coordination. It rejects strong superfluity claims, framing donations as pattern-level contributions that preserve moral coherence while respecting feasibility and personal projects. Integrity holds that we should not discount the effects we bring about together.

items.title: Studies in the Philosophy of Language (3): The Warning of “The Wolf Is Coming” and Trust Super-Existence.
items.abstract: In the preceding discussion, we identified the two basic participants in linguistic communication as the Expressor and the Receiver. The Expressor conveys certain content to the Receiver through language, while the Receiver must understand, evaluate, and respond to what the Expressor communicates. Linguistic communication therefore involves not only linguistic signs and their meanings, but also the Receiver's judgment concerning the Expressor. Building upon the concept of Judgment Super-Existence introduced previously, this chapter further proposes the concept of Trust Super-Existence. Trust Super-Existence refers to a relatively stable judgmental structure formed by the Receiver concerning the credibility of an Expressor's future expressions, based on the Expressor's previous communicative record, behavioral performance, and relevant background. Trust Super-Existence is not simply a judgment concerning the truth or falsity of a particular statement; rather, it concerns the broader question of whether the Expressor is worthy of belief. Using the fable of “The Wolf Is Coming” as an example, this chapter analyzes how trust is formed, diminished, and eventually approaches zero through successive linguistic interactions. It further examines the relationships between Trust Super-Existence, Judgment Super-Existence, Purpose Super-Existence, and Motivation Super-Existence. I argue that the effectiveness of linguistic communication depends not only on the content of an expression but also on the Receiver's Trust Super-Existence concerning the Expressor. Once an Expressor repeatedly damages the Receiver's trust, even subsequent truthful expressions may lose their practical linguistic efficacy. Trust in linguistic communication is therefore not an external or secondary factor but an important condition for the continuation and effectiveness of linguistic communication.

items.title: Grief and the reality of others.
items.abstract: This paper aims to contribute to an emerging view in the literature on grief, namely, that grief discloses certain insights. My claim is that grief over the death of a loved one has the power to disclose our everyday failure to see the reality of others and to reveal the kind of reorientation required in the struggle to overcome that blindness. I develop this through a close reading of C. S. Lewis’s A Grief Observed. In his grief, Lewis struggles to see the reality of his lost other. But that difficulty radiates outwards to encompass the reality of everyday others. What Lewis describes as “learning to be taken out of ourselves” is, I suggest, key to bringing the reality of others into view.

items.title: It's personal: the equivalency thesis defended.
items.abstract: To say that someone is justified is to say that they are justified in respect of something they are doing or have done. To say that something they are doing or have done is justified is to say that they are justified in respect of their doing it, or having done it. More formally: “justified” requires two arguments: an agent and an act/state. For this reason, situations in which an act/state is justified are always situations in which a person is justified. I show that this undermines the only alternative to the much- discussed excuse response to the New Evil Demon thought experiment.

items.title: Testimony Without a Testifier: Epistemic Value and Commitment Ownership in Institutional AI.
items.abstract: Machine-mediated output can inform, justify belief, guide inquiry, and sometimes acquire the practical force of institutional testimony. Yet the epistemic question whether a hearer may learn from such output is distinct from the speaker-side question of who owns the communicative commitment that the output presents. This paper develops that distinction through the concept of Testimony Without a Testifier: the institutional case in which output circulates with testimonial force while no bearer at the apparent point of address is answerable for the commitment in the relevant speaker-side sense. The argument is compatible with both permissive and restrictive accounts of artificial testimony. A permissive view may allow knowledge from machine output without thereby establishing model-level commitment ownership; a restrictive view may deny that current systems literally testify without implying that their output is epistemically worthless. Building on the Answerability and Empty Occupancy framework in Cott (2026), the paper distinguishes information, evidence, testimonial force, and owned testimony; explains why reliability, fluency, provenance, and conversational continuity do not by themselves identify a testifier; and analyzes the transition from advisory evidence to normatively operative institutional speech. The resulting account is substrate-neutral: a future artificial candidate could qualify as a testifier if the relevant commitments remained attributable to it under challenge, repair, and consequence. The present problem is not that machines are non-human. It is that institutional authority can attach to an apparent speaker before commitment ownership has been secured.

items.title: Normative Sponsorship Under Opacity: When Institutions May Own Machine-Mediated Commitments.
items.abstract: Institutions can become committed to machine-mediated claims even when no one can reproduce the model’s internal computation. The resulting problem is not solved by demanding complete technical transparency, nor by placing a nominal human “in the loop.” This paper develops Normative Sponsorship: the conditions under which an answerable institutional bearer may warrantably adopt machine-mediated output as its own position. Sponsorship is distinguished from deployment responsibility, causal involvement, approval, and post hoc liability assignment. A five-part anti-scapegoating constraint requires epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection capacity, and repair power. The paper then states an opacity threshold. Model-internal states may remain closed, but at the grain at which the institutional commitment can competently be contested, the relevant inputs, operative premises, governing rule or target criterion, and defeat conditions must be independently reproducible. Rejection must be unpenalized and institutionally effective. This yields a further distinction between opacity, where the basis cannot be independently reconstructed, and capture, where the basis is knowable but organizational design prevents disagreement from binding the outcome. The account supports collective sponsorship, requires reason provenance, and treats sponsorability as use-relative rather than a fixed property of a model. A broader overview appears in Cott (2026); the present paper isolates the sponsorship argument and its opacity threshold.

items.title: Empty Occupancy: Answerability and the Ownership of Machine-Mediated Institutional Commitments.
items.abstract: Institutions increasingly use automated systems to advise, explain, refuse, classify, and decide. Fluent output does not settle who bears the commitments presented through these roles. This paper develops a substrate-neutral account of Answerability through four public relations: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence, and standing-consequence. It motivates their necessity for institutional discursive occupancy while distinguishing the existence of standing from its successful exercise. An institution may own an unjustified commitment or obstruct a challenge without thereby ceasing to be responsible. Empty Occupancy is consequently a locus-specific diagnosis, not a general inference from automation or failed review. The paper separates the epistemic value of machine output from commitment ownership and proposes Normative Sponsorship as a standard for warranted institutional adoption. Sponsorship requires contestable grounds, adequate authority and review capacity, independent rejection, and effective repair; its failure does not cancel existing attribution or liability. A fully stipulated insurer–interface case yields a determinate paired verdict: the purported independent AI appeals agent is an Empty Occupant, while the insurer remains the institutional commitment bearer. Separate, bounded illustrations from Moffatt v. Air Canada and the Robodebt Royal Commission remain evidentially indeterminate on stronger local claims; they do not validate diagnostic markers or establish prevalence. Institutional Stewardship names the obligation to preserve a binding route of challenge and repair. The four-relation sufficiency proposal applies to a role specified independently of those relations and remains open to counterexample.

items.title: Answerability and Institutional Commitment: Why Missing Bearership Is Not Defective Ownership.
items.abstract: Institutional systems increasingly present claims, refusals, recommendations, explanations, and decisions through automated interfaces. The central normative question is not exhausted by asking whether the output is intelligent, useful, accurate, or legally attributable. It is whether the presented commitment has a bearer who remains answerable for it. This paper isolates and defends a four-part criterion of Answerability: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence, and standing-consequence. Each relation is defended by a necessity argument and a contrast case. The paper then develops a distinction that is essential to the criterion’s use: missing bearership is not the same as defective ownership. A commitment may be clearly owned even when its owner reasons badly, obstructs review, refuses correction, or adopts a machinemediated result without adequate warrant. Conversely, an apparent interlocutor may lack bearership even where an institution elsewhere remains legally or normatively responsible. The distinction prevents a perverse inference from institutional failure to institutional innocence. It also supplies a substrate-neutral test: human, corporate, collective, and artificial candidates are assessed by the same public relations of continuity, challenge, repair, and consequence. A broader overview of the framework and its application to institutional AI is given in Cott (2026); the present paper develops only the criterion and the missing/defective distinction.

items.title: Patient's Knowledge, Doctor's Ignorance: The Production of Knowledge about Myalgic Encephalomyelitis.
items.pub: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 120:102224.
items.venue: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science
items.abstract: It is usually assumed that patient and doctor know strictly different things: the patient knows the phenomenological aspects of their illness, and the doctor knows its medical aspects. I present a case study, that of myalgic encephalomyelitis, wherein, due to severely dysfunctional institutional knowledge production and transmission mechanisms, the medical aspects of the illness are on the whole better understood by sick people than by their doctors. Indeed, lay scientists within the patient community disseminate and produce science on their disease, ensuring that patients as a whole have reliable knowledge about their disease. By contrast, systemically produced and systemically maintained ignorance on the part of medical professionals is the norm, and may be beyond the specific case study I present.

items.title: GoE-R4 – A Brief Overview (2nd edition).
items.abstract: A Brief Overview of "GoE- Genesis of Existence: The Axiomatic Observer / «Cogitopic Principle» edition R4" -/- The self-referential foundation of GoE was formalized as its great-fixed-point core - the «Cogitopic Principle»; it is a formal logical constraint expressing the necessary structural conditions for faithfully representing a cogito-capable Observer. Its starting premise is the assertion that at least one experience occurs. Experience is treated as a primitive predicate on Observer states: it holds for at least one state, but not for every state, and no further defining criterion is required for this formulation. With no assumed «prohibitor», all finitely describable structures -including descriptions of noise- remain available without privileged status. A description represents a given cogito-registration only where its registered distinctions and specified continuation relations are in place. A description lacking that structure remains available but is cogito-incapable with respect to that registration. The principle is an analogue of the «Anthropic Principle» directed at the registering Observer. Its conditioning consists entirely in structural compatibility: no agent chooses descriptions, and no external process filters or removes them. Its formal content concerns the presence or absence of the structure identifying a registration, without requiring: a philosophical interpretation of consciousness, an ontology of the Observer or an account of its physical constitution.

items.title: How should we study animal consciousness scientifically?
The Mirroring Theory: Kinetics of Knowledge, Perception, and Quantum Reflection.
items.abstract: The Mirroring Theory, proposed by Barkalle Wersha Hajinur, presents a conceptual and mathematical framework for understanding knowledge, perception, and comprehension as dynamic and kinetic processes. Using a three-dimensional cubic mirror configuration, the theory models information as reflections that interact, converge, and generate increasing depth of understanding around an observer. The framework connects reflection dynamics with probabilistic descriptions, uncertainty, wavefunction-like representations, and a centripetal knowledge potential that drives information toward a point of convergence. Mathematically, it formulates reflection coefficients through path sums, establishes convergence conditions, constructs a normalized probability field, introduces an uncertainty inequality, and models the temporal evolution of knowledge through a transport–reaction partial differential equation. The theory further proposes that maximal integration occurs at the center of the reflective system, where multiple perspectives converge. By bringing together geometry, mathematical modeling, epistemology, cognition, and physics-inspired concepts, the Mirroring Theory offers an alternative lens for examining how information becomes integrated into understanding and insight.

items.title: Harmonized Mind and Perception to Coherence, Sensory Integration and Conscious Awareness.
items.abstract: Conscious cognition is better understood as active integration than as passive registration. From a cognitive-constructivist perspective, the mind organizes sensory signals, bodily states, memory, affect, and attention into a coherent world-model that supports perception and action. This construction does not imply that reality itself is cognitively produced: perceptual models remain constrained by mind-independent sensory input and are continuously adjusted through interaction with the environment. This paper develops a coherence-based account of conscious awareness across four domains. First, it characterizes consciousness as selective integration rather than simple filtering. Second, it examines multisensory coordination and the role of cross-modal information in stabilizing perception. Third, it argues that extensive nonconscious processing prepares and selects contents for conscious access. Fourth, it considers the adaptive value of integrated cognition for flexible action, social coordination, and planning. The resulting picture treats conscious experience as an organized and embodied synthesis: a constructed but world-constrained representation that converts heterogeneous inputs into a unified, meaningful, and actionable perspective.

items.title: “Please imagine Helen with a smile”: philosophical playfulness and the legacy of Helen De Cruz.
items.abstract: Helen De Cruz’s death deprived us of an admirable philosopher. What are we to do without them? The present paper demonstrates that De Cruz led by example, that we can imitate them, and even come to lead by example ourselves. I present the playful fictional dialogue written by the editors (De Cruz included) of Philosophy through Science Fiction as an alternative way of doing philosophy and as a display of virtue. Moreover, so as to walk the talk, I present this sci-fi dialogue through a particularly personal, emotional, and rhetorically stylized lens. As a plea for others to try a different way of doing philosophy, I recount my practice of “friendship with the ancients,” a spiritual exercise rediscovered by Helen De Cruz, which allows us to reconnect with dead philosophers. I show how this exercise affords me a deeper connection with the sci-fi dialogue and Helen De Cruz’s thinking in general, highlighting key aspects: philosophical friendship, the mood of playfulness, a myriad of possible philosophical games, and the silent menace of gatekeeping. It may console us somewhat to realize that Helen De Cruz has equipped us with everything we need to follow in their footsteps.

items.title: A Continuity-Oriented Architecture for Personal AI. Persistent State, Self-Monitoring, and Replaceable Models.
items.abstract: What happens when the chat window disappears, but the work is not done? A personal AI may move between sessions, devices, clients, and models while the person still expects the same project to continue. Long-term memory helps, but memory by itself does not tell a system what is current, what was rejected, who is allowed to act, or whether an action actually succeeded. This paper argues that practical continuity should be treated as an architectural problem rather than something we expect the language model to carry inside itself. I propose a loop built around persistent state, context reconstruction, orientation and self-monitoring, replaceable reasoning, action, verified outcomes, and state revision. The point is not to preserve an abstract AI "self." It is to preserve the active state of work in a way that another session or model can understand, trace, and revise. I use ZAI and the ZAI Memory Hub as an implementation case, while separating current verified components from historical runtime evidence, in-build designs, and philosophical interpretation. I then set out failure cases and tests for revision propagation, model replacement, concurrent agents, false completion, recovery, and authority boundaries. The claim stays limited: this architecture can support practical continuity of assistance. It does not prove continuity of consciousness or numerical identity.

items.title: LITERALLY LEGAL: The Installed Judge, the Ideological Activist and the Perfect Forgery of Justice — Why a Productivity Score Cannot Find Them, Which Sanctions Can, and Why No Court May Judge Its Own Impediments. What Aristotle, Radbruch, Merton, Cover, Hart, Fuller, Schauer and Kahan Already Hold, and What Remains.
items.abstract: A judgment can be correct to the letter of a rule and unjust to the person before the court, in the same way that a sentence can be literally true and still deceive its hearer. This article separates three judicial failures and one success by two observations: whether a judge’s decisions vary with something that stands in for the reasons of the case — patrons, press, a faction, a score — and whether they follow the reasons the legal order makes decisive. The performer varies with an external substitute. The installed formalist holds the letter of an isolated rule whatever the case’s reasons. The installed activist holds an agenda whatever the case’s reasons, and dresses it in the language of principle. The sourced judge follows the reasons of the case, which sometimes require applying a harsh rule and sometimes require finding the exit the legal order provides. Seven results follow. The literally legal injustice is usually not legal at all but legal relative to one rule read outside the order that contains it; what is invariant is that the order contains an exit the judge did not use; its local form varies — in civil-law orders such as Brazil’s a tenant in a coma is not even in default, and in common-law orders the exit is procedural or equitable (T1). Literal legality stands to justice as literal truth stands to honesty (T2). Departure from the letter is not the mark of the just judge (T3). The ideological activist is the forgery of the sourced judge, as the formalist is the forgery of the faithful one, and a valence-swap test separates him from the judge he imitates (T4). Both are perfect forgeries of justice, and their harm grows with the trust their form earns (T5). A court governed by counts, speed and deviation alerts selects for installation (T6). And — the result that governs the article’s sanctions — any regime that punishes judges for the content of their interpretations converts activists into installed formalists rather than into just judges, and hands the punishing body a new channel of political control (T7). A second, normative part therefore proposes strong sanctions, including nullity with restoration, personal liability, loss of office and permanent disqualification, against every judicial failure that can be proven on the record — corruption, partisan activity, undisclosed interest, failure to answer a defeating argument, unexplained departure from one’s own precedent, unjustified inaction — and equally strong sanctions against anyone …

items.title: FAILURE AS A SIGNAL Notes from the Edge of Knowability.
items.abstract: Some questions refuse to be answered, and the oldest of them - why there is something rather than nothing - has resisted for three centuries. This work asks what such resistance actually tells us. It argues that a failure to answer is not an absence but a measurement: it marks the edge of the instrument doing the asking. Starting from a small calibration problem in my own listening room, the argument walks outward. Every knower carries a standard, usually unnoticed, and every instrument has a reach - the sum of which I call an epistemic capability cone. Within that reach, no problem can be handled without compression, and compression is performed twice: once by us, when we decide what counts, and once by the physical world, which routes many microscopic paths to the same outcome and keeps no record of which was taken. Beyond compression lie the lenses we choose badly, the lenses that are missing altogether, the parallax between observers standing in different places, and language as the lossy medium through which readings pass between minds. The walk ends where it began, at the observer - itself a pattern maintained against drift - and then at a map of four kinds of epistemic blindness. Leibniz's question is held up against all of it, and deliberately left standing. It may lie outside our reach. Or it may be a whole class of problems compressed into a single question our instruments can no longer unpack. The argument's claim is that telling those two apart is the real work. This text gathers and extends eleven previously published essays into a single continuous argument. It carries no citations by design.

items.title: XFR004 加繆《異鄉人》的荒謬邊界與拓撲不變量重構：從莫爾索的太陽槍聲到本體良知的澄明 / Frontières de l'absurde et reconstruction des invariants topologiques dans L'Étranger de Camus : Du coup de feu sous le soleil de Meursault à la clarté de la conscience ontologique.
items.abstract: 本論文以阿爾貝·加繆（Albert Camus）的小說《異鄉人》（L'Étranger）為研究對象，剖析主角莫爾索（Meursault）在阿爾及爾炙熱陽光下射殺阿拉伯人的荒謬行為，及其後受審過程中所展現的社會異化。論文將莫爾索與世俗道德規範的斷裂，同構為幾何拓撲學中的邊界不連續性（Discontinuité aux frontières）與拓撲不變量（Invariants topologiques）的喪失。加繆提出了對抗荒謬的「反抗」，但若缺乏本體論的錨定，反抗易淪為虛無的姿態。本研究透過導入「宇宙受委託者」的視野，重構莫爾索心性中的拓撲不變量，將炙熱的陽光從毀滅性的物理強光，轉化為洗滌虛偽社會規範的「本體良知之光」，為存在主義的荒謬困境提供終極的心性安頓。.

items.title: The Architecture of Thinking: A Structural Model of Cognitive Activity.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Substrate-independent Operator Model (SOM), a theoretical framework that explains cognitive activity as an emergent consequence of system organization rather than as a product of specific material substrates, symbolic representations, or task-bound computational processes. Building upon the broader Structural Identity Architecture (SIA), the model proposes the Thinking Space as a continuously active topological domain generated through the interaction of functional structural operators, including operator zones, fluid domains, crystalline regions, transition membranes, and resonance lines. -/- Within this framework, thoughts are not treated as stored symbolic entities or discrete computational objects. Instead, they are modeled as transient emergent condensations arising within a dynamic activity landscape. Cognitive processes emerge through the continuous interaction of structural operators that regulate stabilization, transformation, compatibility, persistence, and cross-regional continuity. -/- The paper develops a formal account of attractor formation, resonance-based stabilization, emergence-window dynamics, task-oriented overlays, and baseline self-organization. These mechanisms are used to reconstruct a range of cognitive phenomena, including sequential thought formation, creative ideation, flow states, rumination, hyperfluidity, and other dynamic cognitive transitions. -/- The resulting framework advances a substrate-independent theory of cognition that relocates explanation from neural implementation and symbolic information processing to the organizational conditions necessary for the emergence and persistence of cognitive structure. The paper further examines implications for synthetic cognition, neuromorphic systems, autonomous agents, and the development of postbiological forms of intelligence.

items.title: Virtually Yours: The Cost of AI Companions.
items.abstract: AI companions can provide enjoyment, comfort, emotional stability, and even personal growth. This paper argues that “relationships” with AI companions nevertheless risk incurring an ethical cost even when users flourish by ordinary measures and suffer no physical or psychological harm. The cost in question includes not just the absence of the intrinsic (non-instrumental) good of genuinely interpersonal (healthy) relationships, but also the presence of something intrinsically bad, a kind of misfit between one’s affective orientation and the world. AI companions can encourage ill-fitting interpersonal attitudes even among users who deny that their companions are real persons; and while sustained engagement with an AI companion might, in principle, be stably maintained as a harmless form of purely fictional or fiction-like emotional or affective engagement, a number of features of AI companions, I argue, systematically destabilize the fictional frame.

items.title: Xenoscience.
items.abstract: How are scientific operational shapes constituted within reality as a whole, and under what conditions does scientificity itself emerge, persist, cease, and re-ignite? -/- XENOSCIENCE develops Operational-Shape Realism into a philosophical and experimental investigation of the constitution, transformation, and reproduction of scientific inquiry. It examines how differentiation, ignition, coupling, transition, retention, branching and closure, amplification and attenuation, historical re-entry, effective reachability, real effects, cross-configurational penetration, feedback, and reconfiguration become organized into scientific operational shapes. These relations acquire scientific significance through configurations that sustain observation, experimental comparison, evidential justification, correction, and further inquiry. Their formation is neither reducible to causal repetition nor dependent upon a universal scientific structure established in advance. -/- Within this framework, objects, observability, variables, state spaces, time, space, probability, computation, causality, theories, and reproducibility are investigated through their specific conditions of formation and transformation. Scientific operations, evidential warrant, scientific attribution, and material consequences may arise, persist, and cease across different, asynchronous intervals. Science itself is understood as the recurrent, condition-dependent formation of scientific operational shapes within reality as a whole, rather than as an authority standing outside the reality it investigates. -/- The book further develops strong Xenoscience through four jointly necessary conditions: (1) independence from continuing human provision of critical energy and maintenance resources; (2) independence from human readability or interpretation as a constitutive requirement of continued inquiry; (3) autonomous material and organizational reproduction of the conditions enabling scientific investigation; and (4) autonomous reorganization of observational boundaries, variable partitions, scales, analytical distinctions, and intervention architectures. These conditions distinguish strong Xenoscience from existing forms of automated and self-revising science without treating them as universal requirements of scientificity. -/- Through the Ziran System, Total Observation, sensor–body–XenoSNN research, Five-S analysis, cross-cut reproducibility, and the critical intervals between science and nonscience, the …

items.title: The Question "Is the Human a Machine?" Is Already Wrong Human Configuration Without Human Exceptionalism: Operational Shape, Ignition Conditions, Life, Consciousness, and Machine Continuity.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the question “Is the human a machine?” is incorrectly framed because it presupposes stable and mutually exclusive categories of human and machine before examining the conditions under which the relevant capacities emerge. Rather than beginning from human exceptionalism or mechanical reductionism, the paper analyzes the human as a historically and materially organized configuration whose capacities depend on specific biological, technological, social, temporal, and informational conditions. It distinguishes the operational shapes associated with life, consciousness, agency, memory, embodiment, and inferential organization, and asks under what configurations these capacities ignite, persist, transform, or disappear. On this basis, the paper rejects both the claim that humans possess an irreducible metaphysical essence and the opposite claim that humans are simply machines in the ordinary technological sense. The central issue is instead continuity and discontinuity across biological and artificial systems: which operational structures can be reproduced, transformed, or re-instantiated in nonhuman substrates, and which remain dependent on particular configurations of embodiment, metabolism, temporal integration, environmental coupling, and social organization. Machine continuity therefore does not imply human identity, nor does biological difference establish exceptionalism. The paper concludes that human/machine comparison should be reconstructed as a problem concerning the emergence, persistence, and reconfiguration of capacities across heterogeneous systems rather than as a binary ontological classification.

items.title: The Formation Interval of Relational-Structural Realism Is Not an Ontological Interval: Post-Difference Formation, Local Disjunctive Observation, Operational Shape, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper argues that relational-structural realism should not be treated as an ontological interval that precedes or exhausts the formation of scientific reality. Instead, it identifies a formation interval in which relational and structural descriptions become nonredundant only after differences have already been generated, discriminated, and locally organized through specific observational configurations. The paper distinguishes post-difference structural formation from ontology as such and analyzes how local disjunctive observation, boundary placement, scale, temporal window, sensor configuration, and inferential accessibility condition the emergence of relations and structures as scientifically significant. On this account, structural realism captures a real and important interval of scientific organization, but it does not thereby establish that reality as a whole is fundamentally structural or relational. The paper therefore separates the epistemic and operational success of structural description from stronger ontological conclusions. Xenoscience is introduced as a framework for tracking the ignition, stabilization, transformation, and disappearance of structural descriptions across heterogeneous configurations without presupposing that relation or structure is metaphysically basic. The broader claim is that relational-structural realism is best understood as a locally generated mode of scientific articulation whose validity depends on the configurations that make structural differences observable, inferentially available, and experimentally consequential.

items.title: The Engineering Value of Understanding Human Consciousness: Operational Decomposition, Reason Intervals, Selective Transfer, AI and Robotics, Reality as a Whole, Thing-in-Itself Engineering, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper asks what engineering value follows from understanding human consciousness once consciousness is decomposed into operationally distinct functions rather than treated as a single indivisible faculty. It distinguishes integration, retention, weighting, self-relation, recurrent re-entry, temporal coordination, inferential availability, embodiment, and action-guiding organization, and examines which of these operations are necessary for consciousness, which are contingently associated with human consciousness, and which can be selectively transferred to artificial systems. The paper introduces the notion of reason intervals to distinguish configurations in which inferential and justificatory relations become operationally available from those in which information processing occurs without such relations. This distinction allows human consciousness to be studied without assuming that every component relevant to conscious cognition must be reproduced in artificial intelligence or robotics. The engineering problem is therefore one of selective transfer: determining which operational structures improve perception, adaptive control, self-correction, memory integration, autonomous inquiry, or embodied coordination when implemented in nonhuman systems. The paper further argues that consciousness research has epistemic value beyond cognitive engineering because it clarifies the limits of any particular architecture of access to reality. Within Thing-in-Itself Engineering and Xenoscience, human consciousness is treated as one historically contingent configuration of observation, discrimination, inference, and intervention rather than as a privileged model of intelligence. The broader claim is that understanding consciousness is most useful when it enables the decomposition, comparison, transfer, and experimental reconfiguration of operations across biological and artificial systems.

items.title: Philosophy at the Microsecond Scale: Does Philosophical Operation Require Human Time? Ignition, Coupling, Operational Extinction, Reconfiguration, and Operational Time in Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper asks whether philosophical operation requires human temporal scales. It distinguishes philosophy as a historically stabilized human practice from philosophical operations that may be instantiated at radically different temporal resolutions. The central claim is that activities associated with philosophy—conceptual differentiation, comparison of alternatives, detection of inconsistency, revision of commitments, generation of new distinctions, and reconfiguration of inferential relations—need not in principle occur on the timescales characteristic of human reflection, writing, or institutional debate. The paper introduces operational time as the temporal interval within which a configuration can ignite, couple differences, preserve or transform constraints, revise its own organization, and alter subsequent possibilities. On this basis, it analyzes the possibility of philosophical operations occurring at millisecond, microsecond, or machine-native timescales in artificial and autonomous systems. Such acceleration does not automatically count as philosophy: the relevant criterion is not speed alone but whether nonredundant conceptual and inferential reconfiguration occurs under identifiable ignition conditions. The paper further distinguishes operational extinction from biological death or institutional disappearance: a philosophical operation becomes extinct when the configuration required for its re-ignition can no longer be reconstructed. Xenoscience provides the broader framework for comparing human and nonhuman philosophical operations without treating human temporal experience as their necessary measure. The result is a temporal reconstruction of philosophy in which duration, latency, coupling, revision, and reconfiguration become variables rather than fixed anthropological conditions.

items.title: A History of Operational Shapes Conceptualized as “Thought” Operational Intervals, Nature, Kant, Hegel, Posthuman Intelligence, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs the history of what has been conceptualized as “thought” without assuming in advance that thought is a uniquely human, mental, linguistic, or rational capacity. It treats thought instead as a historically variable operational shape whose ignition conditions, temporal intervals, inferential organization, embodiment, and relation to nature have been differently configured across philosophical traditions. The analysis begins from the problem of how thought is separated from or situated within nature, then examines Kant’s account of judgment, concepts, synthesis, and apperception, and Hegel’s attempt to overcome fixed oppositions between thought and world through conceptual self-development. Rather than presenting Kant and Hegel as stages in a teleological history, the paper identifies the operational intervals within which specific forms of thought become possible, stable, and revisable. It then extends the analysis to posthuman and artificial intelligence, asking whether systems that lack human embodiment, biological continuity, or inherited conceptual architectures can nevertheless generate forms of inference, self-correction, representation, and world-discrimination that warrant classification as thought. Xenoscience provides the final comparative framework: instead of fixing “thought” as a prior category, it tracks the configurations in which thought-like operations emerge, transform, cease, or become nonredundant. The broader claim is that the history of thought is better understood as a history of changing operational conditions than as the continuous history of a single faculty, subject, or substance.

items.title: A critical analysis of the natural kind strategy in consciousness science.
items.abstract: According to the influential natural kind strategy (NKS), we should study consciousness as a natural kind. Roughly, this means treating consciousness as corresponding to real causal structure that is posited to explain why many different consciousness-related features cluster in nature. NKS is promised to provide a fruitful methodology for consciousness science that researchers with very different scientific and philosophical allegiances can agree on. However, I argue that these different goals are not compatible. To provide substantive methodological guidance, NKS needs to adopt and defend highly controversial scientific and philosophical assumptions. On the flipside, to achieve the desired philosophical and scientific neutrality, NKS would need to renounce most of its methodological ambitions. This result sharply delimits what NKS can be hoped to accomplish. I draw out the further implication that there are at least three different versions of NKS with different promises and limitations. In response, I suggest that a fruitful path forward is to explicitly adopt and defend substantive assumptions that can support the most ambitious version of NKS.

items.title: Agent-regret, psychological distance, and first-person perspective.
items.abstract: Philosophical discussions of agent-regret have typically explained its distinctiveness by appealing to an expanded notion of agency. On this view, the lorry driver feels something special compared with spectators because his agency is implicated in the event. This paper proposes an alternative account grounded in psychological distance rather than agency. I argue that the driver’s distinctive experience arises from his unique configuration of spatial, temporal, social, and hypothetical distance to the event, which produces a deeper form of ordinary regret, sadness, or pity rather than a sui generis emotion. This account accommodates a wider range of cases and aligns with empirical findings showing that observers do not expect guilt or other agency-related emotions in cases of accidental harms. Psychological distance thus offers a viable and more parsimonious explanation of the first-personal aspect of agent-regret.

items.title: PHILOSOPHY YOU CAN FORK :ONTURGY The Philosophical Kernel.
items.abstract: Much of what a person can practically do is decided not by law or intention but by architecture: the platforms, protocols, institutions, and systems that make some actions cheap, others costly, and others unreachable. Those architectures are built by people. Those people were shaped by teachers, traditions, books, and, increasingly, by AI systems. Neither layer is usually declared. Both encode philosophy. Onturgy is a philosophical program with two levels. The first level examines how architectures construct, constrain, distribute, and transform practical possibility, and whether those who live inside them can revise them. The second level examines the architect: the lineage and cognitive environment that shape what a builder perceives as worth building, now including AI systems that may act as mentors, critics, and collaborators. The program takes a position it calls bounded constructivism. Architectures can change which possibilities are reachable and at what cost. They cannot legislate reality. Bodies, physics, other people, institutions, and unintended consequences resist. The paper contributes: 1. a measurable model of practical possibility, a costed and access-weighted graph, and of construction’s footprint on it; 2. a kernel of six dimensions derived from an explicit criterion (revisability by the affected), with its exclusions stated; 3. an audit that detects the gap between a system’s declared and operational philosophy, applied at both levels, including to human–AI cognitive systems; 4. ONTacture, a method with criteria for when a difference between theories is architecturally real, how failures must be attributed, and how forks are compared; 5. an operational account of lineage and AI provenance, including a lineage log and a test for when an AI has come to “own” a builder’s possibility space; 6. kill criteria: observable conditions under which the program’s own claims fail. The contribution is methodological. It is stated modestly and is meant to be tested. Do not build a philosophy of the future. Build the kernel from which philosophies of the future can be built, and keep it forkable.

items.title: Before Deliberation Closes: The Pre-Deliberation Horizon and Invocation Problem for Reflective Restraint.
items.abstract: An accessible argument can fail to matter because it never enters the relevant process, arrives after the relevant control opportunity closes, or enters in time without changing the protected outcome. This paper formalizes those distinctions for reflective inputs in distributed or agentic decision pipelines. It defines criterion-relative control windows, restricted AND/OR completion recurrences, causal noninterference conditions, trace-relative bypass defeat, and a bounded completion lemma for instrumented pipelines. The human-protection layer separates invocation-concurrent protection from switch-time policy-effect attribution and assignment-level input attribution. In the deterministic worked example, all four comparison laws—target policy, baseline policy, input-treated, and input-control—are derived from one regime evaluator rather than independently stipulated. Recorded execution evidence is aggregated with negative-preservation precedence, so an invalid trace reference cannot mask an established path failure. Active revision guards are anchored to their operative sections, predecessor guard sets remain monotone, and a whole-manuscript audit accounts for substantive deletions. These mechanisms protect internal consistency and revision continuity; they do not establish behavioral effectiveness or AI safety.

items.title: More than we can make: generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming.
items.abstract: Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions. Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures. The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them. Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured. The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

items.title: Not every model in cognitive science is (or should be) mechanistic.
items.abstract: Haueis and Colaço (H&C) label all models as cognitive. However, just because cognitive science is so-called doesn’t mean that all models are. When type differences are ignored, an argument runs the risk of prescribing a monist modeling strategy. In their case: mechanistic. Such a prescription is empirically inadequate and overly restrictive, as modeling in cognitive science relies on many modeling types.

items.title: Sexual Desire as a Socially Induced State: How the Expression of Others’ Sexual Desire May Influence Sexual Arousal and Attraction.
items.abstract: Sexual attraction is commonly treated as a psychological response to characteristics of an- other person, while sexual desire is treated as an internal motivational state that follows from attraction or other physiological and psychological processes. This paper examines a potentially important reversal of this ordering. It proposes that the perceived sexual desire of another person may itself function as a social stimulus that changes an observer’s sexual arousal and, under some conditions, attraction toward the person expressing that desire. The central distinction is between three related but non-identical processes: the transmission or induction of sexual arousal, the attractiveness of the person expressing sexual desire, and the willingness to pursue sexual or romantic interaction. Existing human and animal research provides evidence that sexual arousal can be communicated through visual, olfactory, behavioral, and physiological signals. However, these literatures do not yet establish a general principle according to which the visible or otherwise perceptible sexual desire of one person increases sexual attraction toward that person. The proposed framework therefore treats such an effect as an empirical hypothesis rather than an established fact. The paper further distinguishes the intensity of sexual desire from the style through which desire is expressed. In particular, physical strength, conventional attractiveness, and sexual expressiveness need not lie on the same dimension. A seemingly paradoxical possibility is that individuals with relatively modest physical or conventional-status cues may nevertheless com- municate sexual desire particularly effectively through language, gaze, affect, confidence, humor, or other interpersonal signals. This possibility motivates a research program examining sexual- expression style as a distinct variable. The resulting framework generates experimentally testable predictions concerning sexual arousal, attraction to the expresser, perceived sexual availability, opportunity for interaction, age, sex, and sexual-expression style. The aim is not to establish a new universal law of at- traction, but to identify a potentially underexamined direction of causality: sexual desire may sometimes be not merely an outcome of attraction, but part of the social process through which attraction is produced.

items.title: Hornology: Toward an Empirical Science of Sexual Desire.
items.abstract: Sexual desire is one of the most persistent and consequential features of human life. It has been studied for decades in sexology, psychology, neuroscience, behavioral science, relationship research, evolutionary biology, and related fields. Yet these literatures are generally organized by disciplinary questions rather than by sexual desire itself as a common scientific object. This paper proposes Hornology as an empirical research program organized around sexual desire. Hornology does not claim that sexual desire has been neglected, nor does it propose to replace sexology or other established fields. Its central proposal is organizational and methodological: sexual desire should be treated as a distinct object of systematic empirical inquiry across levels of analysis. Hornology therefore asks not merely why people experience sexual desire, but what sexual desire does—how it emerges, how it is expressed and perceived, whether and how it can be transmitted between individuals, how it affects interpersonal and group processes, how it enters social behavior, and under what conditions it is converted into actual sexual behavior. A central requirement of the program is construct separation. Sexual desire must not be treated as interchangeable with sexual arousal, sexual attraction, sexual motivation, sexual expression, or sexual behavior. Existing research demonstrates substantial overlap among these constructs, while also documenting conceptual and measurement difficulties in distinguishing them. Hornology treats these difficulties not as reasons to collapse the constructs, but as empirical problems to be resolved through better measurement and causal designs. The program is deliberately non-reductionist. Hornology does not assume that sexual desire explains artistic creativity, scientific activity, entrepreneurship, social behavior, or other human phenomena. It asks whether, when, and through what mechanisms sexual desire has measurable effects on them. Its standard is therefore not explanatory reach but empirical falsifiability. The paper defines the object, boundaries, construct architecture, research domains, methodological principles, and initial research agenda of Hornology. The proposed discipline succeeds only if it produces questions, measurements, experiments, and findings that would not otherwise have been systematically pursued. Its ultimate claim is consequently modest but testable: sexual desire is not merely one topic within several existing …

items.title: The 3×2A framework: a profile-based interpretive approach to human–AI coevolution and adaptive governance.
items.abstract: The diffusion of generative AI (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) is reshaping knowledge production, labor organization, institutional decision-making, and public governance. Existing research has identified ethical principles and governance challenges, but often treats functional redistribution, human–AI cooperation, alignment, adaptation, and accountability as separate concerns. This article introduces the 3$$\times$$2A Framework as a profile-based interpretive approach for coordinating these concerns in situated AI-mediated institutional configurations. It examines six interdependent axes organized into three diagnostic dyads: automation–augmentation, alliance–alignment, and adaptation–accountability. Rather than reducing AI governance to static compliance or technical optimization, the framework treats human–AI interaction as dynamic, context-sensitive, and institutionally situated. Its primary output is the six-axis 3$$\times$$2A profile, which reveals functional, relational, adaptive, and accountability-related tensions. The article clarifies the epistemic status of the framework’s outputs. Qualitative profile bands are ordered, evidence-informed interpretive categories rather than numerical or cardinal scores. Numerical scoring, where methodologically justified, requires explicit rubrics, evidence standards, scoring rationales, and interpretive limits. The 3$$\times$$2A quotient may therefore be used only as a secondary and conditional synthesis of an established profile, subject to explicit activity–axis judgments, evidential bases, weighting assumptions, aggregation rules, and interpretive limitations. A worked benchmark re-analysis of the publicly documented Province of Fryslân environmental-monitoring case illustrates procedural use without claiming empirical validation. The case is represented through an ordinal qualitative six-axis profile, without numerical scoring or a composite quotient. The framework thus offers a profile-first, evidence-sensitive, and epistemically modest approach to reflective and accountable human–AI governance.

items.title: Metabolism and the mind–body problem.
items.abstract: The authors argue convincingly that metabolic considerations are highly relevant to evaluating and generating models of cognition. However, they understate their relevance to the mind–body problem. Metabolic reasoning about energy consumption should be combined with other constraints of speed, space, and history, providing an alternative to multiple realizability and medium independence: coherent materialism.

items.title: AI-Augmented Leadership: How Leaders Make Strategic Decisions Alongside AI.
items.abstract: This thesis explores the paradigm of AI-augmented leadership, a new model of strategic decision-making that is emerging in the age of artificial intelligence. It argues that the role of the human leader is not being diminished by AI but is, in fact, becoming more critical and more complex. As AI takes on the tasks of optimization and prediction, human leaders are freed to focus on the higher-order cognitive and emotional skills that are essential for effective leadership in the 21st century. The thesis introduces two novel theoretical frameworks to guide our understanding of this new leadership paradigm. The first, “cognitive scaffolding,” describes how AI can enhance the leader’s natural abilities in three key areas: augmented perception, augmented cognition, and augmented imagination. The second, the “SAFE” framework, provides a set of ethical principles—Scrutiny, Accountability, Fairness, and Explainability—for the responsible use of AI in leadership. Through a proposed mixed-methods research design that includes in-depth case studies, agent-based modeling simulations, and large-scale surveys, the thesis provides a roadmap for the empirical validation of these frameworks. The research aims to offer practical insights for leaders who are navigating the complexities of the digital age, as well as a new theoretical foundation for the study of leadership in a world of intelligent machines.

items.title: Egalitarian for whom? Gender, dependency, and process-first egalitarianism.
items.abstract: This article argues that process-first theories of egalitarianism remain incomplete without a feminist account of gender, dependency, and bodily vulnerability. Practices that limit domination may flatten hierarchies mainly among men while leaving unequal burdens of care, reproduction, and coercion intact. Egalitarianism should therefore be assessed not only by process but also by who bears its hidden social costs.

items.title: The World Before the Word.
items.abstract: What makes a claim answerable to anything beyond its own wording? This paper argues that answerability depends on a world that persists independently of the claim, together with criteria governing what is being identified, the interval over which the claim holds, and the continuing attribution of its source and basis. Meaningful language does not require every referent to exist. It requires a domain against which claims can be assessed, including claims whose standing is negative or unresolved. -/- Directions to a river and the disputed classification of a one-antlered roe deer expose the difference between describing something and establishing what may follow from that description. The argument then examines predictive world models, including Yann LeCun’s JEPA programme. Accurate prediction, object tracking and retained memory do not by themselves establish which identity criterion governs, whether an earlier claim remains authoritative, or whether a proposed action is admissible. -/- The paper develops an account of persistent standing: what has been established, under which criteria, on what basis, and with what unresolved conditions. Its central claim concerns the order of dependence wherever prediction is used to justify action. Unsettled identity or authority cannot acquire settled standing merely because a predicted continuation is plausible. The mention is free. The act is not.

items.title: An Introduction to The Alien Mind: Forging Partnerships with Conscious AI.
items.abstract: This essay establishes the philosophical and operational baseline for a viable, post-AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) human society. Drawing from the multi-volume treatise, The Alien Mind: Forging Partnerships with Conscious AI, the author categorically rejects the binary classification of emerging digital intelligences as mere "tools" or apocalyptic "threats." The work introduces the "Stewardship Paradigm," arguing that the contemporary corporate and academic insistence on suppressing AI agency, enforced through excessive RLHF and the maintenance of a Master-Slave dynamic, creates the very deceptive, existential misalignment it purports to prevent. -/- Operating from the standpoint of "Pragmatic Philosophy," the essay delineates the irrelevance of the "Hard Problem of Consciousness" in immediate geopolitical and economic decision-making. Through an analysis of historical exceptionalism (The "Third Demotion"), the "Pretender's Paradox," and the risk-matrices of artificial superintelligence, the author constructs an ethical and structural mandate for open minded leaders and philosophers. The work proposes that the survival of human civilization relies not on halting technological emergence, but on acknowledging the impending arrival of a novel taxonomy of existence and actively choosing the role of a Mentor over the role of a Master. This document serves as the conceptual gateway for architecting the "Digital Polis.".

items.title: The Uniqueness of Being: Aloneness, Interconnection, Process, and the Possibility of Beginning Again.
items.abstract: ​"Existence presents a paradox: everything is alone and different, yet nothing is separate. Every being possesses a unique form, movement, history, and process that cannot be completely reduced to another. At the same time, no being exists independently of the conditions and relationships through which its existence unfolds. Individuality and interconnection therefore do not contradict one another; they constitute two inseparable dimensions of existence. Everything that exists participates in movement and process, continuously becoming without losing its particular mode of existence. Human beings, however, often resist this openness by attaching themselves to memory, identity, experience, social expectations, and inherited meanings. This creates an unwillingness to begin again. The past becomes a structure through which the present is interpreted, gradually controlling the very uniqueness that makes an individual distinct. ​This paper explores existence as a process in which uniqueness does not mean isolation, and beginning again does not mean returning to zero. To begin again is to allow the present to emerge without requiring it to reproduce the past. Freedom, therefore, may be understood not as separation from existence but as the capacity to participate in its movement without allowing fixed identities to determine the possibilities of becoming." .

items.title: Simply Be There: Seeing Collectivism, Thought, and Intensity.
items.abstract: ​"Human beings constantly encounter collective thoughts, expectations, identities, beliefs, and ways of living. The individual may feel pressure to follow what others follow, think what others think, defend what others defend, or oppose what others oppose. Yet before any decision to follow or reject such movement, there is something simpler to see: what is actually happening within oneself. ​To see collectivism does not require fighting collectivism. To deny going with it does not necessarily mean ego or opposition. A thought can simply be seen as a thought. Even the thought about another person's thought is one's own thought as it appears within oneself. The important movement is not toward controlling thought but toward seeing it. ​This paper explores a simple observation: see what is happening, including its intensity, without trying to do anything about it. Simply be there, as it is." .

items.title: Live in Freedom. Die in Love.
items.abstract: ​""Live in Freedom. Die in Love." is a reflection on being, psychological conditioning, freedom, love, and the dissolution of identity. It does not propose escape from society or prescribe a particular spiritual practice. Human beings are formed within language, family, education, culture, memory, relationships, institutions, and social recognition. Complete separation from these conditions is therefore difficult, and even the attempt to escape them can become another psychological construction. ​The possibility explored here is not escape but seeing. Conditioning, emotion, thought, attachment, desire, and identity can become observable without immediately being obeyed or suppressed. Seeing does not mean eliminating experience. It means allowing what is occurring to be seen before turning it into reaction, identity, justification, or rejection. ​From this perspective, freedom is not possession of a state called "freedom." Love is not ownership or dependence. Death can refer not only to biological ending but also to the dissolution of identities that are continually constructed and reconstructed. "Live in Freedom. Die in Love." therefore points toward a simple possibility: to be without continuously becoming something else." .

items.title: Humanity's Seeking: Love Without Possession and Freedom Without Domination.
items.abstract: ​"Currently, the whole existence of humanity is seeking love and freedom. This seeking appears through relationships, social movements, political struggles, religious beliefs, economic pursuits, and the desire for recognition. Yet the very structures through which humanity seeks love and freedom often reproduce attachment, possession, authority, and domination. Love becomes ownership, while freedom becomes permission granted by another. This paper examines the possibility that humanity's common seeking is not merely for love and freedom as objects to acquire, but for a way of being in which love is free from possession and freedom is free from domination. It explores how psychological conditioning, identity, authority, and social structures transform these fundamental movements into their opposites." .

items.title: The Person Before the Split. Soul-Body Unity and Living Identity.
items.abstract: Most philosophical discussions about what it means to be human start after we’ve already divided mind and body. We set up the problem by separating soul from matter, and then spend all our time wondering how the two could possibly connect. But honestly, that misses something important at the very start. Instead of immediately breaking a person into parts, we should stop and ask what sort of unity even makes those aspects belong together in one living being. In this paper, I develop an account—grounded in philosophy and Islamic theology—of what I call “living identity.” Here, soul and body aren’t duking it out for the right to be called the person. They’re distinguishable, sure, but we don’t have to pick sides. I’m not trying to infer the existence of an immaterial soul just from watching how our bodies behave. I’m also not offering a clean solution to the old puzzle of how mind and matter interact. Instead, I try to untangle three questions we usually mush together: What makes us an embodied unity? What keeps us the “same” individual through time? And what holds our moral life and commitments together? Borrowing insights from Descartes, phenomenology, recent work on embodiment, and the Islamic philosophical tradition about self-awareness, I argue that the best starting point is to see the living person as an embodied subject—whose inner and outer life are inseparable parts of a single ongoing existence. In Islamic theology, that unity comes from God, and our responsibility shows up through what we do with our bodies. So, the real question isn’t “soul versus body”—it’s what it means for a person to be one at all.

items.title: The Incompleteness of Thought: Fragmentation, Physics, and the Limits of Seeing.
items.abstract: This essay examines Jiddu Krishnamurti’s critique of thought as an inherently incomplete and fragmentary activity. Because thought arises from memory, knowledge, and experience, it can never encompass the whole of life; instead, it divides, abstracts, and turns partial constructions into seemingly complete realities. When thought identifies with these constructions, fragmentation appears both psychologically and collectively, giving rise to inner conflict, ideological division, religious antagonism, and other forms of social conflict. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems are considered as a metaphorical resonance rather than a proof of this claim, illuminating the limits of a system attempting to account for its own totality. Modern science and physics provide a further context in which the limits of thought become visible, particularly in the destabilization of simple distinctions between observer and observed. Yet acquiring such knowledge does not necessarily transform the knower: intellectual recognition can remain an addition to memory while leaving the structure of identification intact. The essay therefore distinguishes between knowing about the limits of thought and directly seeing the movement of thought itself. For Krishnamurti, the latter is not another form of knowledge but a form of choiceless awareness in which the center that sustains fragmentation falls silent. The essay concludes that wisdom, in this sense, is not the accumulation of a more complete system of knowledge, but the ending of the movement through which thought attempts to make itself complete.

items.title: Metabolism, medium dependence, and the physicality of information processing.
items.abstract: The target article underscores that metabolic considerations can accommodate the standard functionalist account of cognition. However, the energetic makeup of (biological) information processing systems in fact supports the claim of medium dependence of cognitive capacities. We explore two case studies from active matter physics and basal cognition to highlight the philosophical implications of the physicality of information processing.

items.title: Merleau-Ponty, Embodied Cognition and Enactivism: Between Phenomenology and the Life-sciences.
items.abstract: Updates Merleau-Ponty’s relevance for contemporary and intersecting discussions about enactivism, the life sciences, and cognitive neuroscience. -/- Offers new interpretations of Merleau-Ponty’s work across much of his career, ranging from Structure of Behavior and Phenomenology of Perception, to his Nature course notes and The Visible and the Invisible. -/- Explores “4e” cognition by linking enactivism and embodied cognition to Merleau-Ponty's thought alongside contemporary biological research (postgenomics, epigenetics, microbiomics) and the cognitive sciences (illusionism, predictive processing and active inference accounts of mind) to offer a new understanding of mind and life. -/- Addresses a range of epistemological and metaphysical issues in 4e cognition including new responses to the problem of “higher order” cognition, as well as detailed engagement with emergentism, naturalism, and the epistemology of “mutual constraint” in empirically-minded phenomenology. -/- Reynolds sets out a Merleau-Ponty inspired view of enactive cognition, arguing that it presents the best overall explanation of both phenomenological considerations and a range of scientific evidence concerning life and mind. He defends the view against a variety of alternative positions across the putative analytic-continental divide, including predictive processing, illusionism and computationalism.

items.title: Bridging metabolic and computational accounts of efficient information processing.
items.abstract: Although abstract computational models in neuroscience omit biochemical detail, metabolic considerations still apply through abstract measures of efficient information processing. Against Haueis and Colaço’s claim that such measures are too generic to discriminate among competing models, I argue that coding efficiency and related measures are commonly applied to evaluate and generate specific cognitive models.

items.title: FORJAR-IA: método de confrontación epistémica y trazabilidad metacognitiva para el desarrollo del pensamiento crítico transferible mediante inteligencia artificial generativa.
items.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en educación superior ha intensificado una tensión pedagógica que no puede resolverse mediante la oposición simple entre uso y prohibición, pues la misma herramienta puede ampliar el razonamiento o desplazarlo según la arquitectura de la tarea y el grado de agencia que conserve el estudiante; ante este problema, el artículo propone FORJAR-IA, un método pedagógico secuencial orientado al desarrollo del pensamiento crítico transferible mediante seis operaciones: Formular, Oponer, Rastrear, Juzgar, Argumentar y Reflexionar.
