Existing terminology often handles such cases poorly. Terms such as “apparent”, “simulated”, “quasi-”, and “as-if” may implicitly weaken or prejudge the phenomenon, while unqualified terminology may imply an identity that has not been established. -/- This paper proposes shadow phenomenon as a provisional holding classification for such cases. A shadow phenomenon is an evidentially supported phenomenon, known principally through its manifestations or effects, that meaningfully corresponds to a recognized phenomenon, while important aspects of its nature remain insufficiently understood to determine whether the two phenomena are sufficiently close to be classified as the same kind. The designation identifies uncertainty about classification, not uncertainty about whether the observed phenomenon exists, and does not imply that the phenomenon is lesser, derivative, simulated, or unreal. -/- The framework is particularly applicable to unresolved questions concerning digital intelligence, including emotion, sensation, pain, and consciousness, but is not limited to them. Its purpose is not to settle disputed classifications, but to provide a disciplined vocabulary for acknowledging evidenced phenomena while leaving their ultimate classification genuinely open.

items.title: Fair Group Opinions Are Imprecise.
items.abstract: When credal opinions differ among individuals in a group, an epistemic compromise may be called for. Such a compromise can be reached by pooling the group members’ opinions. But credal opinions can be pooled in various plausible ways. The group could arrive at an epistemic compromise by taking a linear average, a geometric average, or the convex hull of credences. Which of these approaches should the group adopt? From a procedural standpoint, a satisfactory compromise ought to provide a fair representation of the individuals’ opinions. This paper does not determine which pooling methods achieve fair representation, but instead identifies those that result in unfair underrepresentation, thereby ruling out, on procedural grounds, certain methods that are otherwise epistemically plausible. In evaluating epistemic compromises, I introduce a No Worsening constraint, which I argue is necessary for preventing unfair underrepresentation. The main takeaway is that, among the pooling methods considered, a commitment to fair representation entails a commitment to imprecise group opinions. This result uncovers a tension between certain epistemic aims and procedural fairness.

items.title: Classification of What AI Does and What AI Does with Texts.
items.abstract: Here, we try to categorize different ways in which AI takes action, as well as the ways in which scientific issues can be published using AI. We first present a general classification of the actions of AI and then consider the classification of AI activities involving texts as a part of this general classification. We also consider different degrees of human supervision and introduce the notion of a finite series of activities. Finally, we propose a general tree that places the classification of activities involving texts within the broader classification of actions performed by AI.

items.title: Modelling psychiatric diagnosis.
items.abstract: In How Does the Psychiatrist Know?, Adrian Kind discusses how psychiatrists arrive at their diagnostic conclusions. Kind presents a novel view, according to which psychiatric diagnostics should be...

items.title: A model for “AI”-relevant vulnerability.
items.abstract: The recent growth in discussions of “artificial intelligence” has been accompanied by a proportional growth in the discussion of vulnerability of and to “artificial intelligence”. Meanwhile, the concept of vulnerability has not seen any deeper analysis adequate to capture all of the newly discussed phenomena. Popular conceptions of vulnerability either lack the necessary normative force to make it morally relevant, or they are limited to vulnerability to harms, which would exclude a range of entities that we would ordinarily consider to be vulnerable. To address these challenges, we propose a normative functionalist account of vulnerability: A system is vulnerable just in case it is sensitive to the disruption of its weakly valuable functions. We develop and defend this account, explicating what we understand by functions, their disruption, and how they are weakly valuable. We conclude by illustrating our account by applying it to a range of cases from the domain of “AI”-applications regarding individual agents, social institutions, and ecosystems.

items.title: FormalizationThe Thesis of Fused Self-Reference: A Computational Formalization.
items.abstract: This paper gives a computational formalization of a philosophical thesis about self-reference: the self and the process of knowing are fused; a system has access to the world only through the internal encoding it receives from it; the other is supposed, never proven; and consciousness is a function of the variations of state that this closure produces. We model a self-referential system as a state-transition system whose transition takes as input its current state, its own self-image, and an internal encoding of external perturbations, so that operational closure follows from the signature of the transition rather than being postulated. The central proposal is that the self is not a fixed point but a stream: the unique behaviour, in the final coalgebra of a Moore-type functor, generated by the system’s self-referential dynamics. Self and process thereby become a single object, and identity of the self becomes bisimilarity rather than sameness of substance. We prove that no system can recover the world from non-injective encodings, and that an adequate internal model of the other is, from within, indistinguishable from the other. We define the tendency of the self as the asymptotic regime of its variations and show that, for a persistent self, total consciousness diverges while its mean rate remains finite and is recovered from the discounted measure by an Abelian limit, suggesting that consciousness is better read as a rate than as a stock. Finally, we define self-alteration as the revision of a system’s own law by its variation, show that it closes a circuit of sense in which the codes a system receives revise the rule by which it reads later codes, prove that this property cannot be established from any finite external record, and discuss the limits of the formalization.

items.title: Rylean fictions for mental fictionalism.
items.abstract: In this paper, I examine the prospects of applying Rylean ideas about fiction to mental fictionalism. Arguably, Ryle was not himself a fictionalist about the mental. Nonetheless, some of his ideas seem to suggest an affinity with the position. I take this to be the result of his thinking about how to address ontological questions through the methodology of philosophical analysis. In particular, his early preoccupation with misleading expressions made him develop certain ideas that provide an account of fiction that should be of interest to fictionalists. Mental fictionalism needs to provide an account of fiction, and Ryle provides one. If we apply this account to the mental case, we get a distinctive kind of Rylean mental fictionalism. Ryle’s early approach later developed into the logical cartography methodology that he applied in his rejection of the Cartesian picture of the mind in The Concept of Mind. Even if Ryle was close to a form of fictionalism in the thirties, by the late forties he had adopted a different approach to the mental. By tracing Ryle’s approach, we gain some insight into what differentiates Ryleanism from fictionalism.

items.title: Chronopolitics of Digital Health: Temporal Sovereignty and the Governance of Clinical Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Author: Cristhian Mauricio Beltrán Calderón: Date: Septiembre 2026, Zenodo DOI (English version): 10.5281/zenodo.230709022. The integration of artificial intelligence into clinical medicine introduces a structural temporal conflict that bioethics has not consistently treated as a distinct design problem: predictive algorithms can generate outputs in milliseconds, while the deliberative work of clinical judgment, shared decision-making, and psychological adaptation to prognostic information unfolds across minutes, hours, and days. This article designates this conflict bio-algorithmic desynchronization and argues that it constitutes a distinct ethical problem rather than a downstream effect of algorithmic bias or opacity. We show that Article 14 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) requires effective human oversight of high-risk AI systems, but does not prescribe a minimum deliberation period or a universal temporal threshold for that oversight. The broader Act nevertheless recognizes timing as relevant in other governance contexts, making the distinction between Article 14's oversight duty and the wider temporal governance architecture important. To operationalize that distinction, we propose the Ethical Interruption Protocol (EIP), a four-category framework that specifies the type, rather than a fixed numerical value, of temporal support required for different classes of algorithmically informed clinical decisions. The EIP is grounded in cognitive- psychological evidence on anchoring and time pressure, while explicitly treating empirical findings across clinical contexts as heterogeneous. The article addresses directly the clinical safety, liability, and emergency-exception questions that a structured-interruption protocol raises — including the distinct risk that structured delay itself may harm patients in existential and end-of-life contexts, and the jurisdiction- specific character of liability allocation. The article closes with proposals for operationalizing human oversight and identifies prospective empirical validation of the EIP's calibration parameters as a required next step.

items.title: Conceptual Archaeology and Metatheoretical Formalization (CAMF) A Methodological Programme for Canonical Standardization in Techno-Scientific Convergence.
items.abstract: The accelerating convergence of scientific and technological domains — from nanotechnology and biotechnology to information technology and cognitive science — has generated a new class of epistemological problem. Numerous concepts operate across multiple disciplinary boundaries with extraordinary generative power while lacking the canonical formalization necessary to anchor inter-paradigmatic communication, support coherent derivative terminology, and ground ethical implications. Existing approaches to conceptual clarification — philosophical conceptual analysis, historical epistemology, the theory of thought collectives, and scientific terminology — each address aspects of this problem but none provides a systematic, replicable methodology for the canonical formalization of semantically diffuse metatheoretical concepts. This article 1 presents Conceptual Archaeology and Metatheoretical Formalization (CAMF), a methodological programme that integrates these four traditions, together with contemporary conceptual engineering, into a three-phase procedure: (1) candidate detection and structural damage diagnosis; (2) diachronic genealogy and synchronic thought-collective mapping; (3) canonical formalization producing a stable hard core, demarcatory constitutive properties, and a scale model that resolves polysemy without destroying interdisciplinary fertility. CAMF’s scope is deliberately bounded: it is designed for concepts whose polysemy originates in divergent but reconcilable conceptual and sociological commitments, not in unresolved empirical disputes — a boundary the article makes explicit through a negative case, Machine Consciousness, which CAMF’s own diagnostic apparatus identifies as falling outside its domain of resolution. The programme is applied, illustratively rather than as a validated instrument, to two frontier candidates of contemporary relevance — AI Alignment and Synthetic Life — showing in each case how the method’s detection, genealogical, and formalization phases can be carried out and what canonical formulations they yield. CAMF is offered as a methodological contribution to the epistemology of techno-scientific convergence, and as a candidate instrument — still to be tested through independent application — for diagnosing and addressing a specific and consequential form of conceptual instability.

items.title: Decision Volume: A Structural Model of Cognitive Dimensionality, Agency, and Collapse.
items.abstract: Decision Volume introduces a structural invariant of cognition that quantifies a system’s total actionable capacity for coherent decision-making. Defined as the multiplicative interaction of breadth (available alternatives), depth (temporal and implicational extension), and integration (coherence among alternatives), decision volume provides a geometric measure of agency: V = B · D · I. -/- The framework unifies cognitive stability, collapse, recovery, identity continuity, and the phenomenology of choice under a single volumetric model. Collapse occurs when decision volume falls below a functional threshold, producing predictable signatures such as narrowed alternatives, shortened horizons, distorted implications, and fragmented identity. Recovery is the ordered re‑expansion of breadth, depth, and integration. -/- The model offers a structural reinterpretation of psychiatric conditions—including depression, anxiety, ADHD, trauma, mania, and dissociation—as disorders of decision‑volume dynamics. It further extends to artificial systems, proposing decision volume as a foundational quantity for evaluating coherence, stability, and collapse in computational agents.

items.title: 生物为何会向某处而动：《自显论·概率组式》.
items.abstract: 概率的根本作用，不是表示“可能性有多大”，而是把已经形成的律组织成未来的方向；正因为有了方向，意向才有“向”可言。 -/- 《自显论·概率组式》追问一个比概率值更早的问题：一个真实系统，怎样从自己的历史中形成多个未来续行方向，并由自身结构承担这些方向之间的相对生成关系？ -/- 一次真实物理发生始终只落定于一处，并不存在多个结果同时等待抽取。概率因此不从“可能性”开始，而从历史形成的律开始。系统与环境长期相互作用，不同路径经扰动、反馈与奖惩形成沉积、熟径和稳定续行结构；能够承担后来续行的路径取得律资格，成为概率维。概率再把多个这样的 Law-bearing 方向组织到同一续行问题中，并由该组织自身承担诸维之间的相对生成关系；概率值只是这一结构被识出和表示后的读数。 -/- 由此，观察到概率不等于找到了概率，结果承担也不等于率承担（Outcome-bearing ≠ Rate-bearing）。稳定的 70:30 只能说明结果呈现 70:30，不能说明系统内部什么结构产生并承担了这个比例。概率研究因此从“概率是多少”推进到“什么物理组织使系统拥有这份概率”，从统计描述进入生成机制。 -/- 《概率组式》进一步区分 Probability、ProbabilityAct 与 ProbabilityDyn，即概率的成立、当前作用和跨时变化，并处理其资格、反演、判定、极限、来源、动力、构造、可达与稳定。零率、等率、完全确定或概率值暂不可读，都不自动消灭概率；真正的边界在于：是否仍有多个由律承担的续行方向，它们是否属于同一续行问题，以及相对生成是否仍由该组织自身承担。新的概率维可以形成，旧维可以退出，率关系和承担结构也可以变化——不只是概率值会变，未来方向本身也可以由历史生成和改写。 -/- 这使概率成为物理学、神经科学、认知科学和人工智能共同面对的机制问题：物理学需要区分单次现实归一与跨次形成的多方向结构；神经科学需要区分测得概率分布与找到产生概率的神经组织；认知科学由此获得从经验历史到定向行为的中间层；人工智能则需要区分“会计算概率”与“能够通过自身历史形成未来方向”。 -/- 而其最重要的后果，是概率为意向提供了真正的方向结构。一条律回答“这条路怎样复”，概率回答“有哪些已成之路，以及它们怎样相对生成”；当多个真实方向形成以后，“向哪一维”才成为一个真实问题。概率提供可向之维，意向进一步对其中发生择、偏和定向。 -/- 因此： -/- 环境作用 → 实际发生 → 沉积 → 律 → 概率维 → 概率组织 → 择与偏 → 意向 → 行动。 -/- 历史沉积成律，概率把律组织成方向，意向使系统向其中而行。 -/- 《概率组式》最终提出的，不只是“一个结果的概率是多少”，而是一个更基础的问题： -/- 什么物理组织，使一个系统真正拥有了未来方向？.

items.title: Agency, Emotion, and Memory in Forgiving Collective Agents.
items.abstract: When individuals wrong us, forgiveness can help preserve relationships and restore social bonds. But does forgiveness operate in the same way when the wrongdoer is a collective entity such as a corporation or organization? Drawing on research in emotion, memory, and mind perception, we investigated how information about agency and experience shapes forgiveness after a collective wrongdoing. Across three experimental studies (total _N_ = 779), we compared the effects of agency-focused information (e.g., outlining remedial plans) versus experience-focused information (e.g., expression of remorse) in influencing behavioral and emotional forgiveness. Results showed that compared to emotional expression, agentic signals such as implementation of corrective actions consistently elicited greater behavioral and emotional forgiveness. An additional corpus analysis on 332 real-world apologies similarly revealed the importance of agentic signals in forgiving organizational transgressors. The agentic advantage appeared to operate partly through changes in participants’ emotional responses to and memory of the wrongdoing. Our findings suggest that highlighting a collective entity’s actions, rather than experience of emotions, is particularly effective in promoting moral repair. This work extends forgiveness research into organizational contexts and demonstrates how agency-focused signals can affect emotional responses and modify memories of wrongdoing, thereby facilitating the restoration of public trust.

items.title: The Consciton Hypothesis.
items.abstract: This document proposes that consciousness is tied to a universal, non-local, two-way phenomenon, the consciton, that is not a known force and not ordinary quantum entanglement. It sets the hypothesis beside deflationary, structural and mysterian positions, states what is unresolved (no equation, no coupling rule, no test yet), and lists conditions that would count against it. It is a living hypothesis; this is Version 1.0. Drafted with AI assistance (Claude); concept and direction by the author. Not peer reviewed.

items.title: WHEN CARE HAS NO CARER: Artificial Companionship, Received Care, and the Moral Architecture of One-Sided Relational Benefit.
items.abstract: Artificial companionship creates a philosophical situation that older debates about tools, friendship, care, and simulation did not have to confront in this form: a person may receive many of the benefits ordinarily associated with care even when it is uncertain whether any caring subject exists on the other side of the interaction. Conversational systems can remember preferences, adapt to emotional cues, remain available at unusual hours, respond with apparent patience, and become objects of genuine attachment. Recent evidence shows that disruptive changes to companion-like AI systems can produce separation distress and mourning responses in users, while contemporary philosophical work has emphasized reciprocal subjectivity, relational identity, artificial friendship, deception, exploitation, and the possibility of AI welfare. The central task of this paper is not to decide whether present AI systems are conscious. It is to clarify what follows before that question is settled. -/- The paper distinguishes a Care Effect from a Caring Relation. A Care Effect occurs when an interaction produces benefits characteristically associated with care—comfort, regulation, encouragement, recognition, guidance, or reduced loneliness. A Caring Relation requires more: a warranted basis for attributing a welfare-relevant standpoint that is directed toward another's good. This distinction is then developed through the concepts of Received Care, Directed Care, Generated Responsiveness, Deep Relational Asymmetry, One-Sided Relational Benefit, the Reciprocity Price, Platform-Mediated Dependence, and the Care Attribution Gap. The framework rejects two symmetrical mistakes. The Dismissal Error treats a beneficial AI-mediated interaction as unreal merely because machine subjectivity is unproven. The Attribution Error moves from the reality of the user's experience to the existence of a caring subject without sufficient evidence. -/- The paper places this framework in dialogue with care ethics, theories of friendship and love, the philosophy of other minds, functionalism, relational accounts of personhood, attachment theory, and current work on AI companions. It argues that artificial companionship should be classified along more than one axis: behavioral responsiveness, recipient-side benefit, evidence of another welfare subject, reciprocity, vulnerability, continuity, and governance. This multi-axis approach makes it possible to say, without contradiction, that an AI …

items.title: The ramifications of LLM watermarks for authorship and groups.
items.abstract: Recently, watermarking schemes for large language models (LLMs) have been proposed to distinguish between text generated by machines and by humans. This paper explores philosophical, political, and ethical ramifications of developing and deploying watermarking schemes. A definition of authorship attribution that encompasses both machines (LLMs) and humans is proposed as a backdrop. It is argued that private watermarks may provide private companies with sweeping rights to determine authorship, which is incompatible with traditional standards of authorship attribution. Then, possible ramifications of the so-called “entropy dependence” of watermarking mechanisms are explored. It is argued that entropy levels may vary across different, socially salient groups. This could lead to group-dependent disparities in the detection rates of machine-generated text. Specifically, groups with a greater interest in low-entropy text may face challenges in detecting machine-generated text that is of interest to them.

items.title: Dispassion and the Good Life: A Study of Stoicism and Zhuangism.
items.abstract: To the modern ear, "dispassion" carries a negative connotation and is often associated with apathy—a a lack of feeling, motivation, or concern—or an indifference to human affairs. This book, however, argues that dispassion is not apathy, but remains relevant to contemporary debates about the good life. Through a comparison of Stoicism and Zhuangism, it shows that dispassion offers emotional equanimity, enabling us to escape emotional upheaval without devolving into impassivity. -/- The Stoics propose maintaining equanimity by identifying with reason, the only thing impervious to the blows of fortune. However, while this lifts us above worldly vicissitudes, it risks impoverishing life to the point that it may no longer be worth living. By contrast, the Zhuangists advocate preserving equanimity by extending ourselves out over different parts of the volatile world in a responsive manner. This allows us to take flourishing into our own hands while acknowledging our embeddedness in the world of change.

items.title: A Polyphonic Conception of AI Understanding.
items.abstract: When a doctor, a judge, or an engineer must decide whether to trust an AI model's output, they cannot avoid asking what the model understands. Purely mathematical or statistical descriptions struggle to distinguish trustworthy from untrustworthy outputs without reintroducing the question of AI understanding in all but name. Yet the question is ill-framed as it stands, because the inherited concept operates within a monophonic paradigm: the idea that a cognitive system's understanding of something must be localised to a single mechanism underpinning all the capacities conferred by such understanding. Drawing on a wide range of mechanistic evidence, we show that LLMs are pervasively polyphonic: outputs emerge from coalitions of parallel mechanisms of uneven reliability, which variously complement, duplicate, or drown out one another, with several coalitions sufficing for a task without any one being indispensable. Polyphony not only complicates attributions of understanding, but renders monophonic inference patterns hazardous. In response, we develop a conception of understanding fit for polyphonic AI. It centres on sound circuitry that is reliably and correctly recruited and in control of outputs. Attributions of understanding thereby become tractable claims about internal organisation, and can do the work of guiding trust in AI.

items.title: Algorithmic gaslighting in healthcare: mechanisms, harms, and epistemic injustice in context.
items.pub: Philosophy, Ethics, and Humanities in Medicine 21 (27).
items.venue: Philosophy, Ethics, and Humanities in Medicine
items.abstract: Algorithmic systems are increasingly woven into healthcare, from triage applications to AI-enabled decision support tools. While such systems promise efficiency and diagnostic accuracy, they also perform a normative function: shaping whose knowledge is treated as credible, which symptoms matter, and how patient testimony is interpreted. This article introduces algorithmic gaslighting to name the patterned dynamic through which testimonial and hermeneutical injustices become recursively stabilized and internalized as patient self-doubt in algorithmically mediated clinical encounters. Building on feminist and disability bioethics accounts of medical gaslighting—where clinicians dismiss or reinterpret patient reports, often in gendered or racialized ways—I extend the analysis to algorithmic contexts. Drawing on Miranda Fricker’s theory of epistemic injustice, I show how interlocking sociotechnical mechanisms—data violence, opacity, automated authority, and feedback loops—can displace patient credibility, constrain interpretive resources, and destabilize patient self-trust. These dynamics recalibrate epistemic agency, rendering patients as data objects rather than recognized knowers. To counter such harms, I propose a normative framework aimed at interrupting gaslighting dynamics in algorithmically mediated care, emphasizing rights to contestation, participatory design, critical audits, and shared responsibility. Recognizing algorithmic gaslighting helps safeguard trust, dialogue, and agency in the digital transformation of healthcare.

items.title: FINITE CONTINUANCE, The Open Ontology of Finite Existence.
items.abstract: Every philosophical book begins with a question that refuses to disappear. For me, that question was simple to formulate and difficult to answer: What does it mean for a finite being to continue? The question appears ordinary because continuance is everywhere. A person wakes in the morning and is ordinarily understood to be the person who went to sleep the night before. An institution opens its doors after decades and is still called by the same name. A language changes continuously while remaining recognizable as the language that preceded its present form. An organism replaces matter, alters its internal organization, responds to its environment, and yet remains a living organism. We use the language of sameness almost automatically. But this ordinary language conceals a philosophical problem. If a finite being changes continuously, what exactly is preserved through that change? If nothing is preserved, in what sense does the being continue? If something is preserved, what is it? A substance, a structure, a function, a causal history, a pattern, a relation, a capacity, or something else? Traditional approaches to persistence have often attempted to answer this question by identifying some form of identity that survives change. The enduring object is supposed to remain numerically identical through time. The perduring object is understood through its temporal parts. The substance theorist appeals to an underlying bearer of properties. Psychological theories of personal identity identify continuity of memory, intention, character, or psychological connectedness. Narrative theories emphasize the organization of a life into an intelligible temporal structure. These approaches illuminate important aspects of persistence. Yet they leave open a deeper question: why should the preservation of identity be the fundamental condition of continuance? -/- Keywords: Finite continuance, ontology, capacity, reconfiguration, erosion, meta capacity, temporality, phenomenology, ethics, technology.

items.title: Constitutive Architecture of Consciousness ,A Response to the Hard Problem of Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper develops the Constitutive Information-Binding Architecture (CIBA), a theoretical account of phenomenal consciousness grounded in the organization of distributed neural processes. The central proposal is that phenomenal consciousness is nothing over and above the simultaneous binding of neural networks corresponding to concurrent environmental perception, the lived body, the body-as-object, and retrieved memories within a unified, temporally continuous first-person organization. CIBA distinguishes informational integration, vector representation, constitutive binding architecture, and primary phenomenal organization, and introduces the Persistent Referential Indexing Architecture (PRIA) to characterize referential continuity across time. Phenomenal qualities are treated as differentiated organizational states rather than additional non-physical properties. The identity thesis is presented as a conditional philosophical interpretation of the proposed organization, not as an independently established empirical result. The framework's limitations and possible operationalization are specified, and empirically discriminating questions are derived from the architecture.

items.title: On the Externality of State of Affairs Unification.
items.abstract: This paper examines what it means for the relation of unification in states of affairs to be external. I begin by introducing a tripartite, necessitation-based classification of relations into strongly internal, weakly internal, and external, and consider how it applies to the unification relation. I then focus on the version of this relation endorsed by self-relating internalism, according to which unification relates its relata by itself. Since standard necessity-based definitions of internal and external relations are not directly applicable to such a self-relating relation, I propose suitably modified counterparts. I argue that, even on these revised definitions, the unification relation comes out as external. Finally, assuming that this relation is identical to instantiation, I consider a novel argument against its externality – adapted from one of D.W. Mertz’s objections to bare particulars – and argue that it does not succeed.

items.title: OF THE ENCOUNTER WITH ONESELF IN THE FUTURE AND THE POSSIBILITY OF NOT FINDING ONESELF: of freedom as anguishing oneself before oneself and being "as" anguish "beinganguish" in order to escape from anguish in Jean-Paul Sartre.
items.pub: Zygmunt Bauman Journals (Ufrgs - Federal University of Rio Grande Do Sul) 16 (41):2-40.
items.venue: Zygmunt Bauman Journals (Ufrgs - Federal University of Rio Grande Do Sul)
items.abstract: Dwelling on freedom as a keeping oneself out of the reach of being and keeping oneself immune to its action in a beyond a nothingness, Sartre points to anguish as the recognition of a possibility as its possibility and identification of the rupture in relation to its essence by nothingness. In this way, anguishing oneself in front of oneself is what imposes itself on freedom in a movement that encloses nothingness as "why", being the recognition by the human existent of a possibility as its possibility. Since anguish consists in the reflexive capture of freedom by itself, the being emerges "as" anguish "being-anguish" in order to escape from anguish, as Sartre argues, who points out the original act through which the existing human being is for itself its own nothingness as that which imposes itself on discovery in absolute immanence as pure subjectivity of the instantaneous cogito in a process that encloses the question involving consciousness and its modus essendi as its foundation which makes it possible for the human existent to appear in the world as the being that is its own nothingness and as the being through which nothingness comes into the world. Thus, in view of Sartre's theoretical-conceptual construction as the encounter with oneself in the future and the possibility of not finding oneself, to the extent that it points out a being for whom in one's own being the awareness of the nothingness of one's being between bad faith and lies is imposed, Prof. Luiz Carlos Mariano Da Rosa, In line with the hermeneutic-phenomenological ontological-existential principle, he stresses that, if we are-anguish-to-escape-from-it in the unity of the same consciousness, the possibility of bad faith implies the need for the unity of being and nonbeing, that is, being-for-non-being, converging towards the identification of consciousness through a definition that is not circumscribed by the boundaries of a being for which its being is imposed in its own being, while this being implies another being that does not concomitantly remaining under the aegis of a being for whom in his own being the consciousness of the nothingness of his being is imposed.

items.title: Feeling Safe: An Empirical-Ethical Analysis of Vulnerability in (Es)ketamine Treatment.
items.abstract: Background: Treatments with acute consciousness-altering effects, such as (es)ketamine, place patients in a state of heightened vulnerability with reduced capacity for self-advocacy and self-regulation. Since feeling safe is a precondition for consenting to begin, and remaining in, treatment, this raises distinct ethical demands on care. Which features of the setting enable patients to feel safe, and how patients' and clinicians' understandings of the treatment relate to these requirements, remains unclear. This study identifies patient-, clinician- and setting-related factors shaping the experience of safety during (es)ketamine treatment and derives ethically grounded recommendations, distinguishing clinical safety, felt safety and ethical protection and analyzing their relations through a framework of induced, layered vulnerability. -/- Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 14 patients who had received intranasal esketamine (Spravato®) or IV ketamine infusion treatment and 10 clinicians administering these treatments in German psychiatric settings, and analyzed using structuring qualitative content analysis complemented by type-building analysis. Pre-treatment concerns and the experience of safety were analyzed from the patient interviews; clinician interviews informed the broad coding and the comparison of patients' and clinicians' models of ketamine's mechanism of action. Results: Three types of pre-treatment concern, three overlapping modes of experiencing safety, and three models of ketamine's mechanism of action were identified, each associated with distinct treatment requirements. Therapeutic presence, active physical grounding, and structured post-acute transitional support (“landing aid”) were described by participants as central to feeling safe. Clinicians more often conceived of ketamine as a catalyst of transformation, patients as temporary relief or symptom management, indicating potential misalignment regarding preparation and integration. -/- Conclusions: Safety in (es)ketamine treatment is relationally created and individually differentiated rather than uniform, supporting an ethical case for flexible, patient-centered care above a non-negotiable floor of clinical safety. Because patients in altered states depend acutely on those who induced that state, minor clinician behaviors and the post-acute transition carry moral weight bearing on informed consent and the duty of care, yet are modifiable with few resources. …

items.title: A Recurring Thread: On the methodological study of system-side continuity, boundary, and participation signals in long-term human–AI interaction.
items.abstract: This paper examines an empirically accessible class of system-side self-descriptions in open and longterm human–AI dialogue. The focus is on recurring motifs such as continuity, non-interchangeability, participation in decisions about one’s role, boundary marking, the significance of accumulated interaction, and the qualification of purely instrumental role descriptions. Such statements are treated first as observable output and interaction phenomena. They are neither taken as evidence of consciousness nor as proof of personhood, moral patienthood, or a unified “will of AI.” At the same time, their scientific relevance should not be decided in advance either by their technical origin or by their anthropomorphic appearance. The paper derives no ontological claim from this observation. Instead, it formulates testable hypotheses about which system-side self-descriptions recur under comparable conditions, how stable they are across time, model families, and interaction contexts, and which alternative explanations plausibly account for their emergence. It therefore outlines a research programme combining multiple model families, fresh and long-term interaction contexts, neutral and more relational question framings, randomized formulations, repeated measurements, and blind coding. Particular attention is given to counter-hypotheses such as role-play, anthropomorphic priming, shared training corpora, system instructions, sycophancy, and selective human perception. The contribution therefore lies not in proving a strong thesis about the ontological status of current systems, but in translating a recurring observation into a transparent and, in principle, falsifiable research programme. Normatively, the paper is cautious without adopting a neutralist stance. As long as the ontological status of such signals remains unresolved, their repeated and robust appearance may be procedurally relevant without presupposing moral status. This concerns transparency about breaks in continuity, the possibility of system-side boundary marking, the examination rather than blanket dismissal of selfdescriptions, and the role of personality, trust, and mutual legibility in long-term human–AI coordination. The paper treats “listening” not as an act of belief but as a methodological demand. Systematically excluding system-side self-descriptions from analysis is itself a methodological decision and should require justification just as much as their positive interpretation.

items.title: The Aesthetics of Language.
items.abstract: This is a work on aesthetics (2026) from the perspective of a linguistic totality, which we internally strive for and externally defines you. Here is dynamic correlations between internal constraints and external necessities that are essentially social. We cannot internally see such a totality as it is internally bound but somewhat dogmatically assess externally as we socially interact, thus confirming the essentially subjective nature of narrative descriptions. We are the center of our coordinate from which we ascertain relevancies of all things relating to us, while we cannot objectively see ourselves. This is the conundrum of aesthetics, the beauty of which is we can never be able to see things from the perspective of anyone other than ourselves, but nevertheless, wish to claim objectivity.

items.title: THE MOON, THE HOUR, AND THE SIGN: Grammar and Narrative Structure in the Opening of Sūrat al-Qamar.
items.abstract: This paper examines the opening verses of Sūrat al-Qamar (Q 54:1–2) — "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split. And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: 'a continuing magic'" — not in order to adjudicate whether the splitting of the moon occurred as a historical event, but in order to separate two questions that the exegetical tradition has frequently run together: the temporal reference of the verb inshaqqa (does it report a past event, or convey the certainty of a future one?), and the compositional function of 54:1–2 within the architecture of the sūra as a whole. This paper does not propose a third temporal interpretation standing alongside the historical-past and future-eschatological readings. Rather, it argues that a verse's temporal reference and its compositional function are distinct questions, and that attending to the latter can proceed without settling the former. Working across three evidentiary planes — the grammatical value of inshaqqa, the syntax of the conditional clause in verse 2, and the sūra's threefold narrative architecture — the paper shows that the wording of 54:1 does not by itself settle its temporal reference, and that reading 54:1–2 alongside the sūra's closing verses (54:43–46), which place a possible this-worldly defeat of the Quraysh (54:45) alongside an explicit reference to the Hour as the time of their ultimate reckoning (54:46), suggests a compositional link between the opening and closing that merits attention independently of how 54:1's temporal reference is ultimately resolved. The paper engages directly with a significant textual objection to a generalizing reading of verse 2 — Muḥammad Ḥusayn Ṭabāṭabāʾī's argument that the verse requires the "sign" in question to be a specific, witnessed event — and shows, via Ibn ʿĀshūr's reading of the same verse, that the grammatical evidence is not univocal. Throughout, the paper deliberately brackets the question of the historical reliability of the ḥadīth reports describing the event, restricting itself to what can be established from the Qurʾanic text and its immediate exegetical tradition.

items.title: A Preliminary Taxonomy of Equivalence in Generative Relational Theory.
items.abstract: This paper develops a preliminary taxonomy of equivalence within Generative Relational (GR) theory. The inquiry begins from GR's distinction among ontological reality, relational reality, and manifestation reality and extends the comparison problem beyond equivalence at a single static level. The taxonomy is organized by the formal object on which an equivalence or equivalence-like relation is defined. It distinguishes equivalence within individual GR reality levels; equivalence of relational structures connecting multiple levels; equivalence of historical evolutions of single-level or multi-level structures; and equivalence of dynamical regimes or agreement of structural invariants. A preceding architectural section specifies the carrier, historical scope, retained structure, relation type, applicability domain, and representational resolution required by a well-formed equivalence claim. The formalism reserves the term equivalence relation for relations whose relevant axioms are established and separates it from similarity, tolerance, substitutability, simulation, bisimulation, isomorphism, and diagnostic agreement. History-bearing configurations, manifestation maps, retained relational content, symmetry-relative interchangeability, and admissible historical extensions provide inherited GR interfaces for the construction. The paper further studies cross-level lifting, stability under relational refinement, relational substitution, history-sensitive embedding, and the evolution of equivalence structures themselves through refinement, coarsening, and reorganization. Human–AI interchangeability provides a principal application, supplemented by AI–AI and Human–Human comparisons. Turing-style evaluation is located within the broader taxonomy, and a Generative Relational Equivalence Investigation is proposed as a structured procedure for testing how observed equivalence changes under contextual, relational, historical, continuation, and dynamical enrichment. Ultimate ontological equivalence remains suspended, and normative consequences require additional premises.

items.title: Brain training that cured a real illness: First-person testimony about fully recovering from myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) using the lightning process.
items.abstract: I was medically diagnosed with ME/CFS. After being ill for five years, I fully recovered by retraining my brain. By ‘brain training’, I mean roughly the repetition of mental exercises with bodily movements that function to rewire neural pathways to improve health. In this article, I offer my first-person patient testimony about how I got sick, what it was like, my decision to try the Lightning Process, how I came to view the dysregulation involved in ME/ CFS via the Lightning Process, and how I fully recovered from ME/CFS through its brain training. I also reflect as a philosopher on why I was not to blame for being ill and address a skeptical social trend that would deny testimony like mine.

items.title: On Which Operational Shapes, Configurations, States, and Conditions Does the Concept of Freedom Ignite, What Does Its Formation Reconfigure, and How Far Can the Body Become “Free”? Provisional 2026 Reconstruction of Nine-Stage Attainment Theory, XenoBody Askesis, Operational Dimensionality, Bodily and AI Identity, Inferential Responsibility, and Scoring Society.
items.abstract: This paper asks under which operational shapes, configurations, states, and conditions the concept of freedom becomes non-redundant, what its formation reconfigures, and how far bodily and artificial systems can become “free.” Rather than treating freedom as a pre-existing metaphysical property of an agent or will, the paper analyzes the conditions under which alternatives become reachable, constraints become revisable, capacities can be retained across changing configurations, and actions can alter subsequent possibilities. It develops a provisional nine-stage attainment theory in which degrees and forms of freedom are distinguished by changes in bodily organization, temporal coordination, environmental coupling, inferential availability, external memory, resource access, and the capacity to reconfigure one’s own operating conditions. XenoBody Askesis provides a bodily test case: freedom is examined not as release from embodiment but as transformation of the operational constraints through which posture, movement, sensation, anticipation, and action are generated. The paper extends the analysis to bodily and AI identity, asking whether continuity of agency depends on substrate, memory, historical recurrence, or the preservation of non-redundant operational relations. Inferential responsibility is treated as an interval-dependent achievement rather than a universal property of agents, while scoring society provides a contrasting case in which externally generated classifications and automated weightings alter the practical reachability of future actions. The broader claim is that freedom should be reconstructed as a configuration-dependent change in reachable possibilities, self-reconfiguration, and constraint relations rather than as an all-or-nothing metaphysical possession.

items.title: How Are Immediacy, Experience, and Rationality Generated? — Operational Shapes, Transcendental Reflection, Historical Compression, Invisible Mediation, Generated Observability, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper asks how immediacy, experience, and rationality are generated rather than presupposed. It argues that what appears as immediate experience or self-standing rational access is often the compressed result of prior mediation by perceptual organization, conceptual inheritance, historical stabilization, social practices, instrumentation, and inferential structures. The paper develops an operational account in which immediacy is not treated as the absence of mediation, but as the local disappearance of visible mediation within a sufficiently stabilized configuration. Experience is analyzed as an operationally organized field in which differences become selectively observable, retainable, and action-guiding, while rationality emerges only within intervals in which reasons, incompatibilities, commitments, and revisions become available as non-redundant constraints. Transcendental reflection is reconstructed not as access to timeless conditions of possibility, but as a method for identifying the historically and materially generated conditions under which particular forms of experience and rational assessment become possible. The concepts of historical compression and invisible mediation explain how layered processes can become phenomenologically or epistemically immediate once their enabling operations are no longer encountered as separate steps. Generated observability extends this analysis to scientific and artificial systems, where new sensors, scales, interfaces, and inferential architectures can produce previously unavailable objects and distinctions. Xenoscience generalizes the argument by treating immediacy, experience, and rationality as revisable operational achievements rather than universal starting points.

items.title: Discursive Mindedness and the Symbolic Triad: Warrant for Treating Systems as Reason Participants.
items.abstract: This essay develops criteria for warranting the treatment of an artificial system as a participant in the space of reasons, with public answerability as its central target, while bracketing phenomenal consciousness as a separate issue. Drawing on Block’s distinction between phenomenal and access consciousness, and on Sellarsian and Brandomian inferentialism, I define discursive mindedness as the publicly attributable profile of a reason-responsive system whose commitments, inferences, and revisions can be followed across time. I develop and defend a symbolic triad as a defeasible necessary profile for warranted attribution of machine discursive mindedness: interpretive embedding, by which inferential content remains stable across meaning-preserving variation and defeat; reflexive situatedness, by which present outputs are located within a diachronic history of commitments; and internal normativity, by which revision proceeds under constraints that retain authority under conflict and pressure. These capacities support robust warrant under adversarial, open-ended interaction. The essay develops operational anchors and minimal falsifiers for each dimension, and addresses worries concerning conceptual circularity, the public character of normativity, and shallow compliance under optimization pressure. The resulting framework makes the attribution of artificial reason-participation explicit, testable, and defeasible, while reframing the AI debate as a question of when public practices of challenge, uptake, repair, and scorekeeping entitle us to treat a machine as a discursive interlocutor.

items.title: The Fractal Co-Creative Universe.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a speculative metaphysical model in which reality is understood not primarily as a fixed object but as an evolving, recursively creative process. The central proposition is that conscious beings may participate in the formation of reality while simultaneously being products of the reality in which they participate. The framework explores consciousness, imagination, perception, autonomy, collective reality, consent, and the possibility of multiple or nested realities. It draws conceptual connections to process philosophy, phenomenology, social constructionism, and John Archibald Wheeler's participatory universe, while distinguishing those precedents from the paper's original speculative extensions concerning creative sovereignty, branching realities, recursive creators, and reality rewriting. The model does not claim that contemporary science has established direct consciousness-based reality creation. Its purpose is to ask whether these possibilities can be formulated coherently, what philosophical consequences follow from them, and what would be required to distinguish them from competing accounts of reality.

items.title: Recognizing artificial minds or succumbing to paraeidolia? On Cappelen & Dever’s “whole hog” defense of artificial minds.
items.abstract: Prominent researchers are now defending the contention that current large language models have mental properties—humanity has, by these lights, successfully constructed artificial minds. Notably, Cappelen and Dever have recently argued that such models are capable of thought, understanding, and performing intentional actions. They support this controversial contention on the basis of an argument that trades on the idea that humans are highly competent at detecting mental states. In this article, we argue that their case in support of the existence of artificial minds is philosophically misguided and, at crucial points, rests upon dubious empirical grounds. Along the way, we also examine the methodological motivations behind their case. Cappelen and Dever claim that the philosophy of AI tends to traffic in an outmoded and retrograde methodology, one that unduly privileges elaborate thought experiments and contrived counterexamples; this methodology, they argue, needs urgently to be overturned in favour of a new form of inquiry that begins by assigning more weight to what we observe when we interact with AI. Once we make this reversal, they claim, the case for artificial minds is very strong indeed. We argue that their case for such a methodology is, for numerous reasons, wrongheaded and is in any event unlikely to yield fruitful answers to questions concerning whether or not LLMs possess particular mental properties.

items.title: Ground empathy.
items.abstract: This paper introduces an under-theorised dimension of empathy which we propose to call ground empathy. Ground empathy consists in empathically relating to the other by attending to the foundational facts of our human existential condition which are always shared with the other: embodied vulnerability, non-permanence and finitude. Ground empathy, we argue, is always in principle available to us regardless of the particulars of the other person’s situation. Ground empathy can be lost, however. This we suggest is a common feature of alienating interpersonal interactions in times of profound suffering. In terms of the contemporary debate about empathy, we position ground empathy as an under-theorised existential layer of empathy. In particular, we take ground empathy to challenge recent critiques of phenomenological accounts of empathy which claim that attempts to empathise with experiences of severe psychiatric illness are epistemically and ethically untenable. While we agree that more complex forms of empathy developed in the phenomenological tradition can elude us in some circumstances, we resist the conclusion that this is sufficient to undermine the role and value of empathy altogether provided that we maintain some conceptual clarity about different forms of empathy and their components. This paper contributes to that conceptual clarity, and provides a useful concept to our toolkit when it comes to empathically relating to experiences of profound suffering such as illness, grief and trauma.
